stories.summary: A grass native to Eurasia and North Africa, it forms dense clumps with swollen stem bases, especially in drier places. It rarely produces viable seed and usually reproduces through these detachable bases and bulbils held in green, leaflike flower clusters.

A flowering grass whose native origin is not specified, it occurs in tropical regions. It has tall, thick stems, long leaves and pyramid-shaped flower clusters that bloom in the first year. It may be grown as an annual or perennial.

A perennial herb found throughout tropical and subtropical regions worldwide, it thrives in marshes and other wetlands and can tolerate highly saline water. In southern Iraq’s Mesopotamian Marshes, its pollen is reportedly made into a dessert called khirret, though the source flags this claim as needing a full citation.
stories.edibilityNote: In southern Iraq, its pollen is reportedly made into khirret dessert; the source marks this claim as needing a full citation.

stories.summary: An aromatic annual herb probably originating in western and central Asia. Its white or lilac flowers usually appear from July to September, and its delicately aromatic, spicy flavour is valued as a culinary seasoning.
stories.edibilityNote: Used as a culinary seasoning; in Bulgarian cuisine it is mixed with salt and paprika to make sharena sol.

stories.summary: An evergreen pine native to Eurasia, Scots pine is readily recognized by its short blue-green needles and orange-red bark. Mature trees often have a long, bare, straight trunk topped by a rounded or flat mass of foliage.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Pinus sylvestris
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An evergreen conifer with a Holarctic distribution across the cool temperate Northern Hemisphere, common juniper varies from a small tree to a ground-hugging shrub. It has needle-like leaves in threes and berry-like cones that ripen over 18 months from green to waxy blue-black. The bitter cones are not eaten raw; dried and usually crushed, they flavour meats, sauces, stuffings, beer and gin.
stories.edibilityNote: Bitter cones are not eaten raw; they are dried, usually crushed, and used sparingly to flavour foods, beers and spirits.

stories.summary: A small deciduous shrub native to Japan and eastern Asia. It has spiny brown branches, pale yellow spring flowers, leaves that turn red in autumn, and glossy red-to-orange edible berries that persist through winter. It is widely naturalized in China and North America and invasive in many places.
stories.edibilityNote: The glossy red-to-orange berry is edible and matures from late summer through autumn.

stories.summary: A crabapple tree native to China, it bears white flowers and yellow or red fruit. Some varieties are grown for their fruit.
stories.edibilityNote: Some varieties are grown for their fruit.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to southern Ontario and the eastern United States, silky dogwood bears opposite oval leaves and small blue fruits. Its rusty-brown twigs can spread into dense thickets, particularly in wetland habitats.

A floating aquatic fern native to warm-temperate and tropical regions of the Americas. Its tiny branching plants may be green with pink, orange or red edges and can rapidly cover an entire lake surface. It largely dies back during temperate winters but survives through submerged buds.

A perennial fern native to places including Finland, brittle bladderfern grows mainly in shady, slightly moist rocky cracks and ledges. Its leaves are finely divided, with many rounded spore clusters underneath.
An annual plant believed native to the central and possibly eastern United States, procumbent pigweed has smooth, hairless surfaces. It flowers from summer into fall.
stories.edibilityNote: Several Native American groups ate the seeds; Zuni people initially ate them raw and later ground them with black cornmeal and formed them into balls.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb that may be native to the Neotropics or central and eastern North America, redroot amaranth is now introduced across most continents. It can form a tumbleweed and bears dense flower clusters threaded with spiny green bracts.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, stems, young shoots and seeds are eaten raw or cooked; discard boiling water because leaves contain oxalic acid and may contain nitrates.

stories.summary: A strongly scented herb native across much of Eurasia, Macaronesia and North Africa, celery grows naturally in damp, often salty places. Cultivated forms are vegetables selected for edible leaf stalks, swollen stem bases, or leaves and stems, which may be eaten raw or cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: Wild celery was historically a condiment; cultivated forms provide raw or cooked stalks, swollen stem bases, leaves and stems.

stories.summary: Waterside carrot-family plant of unspecified native origin, widespread across much of Europe, Asia, Australia and North America. Its hollow stems bear thread-like leaves underwater and broader leaves above water, while crushed stalks smell of carrot or parsnip. The Zuni use it in schumaakwe cakes.
stories.edibilityNote: The Zuni people use the plant as an ingredient in schumaakwe cakes.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Berula erecta
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An aquatic plant native to North America and parts of South America. It floats or creeps in wet, sandy places and has rounded leaves; it is eaten in salads or cooked as a pot herb.
stories.edibilityNote: Used raw in salads or cooked as a pot herb.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to mountainous and wooded parts of California and Arizona, it is hairy and aromatic. Its narrow fruits are ribbed and bristly, while its tiny flowers are greenish yellow.

A flowering plant native to southern Africa, brass buttons spreads stems along the ground and raises bright yellow, button-like flower heads. It is highly salt-tolerant and favours muddy wetlands and brackish habitats, with fleshy leaves and reddish stems.

A branching subshrub native to southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia as far east as Pakistan. It smells of camphor and has narrow leaves coated in sticky resin. The resin can cause allergic reactions and severe dermatitis, so gloves are advised when handling it.

A flowering plant native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, telegraphweed is tall, bristly and glandular. Its hairy, toothed or lobed leaves become smaller up the stem, ending in bright yellow, daisy-like flower heads and later spherical seed heads with long white tufts.

Annual herb native to parts of Europe, the Mediterranean, the Middle East and the Indian subcontinent. It sprawls through disturbed, shady ground, with many-branched stems and loose clusters of small flowers.

A fast-growing annual herb widespread in North America, with toothed lower leaves and seeds marked by distinctive honeycomb-like pits. It was cultivated by Indigenous peoples in prehistoric North America and remains a crop in Mexico.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, young shoots and seeds are eaten; cooking reduces oxalic acid, and seeds are soaked and rinsed to remove saponins.

stories.summary: A small succulent native to Eurasia, particularly the Mediterranean Basin. Its fleshy foliage changes from green through orange to deep red as it matures, and tiny flowers appear between opposite pairs of pointed leaves.

A fast-growing annual plant native to North America. Its spreading stems form ground-hugging mats, and its small hairy leaves usually bear a central brown spot. Broken leaves or stems release poisonous milky sap that can irritate skin and cause stomach irritation and vomiting if swallowed.
stories.edibilityNote: The poisonous milky sap has been ingested medicinally as a laxative or to induce vomiting, but can irritate the stomach and cause vomiting.

stories.summary: An annual or biennial legume native to much of Asia, southern Europe and northeastern Africa. Its small white flowers form narrow, often drooping clusters, and the whole plant has a sweet scent that intensifies when dried.

An annual or biennial flowering herb native to Europe, it commonly grows in moist places such as marshes, wet fields and rice paddies. Its branching stems carry spikes of small pinkish flowers followed by oval capsules containing many minute seeds.

Annual-to-perennial herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its narrow leaves form a ground-level rosette and are toothed or deeply divided, resembling a buck’s horn. The leaves are grown as a vegetable, especially for salad mixes.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are cultivated as a vegetable called erba stella, mainly for salad mixes.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial native to Eurasia and temperate Africa, greater plantain forms a broad leaf rosette and narrow flower spikes bearing many small, bitter seeds. Young tender leaves are eaten in salads, older leaves can be stewed, and the seeds can be ground as a flour substitute or extender.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten raw; older leaves are cooked in stews. The tiny seeds can be ground as a flour substitute or extender.

stories.summary: A prostrate annual-to-perennial herb considered native in most places and on every continent except Antarctica, but introduced in Venezuela and the Falkland Islands and absent from southern Asia. It inhabits springs, streams and seasonally wet grassland, sometimes forming mats or floating. In Spain and Portugal, wild plants are gathered and eaten as salad, though they are not cultivated.
stories.edibilityNote: Wild plants are gathered for salad in Spain and Portugal but are not currently cultivated.

stories.summary: Succulent plant of unclear native origin, now ranging from North Africa and southern Europe through Asia to Australasia; much of this spread is assumed to be human-assisted, and its status in the Americas is uncertain. It has reddish, mostly ground-hugging stems and small yellow flowers that open briefly on sunny mornings. All parts are edible raw or cooked, and the seeds can be eaten or made into flour, though the leaves contain high oxalate levels.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are edible raw or cooked; seeds are also eaten raw or made into flour.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to the Mediterranean Basin, parts of the Middle East and nearby Atlantic islands, tiny bedstraw has very short upright stems with small leaves arranged in whorls. Its tiny greenish flowers grow singly or in pairs, followed by fruits covered in hooked hairs.

An annual herb native to the Mediterranean area and Western Europe, including northern Africa, Turkey, Iran and eastern North Atlantic islands. Its thin, branching stems carry rings of narrow leaves and tiny greenish-white or purple-tinged flowers; hooked bristles densely cover the fruit. It readily occupies rocky habitats and old stone walls.
A semiaquatic annual flowering herb native to much of the temperate world. It forms low fleshy tufts in mud or wet sand, with spoon-shaped leaves and tiny white flowers sometimes tinted pink or blue.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Limosella aquatica
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A flowering biennial native to Eurasia and North Africa, moth mullein forms a basal leaf rosette in its first year and a slender flowering stem in its second. Its yellow or white flowers have orange stamens covered in purple hairs, resembling moth antennae. It has naturalized widely in North America and is considered invasive there.

A hairy biennial herb native to Europe, northern Africa and Asia. It forms a large leaf rosette followed by a tall stem densely packed with small yellow flowers. Its abundant seeds may remain able to germinate for decades.

A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, turkey tangle frogfruit occurs across tropical regions worldwide and is often grown as ground cover. Its flower heads have a purple centre ringed by small white-to-pink flowers, giving them a match-like appearance.

An annual sedge native to southern Europe, most of Africa and Asia, and Australia. It grows in wet habitats and rice fields, with thin stems, wispy basal leaves and rounded clusters containing many tiny brown flowers.

Tufted herbaceous sedge native to subtropical and tropical South America. It has a short woody rhizome and umbrella-like clusters of small flowers. In some regions, people eat its nut-like tubers raw or cooked, and the stem base is also edible.
stories.edibilityNote: In some regions, the small nut-like tubers are eaten raw or cooked; the stem base is also edible.

stories.summary: A herbaceous emergent plant of unspecified native origin, three-square bulrush is widespread across much of the Americas, Europe, New Zealand and Australia. This long-lived marsh perennial has rough, dense dark-green foliage and small flowers in compact spikelets.

A tiny duckweed native to parts of the Americas, though its exact native range is unknown, least duckweed is the smallest Lemna species. Its translucent green body grows singly in shade and usually in pairs in full sun, and it produces a short-lived flower.

Duckweed native to much of the Americas, Valdivia duckweed is a minute flowering plant that forms mats on calm freshwater. Its flat, translucent, pale green body produces a root and a tiny, short-lived flower, often enclosed in a membrane.

A tufted grass native to much of northern North America and most widespread in the west, western fescue usually grows in forests and woodlands. It has hairlike basal leaves, does not spread through underground stems, and flowers from late June into July.

An aquatic perennial native to Eurasia and the Americas, longleaf pondweed grows in ponds, lakes, ditches and streams. Its submerged leaves are narrow while its floating leaves are oval, and both types are carried on notably long stalks.
Flowering grass native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, but introduced to São Miguel and Terceira in the Azores. Its reddish colour is a distinctive feature.

A clump-forming perennial native to Europe, chives have dark-green rounded leaves and pale-pink, pompom-like flowers. Their mild onion-flavoured fresh leaves and stems are used raw in salads and as seasoning in many dishes.
stories.edibilityNote: Fresh leaves and stems are eaten raw or used as seasoning in salads, soups, potatoes and egg or cheese dishes.

stories.summary: Herbaceous flowering plant placed in the asparagus family by modern phylogenetic classifications.

A small herbaceous perennial found in Europe, the eastern Mediterranean and North Africa, ground-pine resembles a tiny pine tree. Its three-lobed leaves smell like pine needles when crushed, and its seeds can remain alive in soil for up to 50 years.

An annual or biennial herb native to central and southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, field marigold has bright yellow to orange flower heads on slender, hairy stems. Its fruits occur in three shapes, including ring-shaped forms.

Annual herbaceous plant recorded from North Africa, the Mediterranean region, western Asia and Ukraine. It has soft shaggy hairs, yellow flowers and hanging pods with upturned tips resembling a bird's foot; at night, its flower clusters bend beneath raised, folded leaves.

sources.title: Lotus ornithopodioides L.
sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

stories.summary: Annual wild pea native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. It has branched curling tendrils and single flowers in varying shades of red.
stories.edibilityNote: Historically eaten as cicerchia in Milan in 1288, although the species is known to cause lathyrism.

stories.summary: An annual flowering plant native to the Mediterranean region. Garden forms range from yellow flowers surrounded by sea-green leafy bracts to purple flowers with blue bracts; in Europe it flowers from May to August.
A perennial flowering herb endemic to the Mediterranean basin, broad-leaved anemone has fragrant solitary flowers ranging from bluish white or mauve to red-purple. It flowers from March through May.
An annual herb whose native origin is not stated in the supplied information. It is a small, self-supporting plant with broad compound leaves.

A herbaceous annual native to disturbed ground in Europe and naturalized as a weed elsewhere, including North America. Its pink flowers resemble miniature snapdragons, followed by hairy green fruit said to resemble a weasel's snout.

A flowering plant native to southern Europe and some Mediterranean islands, spring sowbread has wide, heart-shaped leaves that are often coarsely toothed or lobed. Its late-spring flowers have long, slender petals and may be deep carmine-pink or white.

Annual flowering herb native to temperate and boreal North America and Eurasia, usually growing beside ponds, streams and other wet ground. It has deeply divided, mostly hairless leaves and small yellow flowers. All parts are considered poisonous, and ingestion can cause burning, pain, tongue inflammation and increased salivation.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are considered poisonous; ingestion can irritate the skin and mucous membranes.

stories.summary: Orchid native to the Mediterranean Basin, including parts of southern Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. Its dense bright-pink flower clusters appear in April, and each flower has a lobed lip resembling a naked person wearing a hat.
An orchid found widely across Europe and Asia, as far north as Germany. It grows in wet meadows with alkaline soil; mass flowering can occur in Jersey and Guernsey from late May to early June.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Anacamptis laxiflora
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A flowering orchid native to western Eurasia and northern Africa, the green-winged orchid usually bears purple flowers, though they may range from white to deep purple. Its green-veined side petals resemble wings, and its flowers produce no nectar.
Herbaceous orchid of Mediterranean distribution. Its dense flower clusters have pink to purple sepals and a paler pink central lip, sometimes marked with fan-like veins.

sources.title: Anacamptis papilionacea (L.) R.M.Bateman, Pridgeon & M.W.Chase
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial orchid native to Europe, northern Africa and western Asia. Its flowers resemble human figures, with petals and sepals forming the head and the divided lip forming a hanging torso and limbs; it usually grows in sunny, often calcareous grassland.
Terrestrial orchid native to the Mediterranean region from Portugal and Morocco to Turkey. Its flower is said to resemble a sawfly, though this resemblance is only purported.

An orchid native across the Mediterranean region from Portugal and the Canary Islands to Turkey and Lebanon, it has flowers resembling female Eucera bees in appearance and scent. Male bees attempting to mate with the flowers carry pollen between plants.

An orchid native to southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, from Portugal and Morocco to Syria. Its flowers may be yellow or have blue-grey or brown velvety spots. Male Andrena bees pollinate it while facing away from the pollen structures, collecting pollen on their abdomen.

An annual herb native to Eurasia, it commonly grows as a weed in disturbed ground and has been introduced elsewhere. Long hairs and bristles cover the plant, including its sharply lobed leaves and the pointed structures surrounding its yellow flower heads.
Annual herb of unspecified native origin, with broad compound leaves. Its flowers are visited by several kinds of mason bee.

Bulb-growing wildflower native to western North America, from southwestern British Columbia to northern California. It has mottled basal leaves and nodding white flowers with yellow-based, upward-curving segments.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Americans reportedly ate the roots raw or cooked; the source does not identify the groups or period.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to western North America, from southern Alaska and British Columbia south to Utah and California. Its hand-shaped leaves have numerous leaflets, while wild plants usually bear tall spikes of blue-to-purple flowers. Newer garden hybrids are highly poisonous and should never be eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Newer garden hybrids are highly poisonous and should never be eaten; low-alkaloid cultivars mentioned are bred for animal fodder.

stories.summary: A small tree or shrub native to foothill woodlands and chaparral, the western redbud is found primarily in Oregon and Northern California. Its bright pink or magenta flowers emerge before the leaves, while clusters of thin, brown or reddish-purple pods persist through winter.

A coniferous tree native to scattered groves on the western slopes of California’s Sierra Nevada. Giant sequoias are the most massive individual trees on Earth, and the oldest known specimen lived for more than 3,200 years.
A biennial plant native to Europe. It has very large leaves and pink-to-purple flower heads whose hooked outer bracts attach to people and animals.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leafstalks, leaves and flower stalks are eaten raw or cooked; roots require boiling with changed water and become woody after one year.

stories.summary: A deciduous conifer native to the mountains of central Europe, with isolated lowland populations in northern Poland. Its light-green needles turn bright yellow before falling in autumn, and old cones may remain on the tree for years. A lifespan near 1,000 years is confirmed, while ages around 2,000 years are considered likely.

A grass native to the southeastern United States, Grenada, Central America and South America. Its folded or flat leaf blades have fine hairs along their edges and may turn purple or reddish when mature; it is often used as permanent pasture.

A root vegetable native to Eurasia, wild parsnip is related to carrot but is paler and more strongly flavoured. Its root and the part just above it are eaten cooked in stews and soups, while other plant parts are toxic. Cultivated since ancient times, it served as a staple before potatoes were introduced.
stories.edibilityNote: The root and adjoining lower stem are eaten cooked; other plant parts are toxic.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to Eurasia, including central and western Europe. It forms a rosette of finely hairy leaves and bears delicate pink-white flowers from May to September.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is documented as edible; fresh leaves have reported nutritional values.

stories.summary: A parasitic broomrape native to the Mediterranean basin in Europe and North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, and Western Asia as far as Iran, bean broomrape commonly lives on faba beans. It lacks chlorophyll, and its stems are gathered and eaten in Apulia, southern Italy.
stories.edibilityNote: Its stems are gathered and eaten in Apulia, southern Italy.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to the Mediterranean region, garland daisy has aromatic, deeply divided leaves and small yellow flower heads. Its greens are eaten in many Asian cuisines, while the stronger-tasting stalk can also be used; overcooking may make them bitter.
stories.edibilityNote: Greens and stronger-tasting stalks are eaten, often simmered, steamed, stir-fried, deep-fried or added to soups; overcooking may make them bitter.

stories.summary: Evergreen pine native to the southeastern United States, from eastern Texas to Florida and north to southern New Jersey. It has yellowish- to grayish-green needles in bundles of three, sometimes twisted, and older trees develop reddish-brown bark with deep fissures and broad, scaly plates.
An annual flowering herb endemic to California. Its spring flowers are bowl-shaped and white with dark veins, dots and a purple spot at each lobe tip.

A herbaceous perennial native to temperate parts of western Asia, Africa and Europe, the sand crocus has thin, narrow, often curled leaves. Its usually solitary pink, pale purple or violet flower has pointed petals, darker veins and a yellow or golden throat, blooming from February onward or between March and May.

A corm-forming iris-family plant native to the Mediterranean region—southern Europe, northern Africa and the Middle East—and Sudan. It has long, slender leaves and small six-part blooms; most varieties flower purple or violet, but some are white or yellow.
A rhizomatous evergreen perennial native to the Juan Fernández Islands, central and southern Chile, and southern Argentina.

A herbaceous perennial native to central and northwestern Europe, marsh gladiolus has sword-shaped leaves and rosy-violet or magenta flowers. Despite its name, it does not grow in marshes, preferring moist, lime-rich meadows and forest clearings that alternate between wet and dry.

Corm-forming herbaceous perennial native to temperate northern Africa, western Asia and southern Europe, from the Mediterranean to the Caucasus. It is a vigorous plant with linear leaves and bright pink flowers in spring.

A perennial herb native to western South Africa, growing from an underground corm. It has long, sword-shaped dark green leaves and curved tubular orange flowers from midwinter to early spring, pollinated by birds.

A herbaceous elder native to southern and central Europe and southwest Asia, dwarf elder forms large groups of upright stems from an extensive underground stem. It bears flat-topped clusters of white, occasionally pink, flowers and glossy black berries. All parts are toxic, especially the seeds, though cooking can neutralize the toxicity.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are toxic, especially the seeds, but cooking can neutralize the toxicity; explicit human food use is not described.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to western North America, silverleaf phacelia grows in habitats from scrub to forest, usually on sandy or rocky soil. Fine silvery hairs cover the plant, and its white or lavender flowers are urn- or bell-shaped.

Herbaceous perennial native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, where it is scarce within its range. It lacks chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise, instead drawing resources from fungal networks associated with trees; its fleshy, fungus-like growth may be yellow, red or yellowish-white.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Monotropa hypopitys
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A biennial or short-lived perennial herb native to southern Europe and parts of Asia, sweet William bears dense clusters of spicy, clove-scented flowers. Wild flowers are red with white bases, while cultivated forms include white, pink, red, purple and patterned colours. Its flowers are considered edible, although the source marks this claim as needing a citation.
stories.edibilityNote: The flowers are considered edible, but the supplied source flags this statement as needing a citation.

stories.summary: Small herbaceous flowering plant native to central and southern Europe, Turkey, the Caucasus and Iran. Its wiry, branching stems bear narrow leaves and solitary pink-to-white flowers at their tips.

An erect annual flowering herb found in central Europe and southern European mountains. Its dense clusters of small pink or purple flowers are surrounded by brown papery bracts, and it grows in grasslands and beside roads.

A parasitic herb of European–Caucasian origin, occurring as an annual or sometimes a perennial. It lacks chlorophyll and draws nutrients from host roots, usually legumes; even its seeds require nearby host roots to germinate.

A non-photosynthetic parasitic flowering plant native to Southern Europe. Its colour varies widely from reddish or yellowish brown to purple or yellow, making identification by colour unreliable. It attaches to many hosts, especially plants in the pea and daisy families.

A plant in the Orobanchaceae family whose native origin is not stated. Its seeds attract wood ants, which carry and disperse them over short distances. It is also a food plant for heath fritillary caterpillars.

A flowering succulent native to South Africa’s southwestern Cape, deltoid-leaved dewplant has silver-blue, three-sided leaves with red-edged teeth and often purple-tinged stems. It produces masses of pink, almond-scented flowers in spring.
A succulent shrub whose native origin is not stated, orange dewplant has a self-supporting form and simple, broad leaves.
A trailing succulent perennial native to South Africa's Eastern Cape, it has hairy stems and small cylindrical or triangular leaves. Its flowers are lavender, pink or occasionally white.

A prostrate flowering succulent endemic to eastern Australia, angular sea-fig usually grows very close to the sea. It has blue-grey leaves, daisy-like light-purple to deep pinkish-purple flowers, and red to purple fruit that ripens mainly in summer and autumn.
stories.edibilityNote: Aboriginal peoples ate the fruit; the fleshy leaves may be eaten raw or cooked, and roasted leaves can serve as a salt substitute.

stories.summary: A creeping flowering plant found in North and South America and the West Indies. Its unusual leaves spread through marshy or wet ground, and it is widely used as a foreground aquarium plant.

A perennial flowering herb native to western North America from Alaska to California. It grows in wet places such as streambanks and is sometimes aquatic. Its parsley-like leaves are divided into serrated, lobed leaflets, and its many flowers have bright white to red-tinged petals.

An erect perennial herb widespread across much of North America, western ragweed also grows as an introduced plant elsewhere. Its hairy stems bear deeply divided leaves and flower spikes, while a creeping root system allows it to sprout as well as reproduce by seed.

A herbaceous perennial native to Europe, western Asia and northern Africa, creeping thistle forms extensive colonies from thick roots that send up many shoots. It has very spiny leaves and pink-purple flower heads, usually on separate male and female plants.
stories.edibilityNote: Roots are rarely eaten and may cause flatulence; leaves and stalks are also edible, though spines make the leaves tedious to prepare.

stories.summary: An annual or perennial flowering herb native to the United States, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America, marsh fleabane inhabits wetlands, coastal habitats and moist inland sites, often on salty ground. It is strongly aromatic and roughly hairy, with toothed oval leaves and clusters of bright pinkish-purple or magenta flower heads.
stories.edibilityNote: In parts of the Caribbean, the leaves are consumed as medicinal tea; use is discouraged during pregnancy and advised in moderation.

stories.summary: A low-growing annual herb native to South America, common soliva has small parsley-like leaves and upward-pointing clusters of tiny, sharp seeds. These seeds make infested ground painful for barefoot people and are also avoided by dogs and cats.

Perennial mustard-family plant native to southern Europe, Mediterranean countries and Asia east to the Himalayas. It has waxy leaves, small white flowers and an extensive deep root network. Its leaves, shoots and fruits are edible; in Ladakh, young growth is boiled and soaked to remove bitterness before being cooked like spinach.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, shoots and fruits are edible; in Ladakh, young growth is boiled, soaked for two days and cooked like spinach.

stories.summary: A small perennial herb native to southern South America. Its sprawling stems have woody bases and glandular hairs, while its flowers bear hairy sepals and five whitish petals.

A circumboreal annual herb that has become naturalized across many temperate regions. It has spreading branches and diamond-shaped leaves, and accumulates environmental salt in its tissues. Its young leaves and shoots can be eaten raw or cooked as a bland spinach substitute.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves and shoots are edible raw or cooked and can serve as a bland spinach substitute.

stories.summary: A flowering saltbush native to Europe, Macaronesia, northern Africa, Ethiopia, the Middle East, western Siberia and Central Asia. It can live in salty environments but does not depend on them.

A perennial herb endemic to Australia and native to Western Australia, South Australia, Queensland and New South Wales. It often forms low mats from a woody taproot and produces succulent fruit structures that turn red or orange when mature.

A clover native to Europe, southwest Asia, northwest Africa and Macaronesia. Unlike other clovers, it develops its seeds underground, and it can thrive in poor soil where other clovers cannot survive.

Perennial flowering aquatic plant native to the Amazon River in South America. Its feathery blue-green to waxy grey-green leaves grow in whorls, while distinctive stems and leaves emerge above the water like small fir trees. It can spread from fragments and form dense surface mats.
Herbaceous annual native to Europe. It has been introduced across almost every region of the United States and Canada, where it is associated with disturbed sites.

An annual flowering herb native to most of the contiguous United States except the Pacific Northwest and New England. It grows in moist places, with green to deep-red linear leaves and small rose-to-lavender flowers clustered at the upper leaf joints.

An annual plant native to Central and East Asia. It has large heart-shaped leaves that release an odor when crushed and has long been grown in China for strong, jute-like fibre. Its leaves were traditionally eaten in Maldivian mas huni, while its seeds are eaten in China and Kashmir.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves were traditionally eaten in Maldivian mas huni; seeds are eaten in China and Kashmir.

stories.summary: A perennial wetland herb native to Australia, North America and South America. Its creeping stems form floating or muddy mats, with clustered leaves and bright yellow flowers; where introduced, it can invade and clog waterways.
stories.edibilityNote: It is not commonly ingested and was originally traded as an ornamental.

stories.summary: Aquatic or semiaquatic perennial herb native across North America, South America, Africa, Asia and Europe. It forms sprawling mats with reddish stems that root where they touch the ground. Its greenish-white flowers lack petals, and its fruits are small cube-shaped capsules.
A perennial herb native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its often oblong leaves narrow at the middle like a fiddle, and the upper stem may bend as the fruit develops.

A perennial herb native to much of western North America, particularly parts of California, Arizona and Nevada, willow dock is extremely variable and divided into many varieties of uncertain identity. It usually grows in wet but unflooded places and has flower clusters spaced along its stem.

A perennial flowering aquatic plant native across most of Europe and Asia, and regarded as native in northern and central Africa and Australia. It grows in shallow fresh water or mud, with numerous small white or pale-purple flowers that open in the afternoon. Its starchy rootstocks can be eaten after boiling or soaking to remove bitterness, and aquatic plants should be cooked to kill parasites.
stories.edibilityNote: Starchy rootstocks are eaten after boiling or soaking to remove bitterness; cooking is advised to kill parasites.

stories.summary: A small sedge native to many regions across Australasia, Eurasia, Africa and the Americas, slender club-rush grows on boggy ground and around ponds. It occurs in freshwater wetlands, salt marshes, dune slacks and other brackish environments.

A small annual rush native to Europe, parts of western and central Asia, and parts of northern, eastern, west-central and southern Africa. Its threadlike stems carry clustered flowers with pointed, leaflike bracts often longer than the flower cluster, and it grows in seasonally moist places.

sources.title: Juncus capitatus Weigel
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

stories.summary: Flowering plant occurring throughout the northern Northern Hemisphere, especially in marshes and other damp habitats. It may be annual or perennial, with fleshy leaves and a dense flower spike resembling sea plantain.

A perennial vegetable of unstated native origin, it produces young shoots harvested in spring from the second or third year. The shoots are prized in English, German and French cooking, while white asparagus is grown by keeping young shoots from light.
stories.edibilityNote: Young shoots are eaten, especially in English, German and French cooking; white shoots are cultivated without light.

stories.summary: A winter annual grass native to eastern and Mediterranean Europe and western Asia. Its rigid late-spring flower spikes bear long, stiff awns, and whole spikelets fall at maturity and spread by animals, wind or water.
A coarse winter annual or biennial grass native to most of South America. It has hairy leaf sheaths and flat, pointed spikelets that may stand erect or droop.

A wild grass native to tropical Asia, barnyardgrass has large, often purplish, millet-like seed heads crowded with seeds, and one plant can produce up to 40,000 seeds annually. Grain from some varieties is eaten during scarcity, while young shoots are eaten as a vegetable.
stories.edibilityNote: Grain from some varieties is eaten during scarcity; in Haryana, seeds are mixed with rice for fasting-day pudding. Young shoots are eaten as a vegetable.

stories.summary: Perennial grass native to most of Europe, Asia, the Arctic and northwestern Africa. Its creeping rhizomes spread rapidly across grassland, producing flat hairy leaves and upright flower spikes.

A perennial grass occurring wild mainly in northern North America and adjacent northeastern Siberia. Its dense, nodding greenish or purplish seed heads bear barbed bristles that readily attach to animals and can seriously injure grazing livestock when dry.
stories.edibilityNote: Kawaiisu people pounded and ate the seeds dry.

stories.summary: Tufted annual grass native to Europe, Asia and northern Africa, and widely naturalised elsewhere. It has green flowers and curved growth reflected in several of its common names.

A perennial bunch grass native to Brazil and Argentina. It forms dense, stiff clumps and spreads by rhizomes, becoming invasive in some introduced areas. Its flower heads have branches neatly lined with beadlike pairs of green to purple spikelets.

Perennial grass whose native range is uncertain, though it probably includes parts of the tropical Americas. It forms clumps, spreads through underground and creeping stems, and usually bears flower clusters on two branches.

A tropical grass native to the highland regions of East Africa, it has very short flowering stems hidden among its leaves. Its rhizomes and creeping stems rapidly form dense mats, helping it spread aggressively and suppress other plants.
A grass native to Africa, Asia and Europe, awned canary-grass has unusually distinctive spikelets. Each spikelet covering bears a hook.

A perennial grass native to virtually all of Europe, North Asia and the mountains of Algeria, Morocco and Tunisia. Its dark blue-green leaves have boat-shaped tips, while creeping underground stems help it form close mats.
An annual grass native to the Mediterranean Basin. Its plume-like flower head is packed with V-shaped spikelets bearing long bristles; elsewhere it occurs as an introduced plant in moist habitats.

A perennial wetland herb native across most of Eurasia and locally in northwestern Africa, narrow-leaved cattail grows in fresh or brackish water. Its slender leaves overtop the flowering stem, whose upper male and lower female sections are separated by a conspicuous bare gap; the female section matures into a rusty-brown, sausage-shaped spike.
stories.edibilityNote: Depending on season, edible parts include dormant root and leaf-base sprouts, stalk cores, green flower spikes, ripe pollen and starchy roots; prepare like broadleaf cattail.

stories.summary: Annual flowering herb native to the Americas and introduced elsewhere as a common weed. It grows from a taproot and bears small, generally white flowers; plants described as xalapensis are glandular-hairy, while those described as peregrina are hairless.

A strongly scented herbaceous perennial native to North Africa and temperate Eurasia. It has silvery-green stems and grey-green leaves covered with silky white hairs. Pale yellow flowers form drooping round heads from early summer to early autumn.
stories.edibilityNote: Used to flavour absinthe and other alcoholic drinks, and historically as a bitter spice in Danish and English beer.

stories.summary: A mound-forming flowering plant native to Madeira. This evergreen biennial or triennial has deeply divided, fern-like leaves and large summer displays of pink flowers on hairy red stems.

A dense, suckering evergreen shrub or small tree native to the Iberian Peninsula and the Caucasus region. It bears violet-purple flowers, often marked with small greenish-yellow spots or streaks. Honey produced with its pollen can be poisonous to humans if consumed in sufficient quantities.
stories.edibilityNote: Honey produced with its pollen can cause severe poisoning when consumed in sufficient quantities.

stories.summary: A flowering shrub native to the tropical and subtropical Americas, though its exact origin is unknown because of widespread cultivation. It has showy clusters of yellow, orange or red flowers, and its immature seeds are reported edible although Caesalpinia seeds are generally poisonous.
stories.edibilityNote: Immature seeds of this species are edible, although Caesalpinia seeds are generally described as poisonous.

stories.summary: A tree endemic to New Zealand’s Kermadec Islands. It is usually multitrunked, bears scarlet, crimson or pink flowers, and is the dominant tree on Raoul Island.

Rhizomatous herbaceous perennial native to cold Northern Hemisphere regions across parts of Europe, northern Asia and North America. It grows in ponds and swamps, with nearly heart-shaped leaves, yellow-green flower spikes and clusters of red berries; the fresh plant is very poisonous, but its rhizomes are edible after boiling or drying.
stories.edibilityNote: The fresh plant is very poisonous, but its rhizomes are edible after boiling or drying.

stories.summary: An aquatic perennial native to Eurasia, flowering-rush grows along the margins of still or slowly moving water. It has long, pointed, twisted leaves and pink flowers. In parts of Russia, its rhizomes are used as food.
stories.edibilityNote: In parts of Russia, the rhizomes are used as food.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Butomus umbellatus
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A submerged aquatic plant native to Europe and northwestern Asia, with rosettes of serrated leaves and white summer flowers. It floats at the surface in summer, sinks in autumn and rises again in spring; in Britain, naturally occurring plants are female and reproduce mainly through offsets rather than seed.

A compact evergreen flowering perennial found wild around coastal areas of the Northern Hemisphere. It forms low clumps with long stems carrying globes of usually bright pink flowers and tolerates dry, sandy and salty habitats.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Armeria maritima
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A slender herbaceous perennial native to Europe, primarily the Alps and locally England. It has tough, unbranched stems, narrow spirally arranged leaves and five-petalled blue flowers that fall if the stems break.

A deciduous shrub native to western North America, occurring from Oregon to southern California and not known east of the Cascade and Sierra Nevada ranges. Its flowers vary from white to pink and often carry a yellow blotch; it usually grows in wetlands without having submerged roots.

A perennial evergreen native to central North America, Great Plains yucca forms colonies of narrow-leaved rosettes with drooping white or pale-green flowers. Zuni people traditionally boil its seed pods for food, and young flower stalks and unripe fruits can also be cooked and eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Zuni people traditionally boil the seed pods; young flower stalks and unripe fruits can also be cooked and eaten.

stories.summary: Annual herb native to southern Europe and the Mediterranean Basin. It has clustered flowers enclosed by broad, claw-tipped bracts, with bright pink, magenta or lavender petals marked by darker veins.
A tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar, lebbeck has very fragrant white flowers and pods containing several seeds. The seeds rattle inside the pods.

Woody shrub native to chaparral and mixed forests in California’s foothills and mountains and some Arizona mountains. It bears spikes of yellow flowers with prominent stamens and shiny, spherical red fruits. The bitter fruits are edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruits are bitter but edible.

stories.summary: A pantropical creeping vine found on sandy tropical shores of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans. It sends long runners across upper beaches and dunes, bearing two-lobed leaves and pink flowers with dark centres. Its saltwater-resistant floating seeds enable ocean dispersal.

A perennial coastal vine whose native origin is not stated, occurring in temperate regions worldwide. It grows in beach sand and has trailing fleshy stems, kidney-shaped leaves and morning-glory-like flowers ranging from delicate pink to vivid lavender.

A perennial flowering herb native to mountainous southern Europe and northwestern Africa. It grows in rock crevices, usually on limestone cliffs, and bears loose flower clusters and dark, crested seeds.

Evergreen perennial flowering plant whose typical subspecies is native to central and north-western Europe, from the British Isles to Austria; another subspecies occurs from Hungary to the Balkans. It has bright oval green leaves and typically golden-yellow flowers, though some plants have blue, purple or blotched blooms.
A small annual herb native to North America. It has woolly, narrow leaves, peg-shaped flower heads in terminal clusters and windborne seeds.
A flowering plant native to mainland Portugal and Madeira, Hedypnois cretica is introduced in the Azores.

A dandelion-like herb native to Europe and North Africa, with a ground-level rosette of leaves. Leafless stalks each carry a single yellow flower head; fruits near the centre of the head are rough, while those at the edge are smooth.

An annual mustard-family plant native to temperate North Africa, western Asia and Europe. It grows in beach sand, with fleshy, often purple-tinted leaves and corky segmented fruits that float. The leaves are edible, preferably cooked and not in large quantities.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are edible, preferably cooked and not eaten in large quantities.

stories.summary: An annual or biennial herb of uncertain origin, though often cited as native to South America. Its inconspicuous flowers may lack petals, while its paired, rounded fruits contain orange or reddish-brown seeds; the edible leaves have a salty cress or mustard flavour.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are edible and have a salty cress or mustard flavour.

stories.summary: A submerged, free-floating aquatic flowering plant native to every continent except Antarctica. It forms bushy masses of brittle, spiny-toothed leaves, which fork only once or twice and help distinguish it from soft coontail.

An annual wild pea native to Europe, North Africa and much of Asia, hairy vetchling has winged stems and paired leaflets ending in coiled, branching tendrils. Its pink, blue or two-coloured flowers are followed by hairy pods, while the rest of the plant is generally hairless.
Herbaceous perennial flowering vine native to Europe. It has winged, hairless stems with branched tendrils and unscented purplish-pink flowers that fade with age.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds are poisonous.

stories.summary: Evergreen flowering shrub indigenous to coastal California, though its exact native range is uncertain and may extend from Point Reyes south to San Luis Obispo County. It bears fragrant, pea-like flowers, usually soft yellow but sometimes lilac or purple. Outside its native range it has escaped cultivation and become invasive in many regions.
A sprawling flowering plant native to the Mediterranean basin. It usually has three-part leaves marked with spots, pale-yellow spring and summer flowers, and unusually coiled, sharply spiny pods.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is stated to be edible to humans, but no parts or preparation are specified.

stories.summary: Annual clover native to Eurasia and North Africa. Its mostly hairless stems range from low-spreading to upright, and its leaf axils carry dense clusters of pink flowers with outward-bending, triangular sepal tips.

An annual herb with no native origin specified in the supplied information, Trifolium tomentosum occurs in Mediterranean and tropical climates and southern Africa. Its fruiting flower cup becomes rounded and hairy while the rest of the plant is hairless. It has three toothed leaflets and heads of pink flowers.

sources.title: Trifolium tomentosum L.
sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

stories.summary: Annual herb native to the Mediterranean basin, parts of western Asia, Macaronesia, Great Britain, Crimea, Chad and Socotra. It is self-supporting and has simple, broad leaves.

An annual or biennial herb found in the Middle East, bull mallow has a hairy, upright stem. Its pinkish to light purple flowers grow where the leaves meet the stem, followed by disc-shaped, segmented fruit. The leaves and stems are eaten, often chopped and fried with olive oil, onions and spices, and historically fed besieged Jewish settlers during the 1948 Battle for Jerusalem.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and stems are eaten, including fried as garnish or cooked like spinach; they fed besieged Jewish settlers in Jerusalem in 1948.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to western North America, occurring in coastal hills and mountains from British Columbia to California's San Francisco Bay Area. Its showy, four-petalled flowers range from pink to pale purple and bloom from late spring into early summer.

A tuft-forming annual grass native to Europe, where it grows in dry sandy ground, rocky outcrops and heath grassland. Its narrow basal leaves accompany tightly clustered, purple-tinged green flower spikes, which appear from April to June.

A perennial grass widespread across much of the Northern Hemisphere, with no specific native origin stated. Its narrow, needle-like bright green leaves form tufts or spreading growth, and it is widely planted as shade-tolerant turf or groundcover.

A clump-forming annual grass native to the Mediterranean Basin and nearby regions, from Madeira and the Canary Islands to Crimea and Saudi Arabia. Its short oval flowerheads change from green to buff as they ripen and are valued ornamentally.

A perennial aquatic plant reported across much of the world, though the extent of that distribution is debated; it generally grows in brackish or saline coastal waters. Its thin submerged leaves can form dense layers, while its tiny petal-less flowers produce fruit on a long stalk that often coils but is rarely seen.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An aquatic annual or perennial herb found worldwide, especially in coastal brackish wetlands. It is a salt-tolerant freshwater plant with thread-thin, grasslike growth and tiny flowers whose pollen may float away on bubbles.

A non-woody perennial native to temperate Asia, Europe, northern Africa and northern North America, it grows in wet habitats. Its creeping stem roots at the joints before rising through surrounding vegetation, bearing very narrow pointed leaves and sparse spikes of pale flowers.
A perennial plant whose native origin is not specified in the supplied information. Moth larvae of Plusia festucae feed on it.

An annual flowering plant with no stated native origin, sand catchfly is widespread in dunes and sandy soils across Europe and western Asia. Its bright pink petals and prominent parallel veins around each flower make it readily recognizable.

A deciduous shrub native to eastern North America. Its red fruits often remain on bare branches into winter, but its seeds, leaves, bark and berries can cause nausea and low blood pressure if swallowed.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds, leaves, bark and berries can cause nausea and low blood pressure if ingested.

stories.summary: A perennial aquatic or semi-aquatic herb native to Canada, the United States and northern Mexico, it grows in shallow water or mud. Long-stalked leaves form a clump around a flowering stem bearing white or pink-tinged flowers.

A herbaceous perennial native to the British Isles, much of the Mediterranean region, the Caucasus, Canary Islands, Madeira and northern Africa. Its white spring flowers give way to showy red fruit, and its flower structure produces heat. In Croatia, corms were eaten during famines, though the leaves, fruits and rhizomes are poisonous and tuber ingestion may be fatal.
stories.edibilityNote: Corms were eaten in Croatia during famines; leaves, fruits and rhizomes are poisonous, and tuber ingestion may be fatal.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree or multi-stemmed bush native to western Eurasia, the European wild apple has a densely branched crown and often spiny branches. Its small fruits ripen in autumn, and frequent hybridisation with cultivated apples can make identification difficult.

A flowering plant of the rose family known from California, Argentina and Chile, Argentinian biddy-biddy occurs on Californian roadsides, dunes, rocky slopes and coastal grasslands. The California population is sometimes treated as a separate species or variety, and that variety is described as confined to coastal scrub and open rocky slopes.

A deciduous shrub native to Japan, Japanese quince has thorny, spreading branches and vivid red, white, pink or multicoloured flowers. Its golden-yellow, apple-shaped fruit is edible but hard and astringent unless bletted or cooked, and is occasionally made into jam, jelly or pies.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is edible after bletting or cooking and occasionally used in jam, jelly and pies; kernels contain small amounts of poison.

stories.summary: A perennial blackberry native to Armenia and northwestern Iran, it grows vigorously into dense tangles of arching, prickly stems and is invasive elsewhere. Its large fruit is edible and sweet when ripe.
stories.edibilityNote: The large fruit is edible and sweet when ripe; immature fruit is hard, red and much sourer.

stories.summary: A woodland flowering plant native across most of Europe, Eastern Turkey and the Caucasus, cuckoo-pint has arrow-shaped leaves and a hooded flower spike that smells of faeces and traps insects. Its autumn berries are extremely poisonous, but the root is edible when thoroughly roasted, and leaves are eaten in parts of Turkey and by Roma in Sliven only after extensive processing.
stories.edibilityNote: The root is edible when well roasted; leaves are eaten after prolonged boiling with yogurt or after drying and boiling with several changes of water.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to South Africa’s Cape Province, it has hairy stems and white-and-yellow flowers. In Western Australia, it grows in sandy soils, lawns and along road verges, flowering from July to October.

A herbaceous perennial native to temperate Europe and Asia, northern Africa and eastern Australia. It forms extensive colonies of square, reddish-purple stems topped with tightly clustered reddish-purple flowers.

A non-vascular land plant called a liverwort, snakewort has a broad Holarctic distribution. It grows in wet or moist, shaded places, often on rocks or thin soil, and tolerates drying and reduced shade better than Conocephalum conicum.
A highly fragrant daffodil native to central and southern Europe. Its flowers have pure-white outer parts and a short pale-yellow cup with a distinct red edge; the plant is poisonous when eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: All narcissi are poisonous when eaten; poet's daffodil is especially dangerous, acting as a strong emetic and irritant.

stories.summary: Tropical and subtropical vine native from the tropical and subtropical Old World to the South Pacific. Its hollow, oblong fruit has a distinctive warty exterior and bitter flesh. Green or early-yellow fruit is generally cooked, while young shoots and leaves are eaten as greens; ripe fruit and mature seeds are toxic.
stories.edibilityNote: Green or early-yellow fruit is cooked; young shoots and leaves are greens. Sweet red ripe pith is eaten raw, but ripe fruit and mature seeds are toxic.

stories.summary: An erect annual herb, it may be native to Australia, the Americas, or both. It has dark green leaves, pale yellow five-sided flowers and yellow-orange fruits enclosed in balloon-like husks. Ripe fruits are eaten raw and the fruit may also be cooked or made into jam, but unripe raw fruits and all other parts are poisonous.
stories.edibilityNote: Ripe fruits are traditionally eaten raw by Toba-Pilagá people; fruit may also be cooked or made into jam. Unripe raw fruits and other parts are poisonous.

stories.summary: A frost-sensitive annual herb native to Mexico. Its small, round green or purple fruit is enclosed in a papery husk that browns and splits as the fruit ripens. The fruit is widely eaten in Latin American green sauces and Mexican dishes, but other plant parts should not be used as food because they contain toxins.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is used in green sauces, salads and garnishes; other plant parts should not be eaten because they contain toxins.

Physalis ixocarpa: new species of genus physalis to the flora of Pakistan from mountainous region of district Shangla, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Pakistan. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database.
