stories.summary: A cultivated cereal grass first domesticated in China’s Yangtze River basin 13,500 to 8,200 years ago. Its major forms include sticky, short-grained japonica and nonsticky, long-grained indica, while the grain may be white, brown, black or red.
stories.edibilityNote: Cultivated as a cereal, with grain occurring in several colors.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to western Europe, the British Isles and Norway, pignut grows in hedgerows, woods and fields. Its chestnut-like underground part is sometimes eaten as a wild or cultivated root vegetable, and cultivation produces larger tubers.
stories.edibilityNote: The chestnut-like underground part is eaten as a wild or cultivated root vegetable; cultivation produces larger tubers.

stories.summary: Evergreen cherry shrub or small to medium-sized tree native to regions bordering the Black Sea in southwestern Asia and southeastern Europe. It has dark green, leathery, shiny leaves that may smell of almonds when crushed, creamy-white sweet-smelling flowers, and small cherries that turn black when ripe in early autumn.
stories.edibilityNote: The astringent fruits are edible, but bitter fruits should not be eaten; seeds and leaves contain more hydrogen cyanide and should never be eaten.

stories.summary: A colonising perennial herb native to Europe and a broad Asian range extending from the Caucasus and Siberia to Nepal and Japan. Its arching stems carry alternate leaves and scented white tubular flowers with green tips that hang beneath them in spring.
stories.edibilityNote: Young shoots may be boiled like asparagus, and the root is used for tea in Korea; stems, leaves and berries may be toxic in large quantities.

stories.summary: An annual wildflower with a subspecies native to Europe and western Asia, yellow rattle has dry fruits whose loose ripe seeds audibly rattle. Its roots can opportunistically draw nutrients from neighbouring plants, especially grasses and legumes.

A bulbous perennial herb native across the Mediterranean from Portugal to the Levant. It bears rounded clusters of up to 25 white flowers with yellow anthers and has become naturalized in many other regions.

A semi-evergreen flowering perennial native to southwestern and south-central Europe. Its hairy, branching stems trail or rise slightly, bearing mainly red or pink flowers with blue anthers from May to August in the Northern Hemisphere.

Prostrate perennial flowering plant native to Eurasia and Africa. It has dark green, heart-shaped leaves and produces several violet flowers in May and June, often along woodland edges, grassland and shady hedge banks.

A flowering plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula, it grows near streams in wet woods. In mainland Portugal, a 2020 assessment recorded it only in the Estrela and Montesinho mountains and classified it as Vulnerable.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Doronicum carpetanum
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to southern Africa. It grows from rhizomes and bulbs, sometimes forms small bulblets above ground, and bears three-part leaves and solitary white-to-light-pink flowers.

Tall flowering shrub or tree native to coastal and tableland areas of New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory. It has dark green, finely divided leaves, golden spherical flower heads and thin, leathery pods. The flowers are eaten in fritters, while edible trunk gum can substitute for gum arabic in fruit jelly.
stories.edibilityNote: Flowers are used in fritters; edible trunk gum can substitute for gum arabic, including in fruit jelly.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to southwestern Europe and northwestern Africa. Its winged stem climbs using coiled tendrils, and it bears red pea flowers followed by smooth pods that split open.

A perennial flowering plant native to Europe. Its three-part leaves are unmarked, while pale pink or whitish flower heads rise on stalks from the leaf joints. It commonly grows in fields and along roadsides.

Bulbous perennial native to Cape Province in South Africa, where it grows among rocks. Its showy, fragrant pink flowers appear on leafless stems in late summer or autumn, before the narrow leaves. All parts are toxic and can cause vomiting and diarrhoea in humans.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are toxic; ingestion can cause vomiting and diarrhoea in humans.

stories.summary: Perennial herb native to Mexico and parts of Central and South America. It grows from small bulbs, spreads by runners and has stemless leaves with three broad, heart-shaped leaflets; its five-petalled flowers are pink, though some varieties have white flowers.

An evergreen shrub native to the Mediterranean Basin. Its greyish, downy leaves sit below pink-to-purple flower spikes crowned with much larger bright lavender-purple sterile bracts. It blooms in spring and early summer, from March in its native habitat depending on the climate.

An annual or biennial herb native to Europe and North Africa, it has sharp bristles with swollen, blister-like bases on its leaves and stems. Its yellow flowerheads have a distinctive outer row of large bracts.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves were formerly eaten as a pot herb; some modern foragers use the flowers to flavour vinegar.

stories.summary: An annual or biennial herb native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, it has low, spreading stems and sharp, needle-like leaves. Its small, mostly self-pollinated flowers lack petals, and its seeds may germinate in autumn or spring under several different life cycles.
A perennial flowering herb native to Eurasia, lesser stitchwort has weak, four-angled stems and narrow leaves. Each white petal is so deeply divided that it appears to be two petals.

A perennial bulbous herb native to South America, large-flowered pink-sorrel now grows in temperate and tropical regions worldwide except Antarctica. In Europe, plants are sterile and reproduce only through bulbs; its leaves have a zesty, lemony flavour.
stories.edibilityNote: Flowers, leaves and roots are edible, but consumption in large amounts is discouraged because the plant contains oxalic acid.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native to western Eurasia, wild cherry has white spring flowers and ripe red to dark-purple fruit. The ripe fruit has been eaten by people for thousands of years, while every other part is slightly toxic.
stories.edibilityNote: Ripe fruit has been human food for millennia; all other plant parts are slightly toxic and contain cyanogenic glycosides.

stories.summary: A parasitic plant native mainly to central and northern Europe and parts of Asia, ivy broomrape lacks chlorophyll and depends completely on ivy. Its brown, purple or sometimes yellow stems bear cream flowers with reddish-purple veins and a pointed top of unopened flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: Dioscorides wrote that the plant could be eaten raw or cooked like asparagus.

stories.summary: An aquatic flowering plant native to North Africa, Europe, temperate Asia and Jammu and Kashmir in tropical Asia. Its round dark-green leaves and white flowers float on water; the daytime summer flowers open cup-shaped and become star-shaped over time.
stories.edibilityNote: In north-eastern India, young leaves and flower stalks are eaten as vegetables, while rhizomes are boiled and eaten.

stories.summary: An annual flowering plant native to most of Europe, the Maghreb, Levant and Caucasus, grass vetchling lacks true leaves, leaflets and tendrils. Its flattened leaf stalks resemble pointed grass blades, while small crimson flowers give way to long pods that become cylindrical as the peas develop.

A rhizomatous perennial flowering plant native to Western Europe. Its heart-shaped leaves have transparent dots, while its rich yellow flowers have petals that are red underneath and dotted along the margins.

A perennial herb found across Europe, western Siberia, Asia Minor, the Caucasus and North Africa, dropwort favours dry, lime-rich pasture. It has fern-like leaves and clusters of creamy white flowers; mature crushed leaves smell of wintergreen. Its tuberous roots and young leaves can be eaten raw or cooked and taste bittersweet.
stories.edibilityNote: Tuberous roots and young leaves can be eaten raw as salad or cooked as a vegetable; their taste is bittersweet.

stories.summary: A member of the carrot family native to western Europe, it bears frilly leaves and a small rounded taproot. The root, once used as a vegetable in parts of western Europe, is edible raw or cooked, while the leaves can serve as an herb or garnish.
stories.edibilityNote: The taproot is edible raw or cooked and was formerly a western European root vegetable; leaves can be used as an herb or garnish.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to continental Europe. It has small blue tubular flowers and coarse hairs, while its unusually bristly, warty-looking leaves help distinguish it from similar species.

An ornamental flowering plant of unstated native origin, hollyhock reached Europe from southwestern China by the 15th century, possibly earlier. It has large, heart-shaped leaves and large flowers, and may grow as an annual, biennial or short-lived perennial while frequently self-sowing.

A flowering plant native to eastern and central North America. Usually living for two years, it forms a low leaf rosette first, then sends up a flowering stem whose yellow blooms open quickly each evening and last until the following noon. Most parts are edible: roots and leaves may be raw or cooked, while young stems should be peeled before eating raw or fried.
stories.edibilityNote: Indigenous North Americans historically used it as food; roots and leaves are eaten raw or cooked, while young stems are peeled before eating raw or fried.

stories.summary: A generally biennial herb with no natural native range supplied, this evening primrose arose as a garden hybrid in Europe. Its showy flower spikes have long red sepals and bright yellow petals that fade through orange to red. Cultivation has helped it spread and become naturalized in many countries.

Perennial herb native to Eurasia, sulphur cinquefoil grows in tufts from a woody taproot and has upright, densely hairy, branching stems. It usually bears pale yellow flowers with five broad, shallowly notched petals from June to August.
A flowering sedge, cyperus sedge grows in marshes, swamps and along ponds, rivers and canals. It bears one male flower spike and several hanging female spikes among bright yellow-green leaves.

A perennial herb native to western North America, it grows from a layered bulb and bears grass-like leaves and blue, star-shaped flowers. Its bulbs are eaten after roasting or boiling, but are easily confused with toxic death-camas bulbs.
stories.edibilityNote: Bulbs are roasted, boiled or made into flour; they are difficult to distinguish from poisonous death-camas bulbs.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to western North America. It becomes covered in white blossoms with a strong orange-and-pineapple scent, and Native American tribes use the flowers to prepare teas.
stories.edibilityNote: Native American tribes use the flowers to prepare teas.

stories.summary: A milky-sapped perennial native to western North America. It bears dense clusters of pale pink to pinkish-purple, star-shaped flowers and rough pods filled with silky-haired seeds. Young leaves and seed pods can be boiled and eaten, but care is needed to distinguish it from highly toxic related species.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves and seed pods can be boiled and eaten; careful identification is needed because related milkweeds may be highly toxic.

stories.summary: An annual flowering garden plant native to southern Europe, North Africa and southwest Asia, love-in-a-mist has flowers nestled among lacy bracts. Its flowers are usually blue but may be white, pink or pale purple, followed by large, inflated seed capsules that turn brown in late summer.

A parasitic plant native to Europe, greater dodder grows on many herbaceous plants and is a notable parasite of lucerne. Its long, thin stems are yellowish or reddish, bearing compact clusters of pink flowers.

Yellow loosestrife is a perennial flowering plant native to Eurasia, including Ireland, and North Africa. It has an upright, downy form, conspicuous yellow flower clusters and leaves spotted with translucent orange glands.
A flowering plant, dense-flowered mullein occurs in Madeira, where it is introduced.

A hardy annual leaf vegetable native to Asia and Europe. Its red, white or green varieties have thin, slightly acidic leaves with a salty, spinach-like taste. The leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked and were once used to colour pasta in Italy.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw in salads or cooked; green leaves were formerly used to colour pasta in Italy.

stories.summary: A low evergreen shrub native to northeastern North America, eastern teaberry has wintergreen-scented leaves and red fruits. Its mildly sweet fruits are edible, while dried leaves and branches are infused as herbal tea; significant essential oil from the leaves requires at least three days of fermentation.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits are eaten; dried leaves and branches make tea. Leaves require at least three days’ fermentation to yield significant essential oil.

stories.summary: A root-hemiparasitic plant native to parts of the eastern and midwestern United States and adjacent Canada. It attaches to oak roots and is recognized by its fern-like lobed leaves and tubular yellow flowers.
A very small annual herb native to continental Europe. It has alternate leaves and glandular hairs, with flowers ranging from pale purple to white and appearing in June and July.

A usually biennial wildflower native to northern Eurasia, ragwort can behave as a perennial under repeated grazing or mowing. It has unpleasant-smelling leaves and dense clusters of bright yellow flowers, blooming from June to November in the Northern Hemisphere.
An annual herb endemic to California. Its densely hairy, glandular stems carry branching clusters of sticky flower heads, each with resin glands and golden-yellow outer florets.

Perennial aquatic flowering herb with a circumboreal range across northern Eurasia and North America. Its straplike leaves may float or stand above shallow water, and its spherical female fruiting heads grow below the male flower heads.

An annual or perennial herb native to eastern Canada and the United States. It has branching stems, gland-dotted leaves and tiny golden-yellow, star-shaped flowers that appear from July to September. It grows in ditches, marshes, shorelines and sometimes moist woods and fields.

Annual nightshade native to the United States and northern and central Mexico, it forms a tumbleweed and has abundant spines on its stems and leaves. Its yellow flowers contain two unequal sets of anthers, and each berry is enclosed by a prickly covering.

A perennial climbing vine native primarily to subtropical and temperate East Asia, kudzu has tuberous, starch-rich roots and stems that root on contact with soil. Its starchy root has been eaten in China since before 540 CE and is still made into starch, flour, noodles and Japanese sweets.
stories.edibilityNote: The starchy root has been eaten in China since before 540 CE and is processed into starch, flour, noodles and Japanese sweets.

stories.summary: Annual flowering plant, sometimes biennial or perennial, native to eastern and central North America. Its coarse-haired leaves and stems bear yellow, daisy-like flowers with prominent dark, dome-shaped centres in late summer and early autumn.

Perennial vine native to the southeastern United States, especially the Cumberland and Blue Ridge Mountains. Its large, heart-shaped leaves form dense cover, while yellowish-green flowers with brownish-purple lobes resemble smoking pipes.

A tropical tree native to Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America. Its trunk and large branches are often crowded with thorns, and it flowers while briefly leafless. The pods contain seeds surrounded by buoyant, cotton-like fibre traditionally used as stuffing and insulation.

A tropical fruit plant native to the tropical Americas, probably southern Mexico and adjacent Central America. Its usually single trunk bears large, deeply lobed leaves near the top, while hard green berries mature into yellow fruit with soft orange flesh. Papayas are eaten fresh, in salads and juices; before ripening, the skin’s milky latex should be removed because it harms mucous membranes.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten fresh, in salads and juices; milky latex from unripe skin should be removed before consumption.

stories.summary: A large tropical tree of uncertain native origin because people have spread it widely. Its branches grow in distinctive tiers, and its corky fruit can travel by water. The slightly acidic fruit is edible; ripe seeds may be eaten raw or cooked but are small and difficult to extract.
stories.edibilityNote: The slightly acidic fruit is edible; ripe seeds can be eaten raw or cooked but are small and difficult to extract.

stories.summary: A perennial flowering tree native from the southwestern United States and northern Mexico south to the Galápagos Islands and northern Argentina. Its tiny leaflets fall in dry weather, leaving green stalks and branches to photosynthesize, while sharp spines and fragrant yellow-orange flowers make it distinctive.

A large, fast-growing tree native to Central America and Mexico, the avocado has glossy leaves and pear-shaped fruit with creamy, fatty, pale green or yellow flesh. Wild fruits are small, while cultivated varieties can be much larger; the flesh surrounding the large seed is edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The edible part is the soft, greenish-yellow flesh surrounding the large seed; the fruit is nutritious for humans.

stories.summary: A tree native to the Neotropics, it grows naturally in well-drained tropical and subtropical forests from Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean to much of South America. Its aromatic, rot-resistant wood is widely used for storage furniture, veneer and musical instruments.

Deciduous flowering tree native to Madagascar. It is remembered for fern-like bright-green leaves and a summer display of large scarlet or orange-red flowers, usually with a larger upright petal spotted yellow and white. It is endangered in the wild but widely cultivated elsewhere.

Evergreen shrub or small tree native to South America, specifically Peru, common guava bears edible fruit that may be eaten raw or cooked. Cultivars have white, pink, or red flesh, and a few have red rather than green or yellow skin.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit can be eaten raw or cooked.

stories.summary: Evergreen coastal tree native across the tropical Old World and Oceania, with a separate subspecies native to tropical America; its status in Hawaii is uncertain. Its yellow flowers turn orange and then red during the day, and its young leafy shoots may be eaten as vegetables.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leafy shoots may be eaten as vegetables; leaves are also used as cooking trays and in tempeh fermentation.

stories.summary: Shrub native to tropical eastern Africa, specifically Kenya, Tanzania and Mozambique. Its distinctive red or pink flowers have frilly, finely divided petals.

A large deciduous tree native to the tropical monsoon forests of Southeast Asia, specifically India, Myanmar, Thailand and Laos. Its pale, durable, relatively light wood is especially valued for shipbuilding, while the tree has large rounded leaves and small clustered flowers.

Evergreen flowering tree native to the western Pacific, Australia, New Guinea, Southeast Asia and India. Its foliage consists of slender, drooping branchlets bearing tiny scale-like leaves, and its woody fruit resembles a conifer cone although the tree is not a conifer.
A flowering plant reported as native to the tropical Americas and now introduced across most continents. It has spines at its nodes and green, petal-free flowers arranged in spikes.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is eaten in Africa and several Asian cuisines; its leaves are dietary in the Maldives, and it is braised or added to porridge in Brazil.

stories.summary: An evergreen subshrub or herbaceous perennial native and endemic to Madagascar, Madagascar periwinkle has glossy green leaves in opposite pairs, each with a pale central vein. Its flowers range from white with yellow or red centres to dark pink, and all parts are poisonous if eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; eating them can cause stomach cramps, heart complications, low blood pressure, paralysis and death.

stories.summary: An erect succulent shrub native to arid and subtropical South Asia, mainly the Indian Subcontinent. Its ridged, angular branches bear short spines and small leaves that fall quickly. Every part contains poisonous, irritating milky latex.

A flowering plant native to Bolivia, Brazil, French Guiana, Guyana, Suriname and Venezuela, golden trumpet is widely naturalised elsewhere in the tropics. It is cultivated as a houseplant and needs bright light, abundant moisture and organic-rich soil during growth.

A climbing plant of unspecified native origin, lesser balloon vine is widely distributed across tropical and subtropical Africa, Australia, South Asia and North America. It has balloon-like capsules that turn brown when ripe and almost black seeds marked with a pale heart-shaped spot.
stories.edibilityNote: The green parts are eaten as vegetables.

stories.summary: A woody flowering vine or shrub native to Brazil, Bolivia, Peru and Chubut Province in Argentina. Its thorny, hairy stems bear heart-shaped leaves, while small white flowers are surrounded by brightly coloured bracts.

Woody perennial herb or small shrub native to coastal sage and chaparral from Southern California into Baja California. It ranges from a low vine to a stout woody climber, with broad triangular leaves and white, pale pink or lavender flowers whose colour often varies with drought or temperature.

A perennial herb native through most of Europe and western Asia, typically growing in damp meadows. Its divided leaves are dark green above and whitish beneath, while its numerous creamy-white summer flowers have a strong sweet scent and are used to flavour drinks, fruit, jams and desserts.
stories.edibilityNote: Flowers flavour stewed fruit, jams and desserts; the aromatic plant also flavours vinegar, wine, beer and Scandinavian mead.

stories.summary: Cactus native to Argentina, particularly the provinces of Salta and Tucumán at lower altitudes. It usually grows singly and produces long, unscented white flowers that open at night.

A tall perennial grass now found worldwide, reed canary grass often forms single-species stands beside lakes and streams or in wet open ground. It spreads underground through thick rhizomes; in many places it invades wetlands and is difficult to eradicate.

A perennial mustard-family plant native to Europe and western to central Asia. It bears white flower clusters and heart-shaped seed pods, while its creeping roots can produce dense, long-lived patches.
Perennial flowering plant native to Europe, with very large oval leaves that may have red stems and slightly wavy edges. Its small greenish flowers turn red as they mature.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves are eaten as greens but soon become bitter; dried seeds can be ground into flour.

stories.summary: A shrub or tree native to southeastern Australia. It has bright to pale-yellow cylindrical flower spikes and straight to strongly twisted seed pods, and is considered invasive in Portugal, New Zealand and South Africa.
stories.edibilityNote: Flowers, seeds and pods are used as food; in Tasmania, ripening pods were roasted and the seeds eaten.

stories.summary: A small deciduous tree native to Japan and southern Korea, it has rounded, many-lobed leaves that begin downy and turn bright orange to dark red in autumn. Dark purplish-red flowers hang in clusters as the leaves open in early spring.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to Korea, Japan, China, eastern Mongolia and far eastern Russia, Japanese maple has sharply pointed, hand-shaped leaves and paired winged fruits. Its seedlings vary notably in leaf size, shape and colour, while cultivated forms range from upright to weeping. The edible leaves are locally pickled for a year, coated with flour, sesame and sugar, then deep-fried as momiji tempura.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are edible; for the Minoh dish momiji tempura, they are pickled for a year, coated with flour, sesame and sugar, then deep-fried.

stories.summary: A large coniferous tree native to Northern, Central and Eastern Europe, Norway spruce typically has hanging branchlets and the longest cones of any spruce. Its seed cones mature from green or reddish to brown.
stories.edibilityNote: The tree supplies spruce beer; in Finland, shoot tips are used in syrup, tea, alcohol, smoothies, salt and desserts.

stories.summary: A fast-growing evergreen shrub or small tree endemic to New Zealand. Its lance-shaped, finely serrated leaves have translucent dots, while its white flowers bear purple spots and are followed by bright red fruit. The berries were occasionally eaten traditionally by Māori, but consumption is not recommended because the plant contains the toxin ngaione.
stories.edibilityNote: Berries were occasionally a traditional Māori food, but consumption is not recommended because of the toxin ngaione.

stories.summary: Evergreen conifer native to the Mediterranean region, although its precise natural range is debated. Young trees are bushy, while mature trees develop broad, flat, umbrella-like crowns. Its pine nuts are edible and have been cultivated since prehistoric times.
stories.edibilityNote: Edible pine nuts have been cultivated for at least 6,000 years and traded since early historic times.

stories.summary: A large evergreen conifer native to northwestern North America, grand fir has flattened needles arranged in nearly level rows. Its foliage has a citrus-like scent, and the taller coastal variety grows west of the Cascades while the shorter interior variety grows to the east.

A deciduous shrub or small tree of unspecified native origin, the plum may be somewhat thorny and bears white blossom in early spring. Its fruit has one large stone and usually sweet edible pulp, although some varieties are sour and require cooking with sugar to be palatable.
stories.edibilityNote: The pulp is edible; sour varieties may require cooking with sugar to become palatable, and the stone is discarded.

stories.summary: A fern native to western Europe, pillwort grows on wet mud and silt around lakes, ponds, ditches and marshes, sometimes in shallow water. Its slender, rush-like fronds curl as they unfurl, and populations may disappear from a site before returning years later.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Pilularia globulifera
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A medium-sized deciduous tree native to western North America, Oregon ash develops dark gray-brown bark with deep, woven-looking ridges. Its light green leaves turn bright yellow and fall early in autumn. When leafless, it can be recognized by stout, oppositely arranged twigs with woolly hairs.

Annual herb native across most of the world, from Arctic to tropical regions, except South America and southern Africa. It has reddish stems with swollen joints, often dark-blotched leaves, and dense, often nodding spikes of tiny pink flowers. Remains were identified in the intestinal contents of Tollund Man in Denmark.
stories.edibilityNote: Remains were found in Tollund Man’s intestinal contents in Denmark; the plant part and preparation are unspecified.

stories.summary: A tiny floating aquatic plant found widely outside polar and tropical regions. Its simple body carries one dangling root and can form green mats over still water, though it also grows on mud or damp rocks.
A fern native to humid warm-temperate and tropical regions worldwide. It has delicate, divided light-green fronds on black, wiry stems and commonly grows in moist, sheltered, shaded places.

A deciduous vine native to western North America, California wild grape climbs other plants or trails across the ground on twisted woody stems. Its small, often sour purple grapes ripen in autumn and are edible, including for making wine or jelly.
stories.edibilityNote: Small, often sour purple grapes are eaten and can be made into wine or jelly.

stories.summary: A large deciduous tree native at least to southwest and central Asia and southeast Europe, though ancient cultivation obscures its exact natural range. Its fruit has a green husk around a corrugated shell and a rich-flavoured edible nut; cultivated trees usually have thinner shells than wild ones.
stories.edibilityNote: The nuts are eaten fresh or pressed for richly flavoured oil; cultivated forms are commonly selected for larger, thinner-shelled nuts.

stories.summary: A pear species native to central and eastern Europe and western Asia. Most orchard pears grown in Europe, North America and Australia derive from it; the fruit is eaten fresh or cooked and fermented into perry.
stories.edibilityNote: Pears are eaten fresh or cooked in desserts and pies, served with meat, or fermented into perry and distilled into pear brandy.

stories.summary: A small pear tree distributed across southern Iberia and northern Morocco. Within Iberia, its distribution is fragmented and trees are often sparse. It has white, occasionally pink-tinged flowers and fibrous green or brown fruits, which mammals often eat whole and disperse.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is described as inedible for people, though the source flags this claim as needing citation.

stories.summary: A deciduous flowering shrub native and endemic to California, California sweetshrub grows along streams and on moist canyon slopes. Its dark red to burgundy flowers appear from late spring to early fall and are pollinated by beetles.

A tall perennial cane native to the Greater Middle East. It forms dense stands in damp places and bears upright, feathery plumes whose seeds are usually absent or rarely fertile; it spreads mainly through tough underground rhizomes. It is widely naturalised and considered invasive in North America and Oceania.

A pine tree native to coastal and inland mountain areas along the Pacific coast of North America, from Oregon to Baja California, sugar pine is the tallest and most massive pine and bears some of the longest cones of any conifer. Indigenous peoples ate its seeds raw or roasted, ground them into flour or paste, ate the inner bark, and consumed small amounts of sweet resin or chewed it as gum.
stories.edibilityNote: Indigenous peoples ate seeds raw, roasted, as flour or paste, ate inner bark, and consumed small amounts of resin or chewed it as gum.

stories.summary: A pine tree ranging from southern Oregon to Baja California, especially northern California and the Oregon–California border. Its twisted yellow-green needles grow in threes, while resin-sealed cones cluster on branches and sometimes the trunk; fire melts the resin and releases seeds for regrowth.

Fern native to the Western Pacific rim, from Australia through New Caledonia and Fiji to French Polynesia. It is commonly known as monarch fern, musk fern, maile-scented fern, breadfruit fern or wart fern.

A herbaceous perennial native to the United States, from Connecticut to Missouri and south from Florida to Texas. Its lyre-shaped leaves form a basal rosette, while hairy square stems carry lavender to blue flowers. It can spread readily into lawns and tolerate mowing and foot traffic.

A flowering plant native to Mexico and Texas. It bears large, spiny-edged leaves and flowers only once near the end of its life, producing a tall stalk of yellow blooms before dying while new shoots continue from its base.
stories.edibilityNote: In pre-Columbian Mexico, liquid from a cut pre-flowering stem was fermented into pulque; heated hearts are also used to produce mezcal.

stories.summary: A herbaceous climbing plant native to eastern and southern Africa. It has shiny, flattened, leaf-like stems and hanging white flowers, while radial tubers cluster close to its underground stem.

An evergreen woody climber native to the Canary Islands, using aerial rootlets to cling to trees, cliffs and walls or spreading as ground cover. It has broad, glossy, slightly leathery leaves, greenish flowers and round fruits that turn black when ripe.

Perennial flowering shrub native to Mexico and invasive in farmland and bushland worldwide. It has creamy-white flower clusters and seeds with feathery parachutes carried by wind; stems can also root when they touch soil.

A perennial cactus shrub with a likely wild origin in central Mexico, the Indian fig opuntia has thick, succulent, paddle-shaped stems and white, yellow or red flowers. Its fruits are eaten raw, while its young stems are cooked and eaten as a vegetable.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits are eaten raw; young stems are cooked as a vegetable called nopalitos.

stories.summary: A shrub or small tree found in chaparral canyons and slopes of Southern California, Arizona and the Baja California peninsula. It is long-lived, with dense evergreen foliage, leathery folded leaves and reddish, hairy, sticky fruit.
stories.edibilityNote: Cahuilla ate fresh, dried or mashed fruits and boiled flower clusters; Kumeyaay cooked, toasted, ground or infused fruits. Seeds are reportedly inedible.

stories.summary: Large evergreen shrub or small tree native to North America, laurel sumac occurs along the Pacific coast of Southern California and Baja California. Its folded, fragrant leaves have bright reddish veins and edges throughout the year. The Chumash made flour from its dried fruit.
stories.edibilityNote: The Chumash historically made flour from the dried fruit.

stories.summary: A tree endemic to Australia, river red gum is strongly associated with inland watercourses and has smooth pale bark and white flowers. Its limbs, and sometimes whole trees, can fall without warning.
A biennial herb native to Great Britain, Italy, France, the Iberian Peninsula, the Canary Islands and Madeira. It grows tall and bears yellow flowers with purple centres.

A small deciduous tree native to southwestern North America, from southern California to Texas and northern Mexico. It has rough, fissured gray-brown bark and noticeably velvety young shoots. Male and female flowers grow on separate trees in small clusters during early spring.

A perennial grass native to southern Africa and Yemen, it grows in many habitats, including shade. It flowers and sets seed throughout the year, and its seeds can produce new plants within a few weeks; it is invasive in several regions.

A perennial grass native to southern Europe, Macaronesia, North and East Africa, western and central Asia, India, Yunnan and Vietnam. It has simple, broad leaves and is a common established newcomer in the UK.
Annual flowering plant believed to be native to the Middle East. It now has a worldwide distribution and grows in cultivated plots.

A variable flowering plant native across parts of Africa, much of Asia and Europe, North America and the Caribbean. It inhabits many damp or aquatic settings and bears toothed or deeply lobed leaves with small, mustard-like yellow flowers.
A rhizomatous perennial grass native to Europe, Asia and North America, it has very rough, finely toothed leaf edges sharp enough to cut skin. Its loose flower clusters have wavy, hairlike branches.

A perennial herb native to the Americas from Mexico through Central and South America to Argentina and Chile, seashore vervain has become introduced worldwide and is sometimes a noxious weed. Its rough, serrated leaves accompany upright spikes of small purple tubular flowers.

A low, hairy flowering herb native to Europe and Asia, it has creeping, much-branched stems with rounded fuzzy leaves. Its solitary, hairy, snapdragon-like flowers combine yellow, white and deep purple and have a narrow pointed spur.

An annual flowering plant native to the eastern United States and the Gulf Coast to Texas. It mainly inhabits coastal salt marshes, though a non-marine weedy variety occurs in the Ozarks. Its upright, hairless stem bears flower heads with bright yellow centres and white to lavender outer florets.
Annual thistle native to the Mediterranean Basin. Fine tangled fibres give it a cobwebbed appearance, while its rigid leaves and flower heads are sharply spiny and its florets bright yellow.

A member of the sunflower family native to the Mediterranean regions of Europe, North Africa and southwestern Asia, smooth distaff thistle is related to safflower. It is naturalized in New Zealand and California.

Wetland grass with a worldwide distribution, often forming extensive reed beds in damp ground or standing water. It bears dense dark-purple flower clusters that later look grey and silky; young shoots, sap, underground stems, seeds and other parts have documented food uses, though some are tough or scarce.
stories.edibilityNote: Young shoots may be eaten raw or cooked; sap, underground stems, roots and seeds are also prepared as food, with some parts tough or scarce.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to warm temperate and tropical regions of southern Eurasia and Africa. Its branching stems often spread into flat patches, while its hard fruits split into sharply spined burs capable of puncturing bicycle tyres and injuring bare feet or grazing animals.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and shoots are eaten in East Asia; stems have been used to thicken diluted buttermilk.

stories.summary: A fully submerged water plant of unstated native origin, it occurs in fresh and brackish water on every continent except Antarctica. Its very narrow leaves contain two parallel tubes, while its underground stems form starchy tubers.

Flowering grass native to southern South America, including the Pampas. It typically grows in moist soils beside waterways in its native range and is widely cultivated as an ornamental, but has become invasive in temperate regions worldwide.

A mustard plant of unstated native origin, it has cultivars grown for leafy greens, swollen stems, roots and oilseeds. Its edible leaves, seeds and stems range from peppery greens to pickles and spicy brown mustard.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, seeds and stems are edible; they are eaten raw, boiled, cooked or pickled, and the seeds provide brown mustard and mustard oil.

stories.summary: An evergreen conifer native to the eastern Mediterranean and Iran. Its dense dark-green foliage and the very narrow crown of most cultivated trees create a distinctive exclamation-mark shape. Some trees are reported to live for more than 1,000 years.
A plant found throughout the Mediterranean basin and along the European Black Sea coast. Its seed pods are edible and are foraged from March to May in Israel (Palestine).
stories.edibilityNote: Seed pods are edible and foraged from March to May in Israel (Palestine).

stories.summary: An upright annual flowering herb native to Eurasia, particularly most of Europe and southwestern Asia. Its dense, elongated flower spikes range from creamy white to rich crimson and appear through spring and summer.
stories.edibilityNote: Flowers and seedling sprouts are eaten in dishes or tea and may be dried into flour; raw sprouts carry a bacterial-contamination risk.

stories.summary: Straggly tree or mallee endemic to southern New South Wales. Its smooth bark and silvery, aromatic leaves are joined by white flowers and woody cup-shaped or cylindrical fruit. It survives in only a few scattered populations on the Central and Southern Tablelands.
Shrubby plant native to the central and eastern Mediterranean Basin. It usually has pink flowers but is very variable, and is widely grown as a decorative plant.

An evergreen fan palm believed to originate in central China, southern Japan, northern Myanmar and northern India, the Chusan palm has a rough, fibre-covered trunk and rounded fans of leaflets whose tips may be straight or drooping. Male and female flowers grow on separate trees, and the young flower buds are cooked and eaten in various ways.
stories.edibilityNote: The young flower buds are cooked and eaten in various ways.

stories.summary: Flowering plant native to Western Europe, including Britain and Ireland, and extending to North Africa, Italy and Greece. Its dull blue or buff-yellow flowers last only a day or so, while winter-persistent green capsules reveal scarlet seeds. Some people find that its crushed or bruised leaves have an unpleasant, beefy smell.
Small flowering herb native to Europe and Asia. Its hairy trailing stems bear widely spaced fuzzy leaves and solitary, spurred, snapdragon-like flowers patterned yellow, white and purple.

A small evergreen tree native to the American tropics. Its flowers grow in clusters directly on the trunk and older branches, while yellow-to-orange pods hold numerous seeds in white pulp. Dried, fermented seeds make cocoa and chocolate; the pulp is also used for drinks, jelly and cream.
stories.edibilityNote: Dried, fermented seeds make cocoa and chocolate; pulp is used for juice, smoothies, jelly, cream and sometimes fermented alcoholic drinks.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to the southwestern highlands of Ethiopia, Arabica coffee has white flower clusters and red-to-purple “cherries” that usually contain two seeds. A drink made from its roasted seeds is recorded in historical Arab scholarship.
stories.edibilityNote: Its roasted seeds were historically brewed as coffee, according to Arab written records.

stories.summary: A gymnosperm tree native to East Asia, ginkgo is the last living species of an ancient plant order. Its distinctive fan-shaped leaves turn bright yellow in autumn, and some trees can live for thousands of years.
stories.edibilityNote: Seed kernels are traditionally eaten cooked in Asian dishes, but large or prolonged intake may cause poisoning; cooking does not destroy the toxin.

stories.summary: Woody shrub or tree native to Australia’s east coast, with outlying populations in Tasmania and on Flinders Island. It is remembered for its wrinkled grey bark, saw-toothed glossy leaves and large yellow to grey-yellow flower spikes that age into woody cones.
A sturdy perennial woody vine native to central and eastern North America. It has tiny scentless flowers and pea-sized orange fruits that are poisonous to humans when eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: The orange fruits are poisonous to humans when ingested.

stories.summary: A woody vine native to China, Japan and Korea. Its thin, spindly vines can climb and encircle trees, while its capsules open to reveal bright red seed coverings; all parts are poisonous.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts of the plant are poisonous.

stories.summary: An annual, biennial or short-lived perennial native to much of Europe, from Portugal and southern Scotland east to Ukraine and the Caucasus. Its slender stems bear deep-pink, white-spotted flowers surrounded by upright hairy bracts, and the blooms close in late afternoon.
A small flowering shrub native across much of Eurasia. Its long runners root at their tips, while its sometimes-prickly stems are bluish-grey. The black, fleshy fruits have a bluish waxy coating.
Low-growing gorse shrub native to southern Portugal, specifically the Algarve and Alentejo. Dense short hairs cover its open branches, stems and slender spines, giving the plant a silvery colour.
A small evergreen perennial native to Asia and Europe. It forms rounded mounds that can be completely covered by clear yellow flowers from mid- to late spring, though cultivars offer other colours.

A thorny tree native to Asia, with an unclear western natural limit in eastern Europe, it has silvery-scaled stems and leaves. Its aromatic creamy-yellow flowers are followed by sweet, orange-red fruit with a dry, mealy texture.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is edible; dried senjed is served in syrup in an Afghan Nowruz fruit salad.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub or small tree native to eastern Asia from the Himalayas to Japan, autumn olive readily colonizes barren land and is invasive in parts of the United States and Europe. It often has sharp thorns, while its leaves emerge silvery and become greener above through summer. The ripe red, silver- or brown-dotted berries are sweet-tart and may be eaten fresh or made into jam, condiments or flavouring.
stories.edibilityNote: Ripe red berries are eaten fresh or processed into jam, condiments or flavouring; they have a sweet-tart taste.

stories.summary: A small deciduous shrub native to cool temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, it grows mainly on wet acidic soils. It has brown stems, blue-green leaves with pale net-like veins, and hanging pale-pink flowers. Its dark blue-black berries have sweet white flesh and may be eaten raw, cooked or dried.
stories.edibilityNote: Berries are eaten raw or cooked, made into jelly, pies or infused liquor, and dried for pemmican.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Vaccinium uliginosum
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A small woody cycad native to the Greater Antilles, it forms low clusters with an often-underground trunk and reddish seed cones. The plant is poisonous, but the Taíno historically obtained starch from carefully leached roots and half-buried stems.
stories.edibilityNote: The Taíno historically used carefully leached roots and half-buried stems for starch; untreated plant material is poisonous.

stories.summary: A pine native to the New World, Pinus coulteri belongs to a group of pines distributed in Canada and the United States, excluding areas adjoining the Mexican border.

A green alga of unspecified native origin, it is distributed worldwide. Its thin, flat, translucent blades have ruffled, often torn edges and attach to rocks or other algae by a small disc. It is eaten in Scottish soups and salads and prepared in several ways in Hawaiʻi.
stories.edibilityNote: Used in Scottish soups and salads; in Hawaiʻi, eaten mixed, salted with raw fish, boiled as soup, or served with seasonings.

stories.summary: A green seaweed originating in the Pacific near Japan and invasive on northern Atlantic coasts. It forms dark green, velvety, finger-like branching fronds. The Atlantic subspecies is used as food in the Far East.
stories.edibilityNote: Only Codium fragile subsp. atlanticum is documented as food in the Far East.

stories.summary: Large deciduous tree native to northern Mexico and the southern United States around the Mississippi region. It bears nuts whose kernels are eaten raw or used in cakes and pies.
stories.edibilityNote: The nut kernels are commonly eaten raw and used in cakes, pies and other foods.

stories.summary: A red macroalga native to the lower intertidal coasts of the northeastern Atlantic, including Macaronesia, and the Mediterranean. It forms loose tufts of dark reddish-purple, flattened fronds, with branches that often shorten gradually toward the tips. It typically grows in tidal pools, coastal lagoons, or shallow water just below the shore.
Flowering plant native to Europe, Asia and Africa. Its small, dull-white flowers have purple tips, and its rounded fruit bears a central crest.

A succulent subtropical subshrub endemic to the western Canary Islands, it bears flattened leaf rosettes at the ends of mostly upright stems. Large pyramidal clusters of bright yellow flowers appear in spring.

A flowering shrub or small tree native to Oahu and Molokai in the Hawaiian Islands, Hibiscus arnottianus grows in tropical rainforest. Its three accepted subspecies occupy restricted parts of Oahu or eastern Molokai, and the species is assessed as endangered.

An orchid that grows on trees or rocks, native to southern China, the Himalayas and Indochina. It forms clumps of stems bearing fragrant, waxy flowers, usually in winter and spring, with colours varying from white to pink and purple.
stories.edibilityNote: Deemed unsafe for human consumption in food supplements without a safety assessment.

stories.summary: An herbaceous perennial native to northeastern and north-central North America, Canada goldenrod forms large colonies through spreading underground stems. Its upright growth carries branching clusters of many small yellow flowers above the foliage.
A perennial herb of damp places across the Boreal Kingdom, Ranunculus flammula flowers in June or July. It is poisonous and can be pollinated by rain.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is poisonous.

stories.summary: A liverwort recorded across Europe, parts of Asia, North Africa, Madeira and North America, cliff scalewort grows mainly in damp, shady mountain habitats. Its branching plants range from light brown to dark green, appearing oily and glossy when wet but dull when dry; reproductive structures are rare.

A moss with no stated native origin, Dicranella heteromalla is widespread through the temperate Northern Hemisphere. It forms dense yellow-green to green carpets and has finely toothed leaves ending in long, sickle-curved tips that usually point to one side.

An evergreen perennial moss occurring on every continent, including Antarctica. It forms bluish-green to grey tufts on wine-red stems, and is distinguished by the long, transparent white hair at each leaf tip.
A biennial flowering plant of uncertain native origin, Alexanders has stout, hairless stems and distinctive divided leaves. Its yellow flowers help distinguish it from similar white-flowered plants.
stories.edibilityNote: Stems are cooked like asparagus; historically, young shoots, leaves and roots were eaten fresh or cooked, especially in northern Europe and Turkey.

stories.summary: Bearberry is a small evergreen groundcover shrub widely distributed across circumboreal regions of the subarctic Northern Hemisphere. It has shiny, thick leaves, clusters of white-to-pink flowers and bright red fruits that persist into early winter.
stories.edibilityNote: Blackfeet people use the fruits and leaves as food; fruits may be eaten raw, made into jelly or cooked with meat, and young leaves brewed as tea.

stories.summary: Grapevine native to eastern North America. Its berries have thick skins that slip easily from the intact pulp, while its varieties are known for pronounced strawberry, raspberry and characteristically grape-like flavours.
stories.edibilityNote: Its grapes and derived varieties are used for wine, juice, jellies, jams, sweets and soft drinks.

stories.summary: A coniferous tree native to the mountains of western North America, white fir has flattened green to blue-green needles. Its green or purple cones ripen pale brown, then disintegrate to release winged seeds about six months after pollination. It can live for more than 300 years.

A shrub or small tree native to the western United States, western juniper usually grows on dry, rocky mountain sites. It bears blue-brown, berry-like cones with a whitish bloom; some Oregon distilleries use these cones to flavour gin.
stories.edibilityNote: Berry-like cones have been used by some Oregon distilleries to flavour gin.

stories.summary: A large evergreen conifer native to the west coast of North America, Sitka spruce is the largest spruce species and can exceed 100 metres in height. It has stiff, sharp blue-green needles and thin, scaly bark.
stories.edibilityNote: New branch tips are used to flavour spruce beer or boiled for syrup, while the needles can be made into aromatic tea.

stories.summary: A flowering perennial native to eastern Africa from Kenya to Mozambique, it has abundant spurred flowers and ripe seedpods that burst open. Its soft stems, leaves, flowers and roots are easily damaged.

A perennial flowering plant native to China, Japan and Korea, it spreads on thin red runners that form new plantlets. Its white flowers have two petals noticeably longer than the other three, and its foliage is occasionally eaten fresh or cooked in Japanese cuisine.
stories.edibilityNote: The foliage is occasionally used fresh or cooked in Japanese cuisine.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native from China through Southeast Asia to the Indian subcontinent, the orchid tree bears conspicuous pink or white flowers. Its mature pods twist into corkscrews and burst open with an audible clack. In South Asia, its edible buds are cooked in curries, stir-fried or pickled, while flowers and buds make Nepalese pickles.
stories.edibilityNote: Buds are cooked in curries, stir-fried or pickled across South Asia; flowers and buds are used in Nepalese pickles.

stories.summary: A perennial moss found on every continent, including Antarctica. Its grey-green leaves have reddish-brown tips and spread wider when moist; it commonly grows on dry, acidic, exposed ground.

A moss widely distributed through temperate and boreal parts of the Northern Hemisphere, common haircap moss also occurs in Mexico, several Pacific islands and Australia. Exceptionally tall for a moss, it usually grows in bogs, wet heathland and beside forest streams; its leaves curve and twist around the stem when conditions become too dry.

Moss with a worldwide distribution outside most tropical areas, growing on wet soil and rocks around streams, lakes, fens and marshes. Its glossy young leaves become dull red-brown with age, extend strongly down the stem and twist when dry.

A deciduous tropical tree native to parts of tropical Asia and Oceania, it bears red, five-petalled flowers in spring before new leaves appear. Its ripe seed capsules contain white cotton-like fibres, while the trunk bears spikes, especially when young.
stories.edibilityNote: Flowers are dried and cooked in Myanmar; dried flower cores flavour Thai soups and curry, and flower-bud calyxes were historically eaten in India.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to tropical Africa from Sudan to the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Mozambique, and to Saudi Arabia and Yemen. It is sometimes planted in butterfly gardens.

An epiphytic flowering plant native to the Philippines. It anchors in debris collected in tree forks and bears long clusters of pink, red or violet flowers with pink bracts, followed by fleshy violet berries.

A perennial evergreen native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico, it forms a crown of rigid, bayonet-like leaves above a conspicuous trunk. Native Americans ate its flowers and fruit raw or roasted and ground its black seeds into flour.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Americans ate the flowers and fruit raw or roasted and ground the black seeds into flour.

stories.summary: Grass native to temperate Europe, although its precise native range is unknown. Depending on conditions, it may be annual, biennial, or perennial; it has a round stem and spikelets tipped with a long bristle.

A herbaceous perennial native across temperate and Arctic regions of Europe, northwest Africa, Asia and the Americas, sea plantain forms a dense rosette of thick, fleshy leaves. Its leaves and seeds are eaten raw or cooked, and the seeds can be ground into flour.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and seeds are eaten raw or cooked; the seeds can also be ground into flour.

stories.summary: An annual flowering herb native to the Americas, garden cosmos has finely divided, threadlike foliage and conspicuous flower heads with pink, violet or white outer petals surrounding yellow centres. It is widely grown as an ornamental and may return by self-sowing.

A filamentous terrestrial green alga, Trentepohlia aurea has no native origin specified in the supplied information. It forms small, bushy tufts ranging from golden yellow to orange-brown and grows on surfaces including rocks, old walls, tree bark, rotting wood, mosses and wet soil.

A deciduous tree native to tropical and southern Asia. Its hard, smooth fruit has six vertical furrows and a sour, bitter, astringent taste; it is eaten raw or cooked and is often pickled in South Asia.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten raw or cooked and used in South Asian pickles, savoury dishes and candied sweets.

stories.summary: Flowering tree native to the Indian subcontinent and adjacent parts of Southeast Asia. It bears abundant hanging clusters of yellow flowers and long, pungent-smelling seed pods. In India, people sometimes eat the flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: In India, the flowers are sometimes eaten by people.

stories.summary: A fast-growing deciduous or semi-deciduous tree native from Assam and southern China through Malesia and Papuasia to Queensland. Its open clusters of pale-pink to crimson flowers have yellow stamens, while its fruit develops in long, cylindrical dark-brown pods.

Cherry tree thought to have originated on the Iranian Plateau or in Eastern Europe, although truly wild populations may no longer exist. Its acidic fruit has edible sour pulp, with dark-red Morello and lighter-red Amarelle as its two main cultivar groups.
stories.edibilityNote: The sour fruit pulp is edible; dried cherries are cooked in savoury dishes and desserts or made into fruit spreads.

stories.summary: An annual, downy herb found in southern Europe, southwestern Asia, North Africa and Macaronesia. It bears rounded or egg-shaped clusters of pink flowers and grows chiefly in sandy, temporarily flooded grassland depressions, sometimes on slightly salty or loamy soil.

Annual mercury is an annual herb native to the Middle East and Mediterranean region. Its branched, ridged stems release watery sap when broken, and its nearly hairless leaves grow in opposite pairs. Plants may be male, female or hermaphrodite, an unusually varied breeding system.
stories.edibilityNote: It is not known whether annual mercury is poisonous to humans; documented poisonings concern the related dog's mercury.

stories.summary: A bulb-forming perennial native to parts of Europe, North Africa and Asia. Its dense spikes carry dark blue flowers with white tips, sometimes topped by a cluster of paler, sterile flowers.

An annual flowering plant native to Europe, southwestern Asia, North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Korea and Japan. It has a sprawling habit, usually bold blue flowers and dull green, toothed leaves; its hairy fruit capsule has two parallel lobes.

Perennial flowering herb native to Europe. It resembles a small strawberry plant but produces no fleshy fruit; its matte, dark-green leaflets usually have a shorter central tooth than the adjacent teeth.

An evergreen perennial native to the eastern and central United States. It forms low mats of hairy, narrow leaves, covered in late spring and early summer by small flowers in shades including pink, white, blue and mauve.

A small herbaceous perennial endemic to South Africa’s western Cape region. It has grass-like leaves and spring flowers that are pink with yellow throats; outside its native range, it has naturalised widely and is considered an environmental weed in much of Australia.

Chilli pepper native to the Americas, with a possible centre of origin in the tropical northern Amazon. Its varieties have distinctive flavours and range from non-spicy to exceptionally hot. Fruits vary greatly in shape and colour, commonly ripening red, orange or yellow.
stories.edibilityNote: Used for millennia in Yucatán and Caribbean cooking, especially in stews, sauces and marinades for meat and chicken.

stories.summary: An endangered, fast-growing deciduous conifer whose remaining wild populations are confined to south-central China. Its bright-green opposite leaves turn reddish brown in autumn, and it can grow into a very tall tree despite being the shortest redwood.

An annual or short-lived perennial native to Florida, Mexico, the West Indies and tropical Central and South America, it grows low with translucent, succulent-like branching stems. Its tiny leaves occur in unequal pairs, and the male flowers explosively eject pollen.

An evergreen vine native to Mo'orea in French Polynesia. It climbs with aerial roots, and its heart-shaped juvenile leaves become irregularly divided when mature. It rarely flowers without artificial hormone treatment.
stories.edibilityNote: Consumption may cause burning or swelling around the mouth and other reactions because the plant contains calcium oxalate.

stories.summary: A perennial ornamental herb whose native range is unclear, Buddha’s hand taro is known only from cultivation and plants near homes or in disturbed places. It has broad, roughly heart-shaped leaves and rarely produces flowers or red berries.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is poisonous when eaten because it contains calcium oxalate crystals.

stories.summary: A perennial flowering plant native to Ecuador and southwestern Colombia, painter's-palette has a brightly coloured red or pink leaf surrounding a projecting white or yellow flower spike. It flowers throughout the year, and the whole plant is toxic if eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: The whole plant is toxic; ingestion can cause mouth and throat irritation, salivation, difficulty swallowing and vomiting.

stories.summary: Small creeping flowering plant native to Europe. It has square stems, opposite blunt-toothed leaves and tiny flowers surrounded by bright yellow-green leafy bracts, typically in damp, shady woodland or beside streams.

A small herb native to the British Isles, Europe, North Africa, Turkey and Iran, it may be annual, biennial or a short-lived perennial. It has mostly basal leaves with rounded leaflets, tiny white flowers and fruits that generally remain below the flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: In Manipur it is reportedly eaten as an aromatic herb and eromba garnish, but the source marks this claim as needing a citation.

stories.summary: A tufted sedge native across Europe and into parts of Asia as far east as Iran. Its flowering stems carry several dangling female spikes beneath one slender male spike, and it typically grows in deciduous woodland on heavy soils.
