Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ybwd3x accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

stories.summary: Flowering plant whose subspecies Nepeta tuberosa subsp. tuberosa is native to mainland Portugal. It belongs to the mint family.

A bushy evergreen shrub native to Iberia, Morocco and western Turkey. Its narrow aromatic grey-green leaves contrast with dense heads of small dark-purple flowers, topped by large purple bracts resembling butterfly petals.
A flowering plant whose subspecies Erophaca baetica subsp. baetica is native to mainland Portugal.

A flowering tree or shrub native to China and Japan, Japanese camellia grows naturally in forests. Its leathery dark-green leaves accompany rose or white wild flowers, while thousands of ornamental cultivars offer many flower colours and forms. Its processed leaves can be made into aromatic tea and contain caffeine and catechins.
stories.edibilityNote: Processed leaves are used to make aromatic tea and contain caffeine and catechins.

stories.summary: Evergreen shrub native to the Appalachians of eastern North America, from Alabama to coastal Nova Scotia. It keeps waxy, deep-green leaves for up to eight years and bears showy white, pink or pale-purple flowers, mainly in June. In the southern Appalachians it often dominates the forest understory, forming dense thickets called “laurel slicks” or “laurel hells.”
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves may be poisonous, but no human food use or ingestion context is given.

stories.summary: Herbaceous perennial native to the Mediterranean region, although its exact natural range is uncertain after 2,000 years of cultivation. Its fringed flowers have a spicy, clove-like fragrance; wild flowers are bright pinkish-purple, while cultivars come in many colours.
stories.edibilityNote: Its fragrance was historically used in vinegar, beer, wine, sauces and salads.

stories.summary: A large deciduous shrub or small tree native to the southern Balkan Peninsula, common lilac bears dense clusters of sweet-smelling flowers, usually lilac to mauve but occasionally white. Its flowers are edible and used to flavour honey, sugar, food and other sweets.
stories.edibilityNote: The flowers are used to flavour honey, sugar, food and other sweets.

stories.summary: A large evergreen flowering tree native to the southeastern United States coastal plain, from Virginia to central Florida and west to eastern Texas. It has stiff, dark-green leaves and large, waxy white flowers with a strong lemon-citronella fragrance.

A herbaceous perennial native across much of western, southern and central Europe, the Caucasus and eastward to central Asia, alpine forget-me-not has a highly restricted British presence. There it occurs at two sites: limestone grassland in the North Pennines and high ground around Ben Lawers.

A perennial orchid native to southwestern Eurasia, from western Europe through the Mediterranean to Iran. Its compact flower head has a distinctive pyramidal shape, with pink to purple, rarely white, flowers and a scent described as foxy.
A small palm native to North America. Its extracts are used medicinally, including traditional use for urinary and prostate conditions.

An agave found only in the Chihuahuan Desert, lechuguilla often spreads through underground offshoots into large colonies. It flowers once, then dies, and has tough, rigid leaves tipped with points sharp enough to penetrate clothing or leather.
stories.edibilityNote: In Mexico, salt- and mineral-rich water stored in flowering stalks is sold as a sports drink.

stories.summary: A palm native to the Philippines, the areca palm grows straight with numerous crowded leaflets. Its nuts are chewed with slaked lime and betel leaves for stimulant and narcotic effects, but they are addictive and linked directly to oral cancers.

A deciduous flowering shrub native to woodlands of the southeastern United States, oakleaf hydrangea has large lobed leaves with silvery-white undersides that turn red, bronze and purple in autumn. Its upright, cone-shaped flower clusters open white and age to pink or brown, depending on the cultivar or seedling.

A critically endangered conifer native to southern Brazil and also naturally found in northeastern Argentina, Paraguay and northern Uruguay. It has thick, triangular leaves with razor-sharp edges, and large cones containing many edible, nut-like seeds that are extensively harvested in southern Brazil.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds are edible, widely harvested in southern Brazil and eaten as a winter snack, including boiled.

stories.summary: An Australian rainforest tree naturally distributed from northeastern New South Wales to tropical Queensland. Its bright red flowers form circular, wheel-like clusters, while its boat-shaped fruits hold many thin seeds.

Perennial herb native to eastern Australia, with long, strap-like leaves arising from underground stems. Its leaf tip has three prominent points, with the side points as long as or longer than the middle one. Seeds may be ground into flour, while the flowers and leaf bases are also edible.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds may be ground into flour for Indigenous Australian damper; flowers and leaf bases are also eaten, with leaf bases chewed for water.

stories.summary: A woody climber native to Australia, Malesia and the southwestern Pacific region. Its juvenile and mature leaves differ, and it bears white or cream tubular flowers with purple markings followed by capsules containing winged seeds.

Fruit tree native to the eastern and central United States. Its deeply plated bark is distinctive, and its orange fruit is astringent when unripe but sweet when ripe; ripe fruit may be eaten raw, usually after softening, or cooked or dried.
stories.edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten raw, usually after softening, or cooked, dried, fermented or made into desserts, jam, molasses and candy.

stories.summary: Deciduous tree native to China, the Japanese persimmon has broad, stiff leaves and sweet, slightly tangy fruit. Astringent varieties are edible only when soft-ripe, while non-astringent varieties such as ‘Fuyu’ can be eaten firm.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten ripe or dried; astringent varieties require soft ripening, while non-astringent varieties may be eaten firm.

stories.summary: A rock-growing orchid endemic to eastern Australia. It usually grows on rocks, sometimes forming large colonies, and bears spikes of usually pink flowers from late winter to spring, though timing varies with climate.

A large plant widespread in eastern Australia, the Queensland grasstree can develop a tall, many-branched trunk and grey or bluish-green leaves. Ngunnawal people make a sweet drink by soaking its flower spike and eat the growing leaf-stem portion and white leaf bases.
stories.edibilityNote: Ngunnawal people soak the flower spike for a sweet drink and eat the growing leaf-stem portion and white leaf bases.

stories.summary: Shrub or tree endemic to eastern Australia, including Lord Howe Island. It has thin bark, usually white flowers borne singly on short side shoots, and fruit that can remain on the plant for a few years.

Palm tree endemic to the east coast of Queensland and New South Wales, Australia. Its single trunk has a swollen, regularly scarred base, while its long fronds often twist so their outer leaflets stand nearly vertical. Ripe fruits are bright red and contain one seed.

A large shrub or small tree native to the eastern coast of tropical South America, extending south to Uruguay and parts of Paraguay and Argentina. Its ribbed fruit changes from green through orange and scarlet to maroon; the edible fruit ranges from tart to sweet with cultivar and ripeness and is used mainly in jams and jellies.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten and used in jams and jellies; taste varies from tart to sweet with cultivar and ripeness.

stories.summary: A shrub native to eastern Asia—northeastern China, Japan, Korea and southeastern Siberia—the rugosa rose naturally grows along sandy coasts. It forms dense, prickly thickets and has deeply wrinkled leaves with scented flowers ranging from dark pink to white. Its hips are edible raw or prepared as jam, syrup or tea.
stories.edibilityNote: The hips can be eaten raw or made into jams, syrups or tea.

stories.summary: A deciduous succulent endemic to southern Madagascar, it grows as a spiny shrub or tree with thick, water-storing stems. Its leaves fall during the long dry season, and young plants begin as tangled stems before developing a strong central trunk.

A perennial herbaceous orchid widespread across central and southern Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. Its flower has a hairy, variably patterned petal resembling a bee’s abdomen; northern populations are almost exclusively self-pollinating, while a solitary bee pollinates it in the Mediterranean region.
stories.edibilityNote: Root tubers were ground into salep in the Ottoman Empire; salep remains used in traditional dishes in Turkey and across the Middle East.

stories.summary: A liverwort, it was typically absent from urban sites in one tropical Ecuador study despite occurring at a nearby pristine site. The study suggested sensitivity to human effects such as wastewater and heavy-metal pollution.

A sprawling annual weed whose native origin is not stated, red nightshade occurs in Europe, western Asia and northern Africa and is naturalized in Australia and North America. It is hairy, with white or purple-tinged flowers followed by dull red or orange-yellow berries, depending on the subspecies.

A medium-sized deciduous tree native across Europe and temperate Asia and to northern Morocco, silver birch is mainly mountainous in the southern parts of its range. It has white, peeling bark and slender, often drooping twigs, while its roughly triangular leaves turn yellow in autumn.
stories.edibilityNote: In spring, tapped sap may be drunk fresh, concentrated like maple syrup, or fermented into wine.

stories.summary: A flowering bromeliad indigenous to warmer parts of the Americas, from the southern United States to northern Argentina and Chile. It forms rounded clumps on trees, fences and wires, using hosts mainly for support rather than nourishment.
stories.edibilityNote: The Pima of Mexico occasionally eat its flowers for their high sugar content.

stories.summary: An Arctic–alpine fern native to Europe and parts of Asia. It produces separate sterile and fertile fronds and colonises acidic rocky slopes, often where snow remains late in the year.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Cryptogramma crispa
sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: An evergreen trailing rock-rose native to most of Europe. Its bright yellow, saucer-shaped flowers have touch-sensitive orange stamens, while garden varieties range from white to deep red. Individual blooms are short-lived, but flowers appear in abundance through summer.
Annual flowering herb native to Great Britain, Iceland, central Europe and Western Asia. It blooms in July and August and is a known host of flax rust.

A perennial flowering herb whose native origin is not specified, wild basil has square, upright, hairy stems and pink, violet or purple two-lipped flowers. Its leaves are used to flavour food and make herbal tea.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are used as an aromatic herb in food dishes and to make herbal tea.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree endemic to woodlands of the southeastern and south-central United States, winged elm grows slowly and tolerates many soils. Broad, thin corky wings develop along older branchlets, and the leaves turn bright yellow in autumn.

A large deciduous tree native to the Balkans, horse-chestnut has fallen-leaf scars shaped like horseshoes with seven “nails.” Its spring flowers are usually white with yellow-to-pink markings, followed by green spiky fruits containing glossy brown conkers.
stories.edibilityNote: Raw seeds, leaves, bark and flowers are toxic and should not be eaten; young, fresh seeds can cause sickness.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to the Americas east of the Rocky Mountains and south to Bolivia. It bears large clusters of white summer flowers and drooping clusters of dark purple-black fruit; only ripe berries cooked with their seeds removed are suitable for food.
stories.edibilityNote: Only ripe berries should be cooked and have their seeds removed; traditional jams, jellies and syrups use cooked, strained fruit.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial of unstated native origin, lady's bedstraw is widespread across most of Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia. In medieval Europe its dried plants stuffed mattresses and its flowers were used in cheese making; in Denmark, it is traditionally infused into spirits.
stories.edibilityNote: In Denmark it is traditionally infused into spirits; its flowers were used in medieval European cheese making.

stories.summary: Annual herb of unstated native origin, found on Mediterranean scrubland hills and beneath stonework or concrete structures. It has alternate leaves that may be divided two or more times.

Annual flowering plant native to North Africa, Europe, and parts of western and central Asia as far as the western Himalayas. Its pear-shaped fruits carry a small, toothed crown formed by the remains of the flower.

A perennial flowering herb native to Europe and Asia, greater knapweed bears purple, thistle-like flower heads crowned by ragged purple-pink outer parts. Its deeply divided leaves form a clump at the base, and its flowers attract bees and many butterflies.

A perennial flowering herb native across temperate Eurasia from Britain to Japan. Its violet-blue or purplish-blue bell-shaped flowers grow in tight clusters and bloom from June to September. Garden varieties also include white, pink and blue forms.

Epiphytic fern native to tropical southeastern Asia, eastern Australia, Hawaii, Polynesia, Christmas Island, India and eastern Africa. Its large, banana-like fronds form a nest that collects water and decaying plant matter. Sprouts are eaten in Taiwan, while young fronds are eaten in Polynesia, often cooked with coconut cream.
stories.edibilityNote: Sprouts are stir-fried or boiled in Taiwan; young fronds are eaten in Polynesia, often cooked with coconut cream.

stories.summary: A slow-growing tree fern native to Hawaii, hāpu‘u pulu produces fiddleheads that supply pulu, a material used as mulch or padding. Women also used pulu as a menstrual absorbent.

A tropical flowering tree native to tropical Asia and Australia. It has glossy leaves, bright pink or red flower clusters and bell-shaped fruit that ripens red, pink or white-streaked. The ripe fruit is eaten raw despite its bland flavor; flowers are eaten in Indonesian salads, and the skin is cooked into syrup in Guyana.
stories.edibilityNote: Ripe fruit is eaten raw; Indonesians eat the flowers in salads, and in Guyana the fruit skin is cooked into syrup.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to south Texas, Mexico, Belize, Venezuela and the Caribbean. It bears yellow flower heads throughout the year and commonly grows as a weed in lawns, roadsides and paths.

A tall perennial flowering plant native to North Africa, most of Europe and parts of Asia. Its robust stems and narrow leaves are densely hairy, while the large purple-pink flowers have four notched petals.

An evergreen shrub native to Mexico and naturalized in Florida. Its white flowers emerge from chains of red or salmon-pink bracts resembling shrimps, and its long blooming periods attract hummingbirds and butterflies.

A perennial yam vine native to Africa, Asia and northern Australia, air potato forms bulbils on its stems and potato-like tubers underground. Its twining stems always twist counterclockwise around supports.
stories.edibilityNote: Some varieties have edible tubers; boiling removes their bitterness. Tiwi people ritually cook and eat the tubers during the kulama ceremony.

stories.summary: A low, spreading deciduous shrub native to central and eastern Canada and the north-central and eastern United States, lowbush blueberry has glossy blue-green leaves that turn red in autumn. Its white or pink bell-shaped flowers produce small, sweet, dark blue to black berries.
stories.edibilityNote: Wild blueberries are used in Maine’s state dessert, blueberry pie.

stories.summary: A biennial flowering plant native to central and eastern North America. It has square, narrowly winged stems and fragrant pink, occasionally white, flowers with yellow markings that form a central star.

Perennial sunflower native to North America, including south-central Canada, the eastern and central United States, and northeastern Mexico. Its stems and leaves have stiff hairs, and it spreads through underground rhizomes in sunny open forests and forest edges.

An evergreen shrub native to southern Argentina and Chile and symbolic of Patagonia. It has shiny, box-like leaves, arching thorny branches and blue-black berries eaten fresh or made into jam and alcoholic drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: The blue-black berries are eaten fresh, made into jam and added to alcoholic drinks such as calafate beer.

stories.summary: A flowering plant primarily native from eastern Siberia to Korea and northern and central Japan.

A woodsorrel that likely originated in North America and is now found worldwide. Its clover-like leaves have three leaflets, and its small flowers have five yellow petals; it is often considered a weed.

An evergreen tree native to the Brazilian states of Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, Goiás and São Paulo. Its round, purplish-black fruit grows directly on the trunk and contains sweet white or pink flesh; it is eaten raw or made into preserves, juice and alcoholic drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten raw or made into jellies, jams, juice, wine, tarts and liqueurs; it has been cultivated in Brazil since pre-Columbian times.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native to the Appalachian, Ozark and Ouachita mountain regions of the eastern United States. Its large leaves cluster at branch tips like umbrellas, while its large, unpleasant-smelling spring flowers develop into red, cone-shaped fruits.

A shrub or occasional small tree native to eastern North America, eastern Mexico, the Bahamas and Cuba, groundsel tree often grows in salty or brackish wetlands. Female plants develop conspicuous snowy-white, cotton-like flower heads in autumn. Its seeds are toxic to humans.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds are toxic to humans.

stories.summary: An evergreen shrub or tree originating in Southeast Asia, rose-apple has glossy mature leaves and white or greenish-white flowers with many long stamens. Its ripe fruit has a strong floral scent, crisp watery flesh and usually one or two loose seeds; it is eaten raw, cooked in regional recipes or served with spiced sugar in Southeast Asia.
stories.edibilityNote: The ripe fruit is eaten raw or cooked in regional recipes and is often served with spiced sugar in Southeast Asia.

stories.summary: Non-stinging nettle-family plant that grows on walls and rubbish. Its pollen can cause allergies.
stories.edibilityNote: It was once used to make certain metheglins.

stories.summary: A very small fern native to Europe, East Asia and eastern North America. It grows exclusively on limestone and other calcium-rich rocks, with bluish-green, heavily divided fronds.

Herbaceous perennial native to Europe, from Spain north to Belgium and Poland and east to Ukraine. It has slender green to grey-green leaves and tight clusters of usually dark pink to purple flowers, which are occasionally white.

A creeping aloe native to South Africa’s Western Cape and adjacent parts of the Northern and Eastern Cape. It sprawls over rocky ground, while its leaf-bearing tips often turn upright; drought can redden and curl its fleshy leaves inward. Unlike most aloes, it flowers in summer.

Lily native across Eurasia, from Portugal through Europe and Asia to Mongolia. Its scented, backward-curving flowers are usually spotted pink-purple but can range from nearly white to nearly black, with numerous blooms on vigorous plants.

sources.title: Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental — Lilium martagon

stories.summary: A flowering perennial native to Europe, Africa and western Asia, with grey-green leaves and pale lavender or blue flowers from summer into autumn. In the European wild, it favours grassland on lime-rich soils.

A flowering plant of unspecified native origin, lesser skullcap has a southern temperate European distribution. It bears narrow, opposite leaves and small pinkish-purple flowers, and grows in wet heaths and open woodland on acidic soils.

Hairless flowering perennial native in southern Britain only to counties including Somerset, Dorset and Hampshire, but distributed more widely through Europe, western Asia and North Africa. Its egg-shaped root tubers sit away from the stem base, and its fruiting heads are distinctively flat-topped; unlike other water-dropworts, it can occupy dry lowland habitats within its natural range. In Turkey, locals reportedly eat the tubers roasted, cooked with yoghurt and bulgur, or pickled and cooked in winter.
stories.edibilityNote: In Turkey, tubers are reportedly eaten roasted, cooked with yoghurt and bulgur wheat, or pickled and cooked during winter.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to Europe from Britain to the Caucasus, zigzag clover resembles red clover but has narrower, unmarked leaflets. Its narrow stipules lack bristle points.

A perennial pea native to Europe and parts of Asia. It has dark root tubers and red flowers that become bluer with age. The tubers can be eaten raw but are better cooked like chestnuts; they were historically eaten in the Scottish Highlands during food shortages.
stories.edibilityNote: Tubers are edible raw but preferably cooked like chestnuts; they were historically eaten during Scottish Highland food shortages and used to suppress appetite.

stories.summary: A willow shrub distributed across much of Europe, eared willow is distinguished from the similar grey willow by reddish leaf stalks and young twigs. Kidney-shaped appendages persist along its shoots.

A palm tree endemic to New Zealand and the only palm native to its mainland. It has a smooth, bulging crownshaft, lilac-to-pink flowers and red ripe fruit; island forms vary, with the Chatham Islands form having larger fruit and hairier fronds.
stories.edibilityNote: Māori traditionally ate inner leaf bases and young flower clusters raw or cooked, rarely harvested palm heart, and ate unripe berries; ripe berries are inedible.

stories.summary: A long-lived tree native only to New Zealand, with stiff, needle-like leaves and bark that peels in papery flakes. Its rot-resistant wood has traditionally been prized by Māori for building large canoes.
stories.edibilityNote: The red fleshy part of the berry-like cones is documented as edible.

stories.summary: A rhizomatous herbaceous perennial native to North America from eastern Canada to northern Mexico, obedient plant bears dense spikes of tubular pink flowers resembling snapdragons. A flower pushed aside often stays in its new position.

A perennial herb native to parts of Eurasia. It bears numerous drooping, usually bright blue-violet flowers and can be extremely invasive in North America, spreading through abundant seed and underground rhizomes and tubers.
stories.edibilityNote: Historically grown for food; roots are eaten raw or cooked, while shoots and leaves are edible and basal leaves are often cooked.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial native to Europe, western Asia and northern Africa, it grows in meadows, fields and woodland borders. Wild plants usually have bluish-violet flowers with an arched upper lip, above a clump of ruffled, toothed leaves.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant was historically used as a flavouring for alcohol.

stories.summary: An herbaceous perennial native to eastern and central North America, sweet Joe-Pye-weed forms clumps of upright purple stems with rings of leaves. Its large, loose clusters of purplish flowers bloom from mid to late summer and attract many nectar-feeding insects.
A cactus native to southern Mexico, queen of the night opens its large, very fragrant flowers at night, and they wilt before dawn.
Perennial herb native to the Mediterranean region. It is usually densely covered with white hairs and has yellowish-white flowers and stem leaves that are often deeply divided into narrow lobes.

stories.summary: A tall herbaceous perennial native to Europe and parts of western Asia, white hellebore has pleated leaves and white flowers marked with green. Every part is poisonous, and mistaken identity with wild garlic or yellow gentian has caused poisonings.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; accidental consumption after confusion with wild garlic or yellow gentian has caused poisoning.

sources.attribution: Andre Carapeto % Ana Francisco, Paulo Pereira, Miguel Porto, felipe (2020). Lista Vermelha da Flora Vascular de Portugal Continental. Plazi.org taxonomic treatments database. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ge693f accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-12.

stories.summary: A perennial wild onion from mountainous Eurasia, including Europe, the Caucasus and the Himalayas. It has broad leaves, a sheathed bulb and whitish-green flowers; East Asian and Alaskan populations formerly included in this species are now often treated as Allium ochotense.
A herbaceous perennial native to western and central Europe, from the UK to Ukraine, Cheddar pink bears fragrant rose-pink flowers in May and June. It cannot tolerate wet winter soil.

Woody evergreen flowering subshrub reported as native to southern Europe from the western Mediterranean to southern Italy. Its small grey-green leaves are highly aromatic, and it is the main source of thyme used in cooking.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is the main source of the herb thyme, used as an ingredient in cooking.

stories.summary: A sedge native to the northern United States, Canada, Iceland, Europe, the Atlas Mountains, the Transcaucasus and parts of Siberia. It favors calcareous mires and damp woodland, particularly peaty soil flushed by water from nearby limestone.

Herbaceous perennial native to North American floodplains, stream banks and moist forests. It has deeply divided leaves and late-season flowers with greenish centres and pale-yellow rays, and can spread rampantly through underground stems.
stories.edibilityNote: Young wild leaves were traditionally gathered in early spring and eaten as cooked greens; raw use is suggested by some references.

stories.summary: Evergreen perennial native to Corsica and Sardinia. It has large, leathery leaves divided into three spiny-toothed leaflets and produces green, bowl-shaped flowers in late winter and early spring.

Evergreen conifer native to the northern temperate and boreal forests of Canada and the United States. Its narrow, conical young crown becomes column-shaped with age, and its thin bark flakes into small plates. New growth or tips are used in beer, gin, soda flavouring, candy, pickles and preserves.
stories.edibilityNote: New growth or tips are used in alcoholic drinks, flavoured soda, candy, pickles and preserves.

stories.summary: Large forest tree native primarily to the Appalachian belt, with scattered populations elsewhere in the southeastern United States and southern Ontario, the cucumber-tree is among the largest and cold-hardiest magnolias. Its small yellow-green flowers grow high in the tree, while cucumber-shaped green fruit ripens to a striking reddish orange and releases bright red seeds.

A deciduous tree native primarily to the Midwestern and Upper South regions of North America, it is distinguished from most oaks by shiny, laurel-shaped leaves with smooth margins. Its hard wood was historically important for making shingles.

A deciduous tree native to the eastern United States, commonly occurring in floodplains and swamps. Young bark peels in thin, curling salmon-pink to brown-grey layers, becoming darker, thicker and deeply furrowed with age. Unlike most birches, its fruit matures in late spring.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Americans used boiled sap as a maple-like sweetener and ate the inner bark as survival food.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to central and northern China, Japan and Korea. Its stems bear four corky wings, and it develops vivid red autumn foliage and brightly coloured fruit. All parts are toxic if eaten and cause severe discomfort.
stories.edibilityNote: All plant parts are toxic if eaten and cause severe discomfort.

stories.summary: Annual vine native to eastern North America. It trails in mats or climbs with tendrils, producing clusters of small, bristly fruits that each contain one seed and catch on animals for dispersal.
stories.edibilityNote: The foliage can be cooked and eaten as a green vegetable.

stories.summary: An herbaceous perennial native to parts of the eastern and central United States, fall phlox bears often strongly fragrant flowers from summer into autumn. Wild flowers are typically pink or purple and rarely white, arranged in branching clusters.

Herbaceous perennial native to eastern North America, where it grows in moist prairies and meadows. Its tall purple flower spikes resemble bottle brushes or feathers, and the flowers smell of vanilla when dried.

A red alga distributed across the Atlantic and Mediterranean. Its pink to dark-red body attaches to rock or other algae by creeping cylindrical filaments and develops flattened, irregularly branched upright axes; it commonly occupies dim, shallow rocky habitats year-round.

A bulb-forming flowering plant native to southern Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. Its spring leaves die away before a tall flower cluster appears in autumn, and all parts contain the toxic compound scilliroside.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts contain toxic scilliroside, and the plant has been used as a poison.

stories.summary: A mat-forming flowering perennial native along Atlantic and Baltic coasts of Europe and on several Atlantic islands. It has fleshy, wax-coated grey-green leaves and usually solitary white flowers with deeply notched petals and an inflated, bladder-like base. It grows mainly on stable coastal shingle, dunes and beach strandlines.

A flowering heath native in the British Isles only to Dorset, Devon, Cornwall and one County Galway location, it inhabits bogs and wet heaths there. It has glandular, hairy leaves and bright-pink flowers arranged in long clusters.

Deciduous shrub native to the Appalachian Mountains of the eastern United States, though it may be gone from Pennsylvania and Alabama. Its clustered, unscented flowers usually range from yellow through orange to red, sometimes with several colors on one plant.

A herbaceous perennial native to Europe, fragrant agrimony has yellow glands beneath its leaves that release a sweet aroma. Its brown, grooved fruits bear hooked bristles, some distinctively pointing back toward the stalk.
stories.edibilityNote: Herbal tea reports usually concern common agrimony, and it is unclear whether fragrant agrimony was distinguished.

stories.summary: A perennial flowering herb native to Europe and introduced in a small part of the north-eastern United States, saw-wort has spineless, hairless stems and reddish-purple, thistle-like flowerheads. Its leaves provided a yellow dye used until the 19th century.

An aquatic flowering plant with no stated native origin, found around European, Turkish and North African coasts. Its flowering stems rise above the water and carry small three-petalled flowers; a Newfoundland population was recently found and may have been introduced.

A biennial native to Europe, northern Africa and Asia, carline thistle grows in alkaline grasslands and dunes. Its tiny brown flowers have dry, spiky golden-brown surroundings, making the plant appear to be dying even when fully flowering.

An herbaceous perennial of unstated native origin, European goldenrod is widespread across much of Europe, North Africa and Asia. It flowers profusely in late summer, producing many small yellow flower heads at the tops of its stems.

A flowering perennial native to Western Europe, growing in wet, boggy moorlands. It bears spikes of bright yellow, star-like flowers and deep orange fruit; Shetland Islanders have used the fruit as a colourant replacing saffron.
A wildflower of unspecified native origin, marsh gentian grows in marshes and moorlands. It supports the Alcon blue butterfly and is the only plant on which that butterfly lays its eggs.

Flowering perennial native to Atlantic Europe from southwestern Sweden to southwestern Iberia, common sea-lavender grows in clumps in salt marshes and other coastal habitats. It is probably a group of closely related species.
A biennial or short-lived perennial herb native to Europe, Greenland and the Azores. It commonly trails along northern European coasts, with fleshy, finely divided leaves and daisy-like flower heads.

A liverwort with a Holarctic distribution across Eurasia and North America, it typically grows on tree bark and rocks where rainfall is adequate. Its rounded leaf tips have flat edges. It can remain dormant while dry for months or years and revive quickly when moisture returns.

A perennial orchid probably native to the Mediterranean. Its tiny white flowers, each marked with green, spiral around a slender stalk after summer; its leaf rosette appears around flowering and remains green through winter.

A cultivated autumn-flowering perennial probably originating in southern mainland Greece, it is unknown in the wild. Its sterile purple flowers bear three red or orange stigmas, which are used as the spice saffron, and the plant depends on vegetative propagation.
stories.edibilityNote: The flower stigmas are used as the culinary spice saffron.

stories.summary: A seagrass endemic to the Mediterranean Sea. It forms large underwater meadows of ribbon-like leaves, while its floating fruits are called “sea olives” and fibrous balls made from its foliage often wash ashore.

A green marine alga recorded from the Canary Islands to Ireland and elsewhere in Europe, its origin around Ireland may lie farther south. It forms a dark-green, velvety, spongy sphere and attaches to submerged rock by filaments.

A deciduous tree native to northern Europe and northern Asia, downy birch has dull grey-white bark and finely hairy shoots. Its inner bark was ground into bread during famines, while spring sap is drunk fresh or made into syrup, ale, wine and liqueurs.
stories.edibilityNote: Inner bark was used in traditional and famine breads; spring sap is consumed fresh or made into syrup, ale, wine and liqueurs.

stories.summary: Herbaceous perennial native to northeast Mexico and the south-central United States. Its mildly fragrant, canary-yellow, cup-shaped flowers open in the evening, close the next morning and last just one day; its seed pods have four wings.

An annual herb native to Southeast Asia and the Indian highlands, perilla has square hairy stems and a strong mint-like smell. Its leaves and seeds are eaten in several Asian cuisines, often fresh, pickled, ground or roasted, and toasted-seed oil is used for cooking; large amounts of seeds have caused anaphylaxis.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and seeds are eaten fresh, pickled, ground or roasted, and seed oil is used in cooking; large seed amounts have caused anaphylaxis.

stories.summary: An annual herb native to South Africa and Namibia. Its narrow leaves may be smooth-edged, toothed or deeply divided, while its white to yellowish ray flowers sometimes bear blue or purple markings.
A tuber-forming plant native to India. It grows mainly in seasonally dry tropical regions.

sources.title: Cyanotis tuberosa (Roxb.) Schult. & Schult.f. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

stories.summary: Slow-growing succulent perennial native to Arizona, New Mexico and northern Mexico. Its grey-green leaves retain impressions from earlier leaves and end in a contrasting dark spine. A mature plant produces one tall stalk of bright yellow flowers and then dies.

Aromatic perennial herb native to southern India. Its three-sided yellow-green pods contain black and brown seeds; the green pods are dried and the seeds used whole or ground in sweet and savoury Asian cooking.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds from dried green pods are used whole or ground in Indian and other Asian cooking.

stories.summary: Dwarf shrub native to Europe and northwestern Africa, including Madeira and the Azores. It is widely branched, with small triangular leaves that clasp the stem and pale pink or violet flowers.

Bulbous perennial flowering plant found in South Africa. Its white tubular buds have curved scarlet petal edges resembling candy canes. The flowers open in full sunlight but remain furled at other times.

An annual aquatic herb endemic to wetlands of South Africa’s Western Cape. It produces white or pink cup-shaped flowers, while its form varies between short, reddish tufts on moist soil and longer buoyant branches when submerged.

An annual flowering plant endemic to South Africa, it grows mainly on sandy coastal slopes and flats in the Northern and Western Cape. Its slightly fleshy, branched stems carry hairy leaves and orange, yellow or cream flower heads, which may appear in large numbers during spring.

A hairy perennial shrub from the fynbos of the Cape Peninsula and nearby southwestern Cape, wild mallow grows upright from an underground rootstock and becomes woody at the base. Its crowded, sometimes hood-shaped leaves are fragrant when rubbed, and its flowers range from white to purplish red.

Low-growing perennial herb native to southern Africa, from Angola, Zambia and Mozambique southward to South Africa. Its yellow or white flowers appear soon after the first rains and open only in strong sunlight; damaged leaves release a milky sap.

A parasitic mistletoe indigenous to South Africa, with a range extending north to Namibia, Cape mistletoe has jointed stems and tiny scale-like leaves. Its yellowish-green flowers produce translucent pale berries, and male and female flowers occur on separate plants.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is poisonous, though it is traditionally boiled as a medicinal tea to soothe asthma.

stories.summary: Herbaceous perennial occurring across most of Europe, North Africa and western Asia to Kashmir, and also in the United States and Canada; its native range is not identified. Its erect stems are densely hairy, with tiny pale pink or purple flowers and wind-carried seeds, and it grows in very moist to wet places.

An erect, branching herb native to Eurasia and northern Africa, narrow-leaved lupine has slender leaflets and flowers ranging from blue and violet to pink or white. Its seeds have served as food for over 6,000 years, but alkaloid levels vary by variety and can be poisonous in high amounts; low-alkaloid “sweet” cultivars were bred for food.
stories.edibilityNote: The edible seeds have been cultivated as food for over 6,000 years; low-alkaloid varieties are used because high alkaloid levels can be poisonous.

stories.summary: A flowering tree found along tropical coasts and rivers across parts of the Old and New Worlds. It has spiny bark, light orange flowers and buoyant seeds that can disperse across oceans. Its buds and leaves are eaten as vegetables, including leaves in Thai miang kham, although its alkaloids are poisonous in larger amounts.
stories.edibilityNote: Buds and leaves are eaten as vegetables; in Thailand, leaves are often used in miang kham.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native to South Africa. It can remain leafless for four or five months; dense clusters of scarlet flowers appear before the spring leaves and attract many birds and insects. Hooked prickles occur on the trunk, branches, leaf stalks and central leaf veins.

A large deciduous maple native to Central Europe and Western Asia, the sycamore maple has a broad, rounded crown, bark that flakes into irregular patches with age, and paired winged seeds that twirl as they fall. Its spring sap has been tapped for a drink and used to make sugar, syrup or beer.
stories.edibilityNote: Spring sap has been tapped for a drink and used to make sugar, syrup or beer.

stories.summary: Deciduous hardwood tree native to central and eastern China. It grows extremely quickly, disperses seeds readily, and is invasive in parts of North America. Large, fragrant violet-blue flowers appear before the leaves in early spring.

A deciduous pear tree native to mainland China, Japan, Korea and Taiwan, Callery pear produces abundant white flowers in early spring. Its tiny, hard fruits soften after frost. The fully softened pulp is palatable to people, though the fruits contain abundant cyanide-laced seeds.
stories.edibilityNote: Fully softened fruit pulp is palatable to humans; the fruits contain abundant cyanide-laced seeds.

stories.summary: A semi-evergreen or deciduous shrub native to central and southern Europe, North Africa and southwestern Asia, common privet has creamy-white summer flowers with a strong scent many people find unpleasant. Its glossy black berries are poisonous to humans but eaten by thrushes.
stories.edibilityNote: The glossy black berries are poisonous to humans.

stories.summary: A short-lived herbaceous perennial native to eastern and central Canada and the United States, it blooms from August to October. Its blue, violet or occasionally white flowers use three fused lower petals as a landing platform for bumblebees, which trigger contact with the flower's stigma.

A cactus that grows on other plants, native to Central and South America, the Caribbean and Florida, mistletoe cactus also occurs naturally in tropical Africa and Sri Lanka—the only cactus species found naturally outside the Americas. It is highly variable, with numerous subspecies.

A climbing or trailing vine indigenous to North America, it is long-lived and can reach the canopy of tall trees. Its juicy blue-black grapes are edible but usually sour and herbaceous, and are sometimes made into homemade jelly, jam and wine.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeded, juicy grapes are edible but usually sour and herbaceous; they are sometimes used for homemade jellies, jams and wine.

stories.summary: Cactus native to Mexico and the United States, with populations primarily in Texas. It typically grows in relatively moist habitats with deeper soils.

A tall perennial flowering plant native to the southeastern United States, frostweed bears white flower heads from late summer through fall. In winter, water exuded from the stem bases can freeze into ribbon-like ice structures.

A water moss of unstated native origin, it grows on shady, moist ground, walls and rocks, including recently burned places. In an artificially lit cave without natural light, it developed longer spaces between leaves and longer, narrower leaves.
Small flowering shrub native to the southeastern United States, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It grows in dry woods on acidic soil and bears yellow flowers with four petals.

A perennial shrub native to the southeastern United States from Texas to Florida. Its orange-yellow, sometimes red-lined flowers are followed by four-winged pods whose loose peas rattle inside; the seeds are poisonous.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds are poisonous and contain the toxin sesbanimide.

stories.summary: Flowering plant native to South Africa’s Western Cape and Northern Cape provinces. Its flowers range from yellow to reddish orange, often with brown or black patches at the petal bases, while its narrow leaves may be divided or simple.

An evergreen coniferous shrub or small tree native to western North America. Its dark-blue, wax-coated, berry-like cones usually hold one seed, while its peeling gray-brown bark reveals orange-brown beneath. Historically, Navajo people ate the ripe cones in fall or winter.
stories.edibilityNote: Historically, Navajo people ate the ripened cones in fall or winter.

stories.summary: Moss native to Europe and North America. It forms tight, smooth mats that are usually pale or white-green with hints of pink.

A succulent native to South Africa and Namibia. Tiny light-green leaves densely surround thin stems, giving them a square shape, while the plant forms an intricate bush with very small yellow-green flowers.

A hairy annual grown for large, showy daisy-like flower heads, native to Namibia and South Africa. Its lobed leaves form basal rosettes and also grow along the stems, while cultivated forms have varied petal colours and dark centres.

An annual flowering plant native to Namibia and South Africa’s Western and Northern Cape provinces, yellow gazania bears yellow flowers. Its slender, smooth flower-head coverings have a flat, often collar-like base, while the toothed leaves are woolly underneath.
Annual flowering plant native to south-central North America, including Coahuila in Mexico. It bears pink to white flower heads in late summer and autumn, when its narrow leaves are often wilted.

Herbaceous perennial native to subtropical and tropical conifer forests in central and eastern Mexico. Its usually white flowers emerge from coloured bracts, forming prominent, arching, velvety blue or purple flower clusters. The soft green leaves have whitish, hairy undersides.
Evergreen climber native to Central America and the Caribbean. It has glossy, heart-shaped leaves and rarely produces white flowers when mature.
stories.edibilityNote: The plant is toxic under certain conditions; its parts contain varying concentrations of calcium oxalate crystals and may be harmful if ingested.

stories.summary: Small annual native to parts of temperate North America, from eastern Canada to the southwestern United States. Grey-green leaves give way to terminal whorls edged in broad white bands, which combine with white flowers to create a snow-covered appearance.

A small to medium-sized tree native to New Caledonia, Papua New Guinea and coastal eastern Australia, it often grows in swamps, floodplains and beside waterways. Its trunk has thick, peeling papery bark, while cream or white bottlebrush-like flowers appear from late spring to autumn.
stories.edibilityNote: Traditionally, nectar was washed into water and consumed as a beverage; its flowers also yield a strongly flavoured honey.

stories.summary: Perennial bunchgrass native to the tallgrass and mixed-grass prairies of central North America, from Texas to southern Canada. It forms a mound of leaves beneath airy, branched flower clusters whose small spikelets each hold one fertile floret.

Large conifer endemic to Taiwan’s central mountains. It is slow-growing and long-lived, with red-brown, stringy bark and foliage arranged in flat sprays. Its strongly scented, decay-resistant wood is highly valued, while habitat loss and excessive cutting threaten the species.

A tree native to Florida, the northern and western Caribbean, southern Mexico and Central America south to Panama. It usually begins life in another tree’s canopy, then sends roots to the ground and gradually encircles its host before becoming free-standing.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit was eaten by Native Americans and early Florida settlers and is still occasionally eaten as backyard fruit.

stories.summary: Flowering shrub native to the American South, Mexico, Central America and South America. Its flowers never open fully and attract butterflies and hummingbirds; in Texas it commonly grows beneath taller vegetation.

A cool-season annual plant native to Guatemala, Belize and adjacent parts of Mexico, bluemink has dense clusters of fluffy, threadlike flowers, usually blue but sometimes white, pink or purple. It attracts butterflies and can become invasive outside its native range.

A perennial carnivorous plant native to almost every European country, as well as Russia, Canada and the United States, common butterwort grows in damp habitats such as bogs and fens. Its sticky, gland-covered leaves trap and digest insects, while its funnel-shaped flowers are purple and occasionally white.
Small carnivorous butterwort growing wild from Atlantic western Europe to Morocco. It has pale pink, yellow-centred flowers and may live as a perennial or die after one growing season.
A tropical annual herb apparently native to Asia, lilac tasselflower has branching stems and several pink or purplish flower heads. Its leaves sometimes turn purplish with age.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves and young shoots are eaten raw or cooked, mainly before flowering, although the plant contains liver-toxic alkaloids; young leaves are foods in Java and Puerto Rico.

stories.summary: A rainforest strangler fig endemic to Australia, it occurs in two separate populations in Queensland and northeastern New South Wales. Its paired fruits turn purplish-brown to black and have a nipple-like tip.

A large red-oak tree found across parts of the southern United States, with scattered populations reaching New Jersey, Texas and Oklahoma. Its grey bark has narrow, scaly ridges, while its shiny leaves have deep, often unevenly arranged lobes.

A bamboo endemic to the south-central and southeastern United States. Its hollow stems rise from thick underground stems to form colonies called canebrakes, once extensive but now endangered ecosystems. Indigenous people historically used it as a vegetable as well as for construction and crafts.
stories.edibilityNote: Indigenous people of the southeastern United States historically used river cane as a vegetable and food.

stories.summary: A large tree abundant in northern and central inland Portugal and long known in the Iberian Peninsula. Its chestnuts were a major Portuguese staple until the 17th century and are still commonly eaten roasted or boiled in autumn. Its high-quality wood has been used for construction, furniture and interior decoration.
stories.edibilityNote: Chestnuts were historically a Portuguese staple and are now commonly eaten roasted or boiled in autumn.

stories.summary: Perennial flowering herb native to the southwestern United States and northwestern Mexico. Its golden-yellow flowers have long backward-pointing spurs, and it grows in moist mountain habitats.

Long-lived coniferous tree native to eastern North America, from Nova Scotia and southeastern Ontario south through the Appalachians to western North Carolina and eastern Tennessee. It has a narrow conical crown, sharp four-sided yellow-green needles and hanging glossy red-brown cones, and young trees tolerate deep shade.
stories.edibilityNote: Leafy twigs are boiled with sugar and flavoring to make spruce beer or spruce pudding.

stories.summary: Wildflower native to the New World, occurring widely in Mexico and parts of the southwestern United States. It resembles a dandelion but has white-to-pink flowers, with reports that white blooms become pinkish as they age. Injured parts release white latex, and its stems bear a few leaves.
A small tree endemic to south-western Western Australia, it has rough, fibrous bark and bright red, pink or orange flowers. Its buds grow in groups of seven and develop into woody, urn-shaped fruit.

A deciduous flowering shrub native and endemic to Japan, mophead hydrangea bears large pink or blue flower heads in summer and autumn. Wild plants have flat flower heads with small fertile flowers ringed by a few large sterile ones, while cultivated mopheads usually form rounded heads dominated by large sterile flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: Amacha is a Japanese beverage made from fermented leaves of H. macrophylla var. thunbergii.

stories.summary: A large deciduous tree endemic to tropical and subtropical eastern Australia. When leafless, it can be covered in bright scarlet, bell-shaped flowers; its pods contain yellow seeds surrounded by hairs that irritate on contact. Indigenous Australians ate Brachychiton seeds raw or roasted after removing these hairs, and also ate young-tree roots.
stories.edibilityNote: Indigenous Australians ate Brachychiton seeds raw or roasted after removing irritating pod hairs; young-tree roots were also eaten.

stories.summary: A very large rainforest fern native to Southeast Asia and Oceania. Its arching, glossy fronds are believed to be the longest of any fern. Its starchy rhizomes are eaten only after lengthy processing to remove toxins, and Indigenous Australians historically ate the pith.
stories.edibilityNote: Starchy rhizomes require lengthy processing to remove toxins; Indigenous Australians historically ate the pith.

stories.summary: A small tree endemic to south-eastern Australia, the drooping she-oak has long, hanging branchlets with leaves reduced to small scales. Its barrel-shaped mature cones contain dark brown, winged seeds, and it can flower throughout the year.
stories.edibilityNote: An 1889 account says bushmen chewed the foliage to relieve severe thirst, while children chewed the young cones, called “oak apples.”

stories.summary: Clump-forming perennial herb native to China’s Shanxi Province. It has flat leaves with a garlic-like flavour and round clusters of white flowers. The leaves, stalks and unopened flower buds are used in cooking, including as flavouring and in stir-fries and dumplings.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, stalks and unopened flower buds are eaten; leaves may also be blanched, and flowers are fermented into sauce.

stories.summary: A small, variable, compact succulent widely distributed across northern South Africa, Namibia, Zambia, Angola, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. It grows in dry thickets and sometimes marshy riverside meadows, freely producing offshoots that form dense groups.
stories.edibilityNote: Along Angola’s Kunene River, people prepare cakes from the pressed and boiled flowers.

sources.title: Aloe zebrina | PlantZAfrica
sources.attribution: PlantZAfrica, South African National Biodiversity Institute

stories.summary: A large shrub endemic to New South Wales, Australia. Several stems rise from a pronounced woody base, and striking red spring flowerheads contain hundreds of individual flowers visited by birds, insects and eastern pygmy possums.

A short bulbous perennial native to Portugal, Spain, Sardinia, Sicily, Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia. Its narrow leaves usually appear after the late-summer or autumn flowers, which are white with pinkish bases, or less commonly entirely pink.

A weeping subshrub native to Mexico and Guatemala. Its bright-green arching stems form a fountain-like mound and bear profuse small red flowers; in tropical and subtropical climates it can bloom year-round.

Climbing flowering plant native to humid tropical forests in southern Mexico, Costa Rica, Guatemala and Panama. Its glossy, heart-shaped leaves develop deep divisions and large natural holes as the plant ages. The ripe fruit is sweet-scented and edible, but unripe fruit can irritate the mouth and throat.
stories.edibilityNote: Only ripe fruit is edible; unripe fruit can irritate the mouth and throat because it contains calcium oxalate crystals.

stories.summary: An open-clumping bamboo native to Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia and southern China, it commonly has lemon-yellow stems striped with green. Flowering is uncommon and fruit is rare. Its young shoots are eaten cooked or pickled across Asia; they contain a highly toxic compound that readily breaks down in boiling water.
stories.edibilityNote: Young shoots are eaten cooked or pickled across Asia; their highly toxic taxiphyllin readily degrades in boiling water.

stories.summary: A perennial clonal moss widespread in Northern Hemisphere boreal forests, it forms feathery, step-like fronds. A new level grows each year, so the steps can be counted to estimate its age.
Summer-blooming annual found in western North America from Nebraska and Colorado to Arizona and Mexico. Among the Hopi of Arizona, it was eaten boiled with green corn.
stories.edibilityNote: The Hopi of Arizona historically ate the plant boiled with green corn.

stories.summary: A moss widely distributed in eastern North America and Europe, with no native origin specified. It inhabits Northern Hemisphere temperate forests, and its structure can absorb metal ions.
A fern native only to Hawaii, resembling a small tree fern with a short trunk. Its young fronds are often reddish, and it grows on lava flows, in open areas and in wet forests.
stories.edibilityNote: Pith and young fronds are eaten roasted or steamed.

stories.summary: Flowering shrub originating in Australia and now widely distributed across warm regions worldwide. It has tough, variable leaves that secrete resin and red capsules that ripen brown, each with two to four wings.
stories.edibilityNote: Australians formerly used the plant instead of hops in beer brewing.

stories.summary: A small evergreen tree native to Sri Lanka, Ceylon cinnamon has inner bark historically used as the spice cinnamon. It also bears distinctly scented greenish flowers and purple fruit containing one seed.
stories.edibilityNote: The inner bark is historically used as cinnamon spice and sold dried in sticks or ground into powder.

stories.summary: Pear tree native to southern China and northern Indochina. Its large, fragrant edible fruit has a crisp, grainy, juicy texture and is commonly served raw and peeled.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is commonly eaten raw and peeled; ground pears also sweeten sauces and meat marinades.

stories.summary: A deciduous tree native to Japan and Korea, Japanese chestnut produces spiny cases containing several brown nuts in autumn. Its sweet nuts are edible and heavily produced, making the tree important in Japan and Korea; selected cultivars have especially large nuts.
stories.edibilityNote: Sweet edible nuts are heavily produced in Japan and Korea; some cultivars were selected for larger nuts.

stories.summary: A wild chili pepper native to Mexico and Central and South America. Its small, upright, pungent berries usually mature from pale yellow to bright red; some cultivars supply sauces, condiments and cooked dishes, and the Philippine cultivar's leaves are eaten as a vegetable.
stories.edibilityNote: Cultivar fruits are used in sauces, condiments and dishes; leaves of the Philippine cultivar are eaten as a vegetable.

stories.summary: A tree native to Central America and the Caribbean, allspice has smooth grey bark, leathery leaves and berry-like fruits. Its dried fruits are used as a spice, with a flavour recalling cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves; the two seeds inside are prepared for seasoning preserves, meat and shellfish.
stories.edibilityNote: Dried fruits are used as a condiment; prepared seeds season preserves, meat and shellfish, while ground spice flavours baked goods, soups and sauces.

stories.summary: A thorny understorey shrub or small tree native to southeastern Queensland and northeastern New South Wales, Australia, the finger lime has aromatic leaves and cylindrical, slightly curved fruits. Its edible fruits contain tangy, pearl-like juice vesicles used fresh or in recipes; they are also made into marmalade and pickles, while dried peel is used as a spice.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits are eaten fresh or used in recipes, marmalade and pickles; dried peel is used as a spice.

stories.summary: An annual flowering plant native to western Asia and eastern Europe, specifically from the Levant, Cyprus, Turkey, Iran and Iraq to Bulgaria and Romania. Its delicate pale blue-and-white flowers produce inflated capsules containing numerous seeds, which are widely used as a spice.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds are used as a spice, including ground into Palestinian qizha paste or dry-roasted to season many foods.

stories.summary: Climbing legume of Andean and Mesoamerican origin. It bears pale flowers and strongly curved pods containing seeds valued as food.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds are valued as food.

stories.summary: A herbaceous annual native to the Americas, the common bean may grow as a climbing vine or, among many cultivars, a bush. Its beans and unripe green pods are eaten, but raw dry beans contain a toxin that can be deactivated by boiling them for 30 minutes.
stories.edibilityNote: Beans and unripe green pods are food; leaves are occasional vegetables. Raw dry beans require 30 minutes’ boiling to deactivate phytohaemagglutinin.

stories.summary: A perennial climbing legume originating in the mountains of Central America. Most varieties have red flowers and multicoloured seeds, although some are white. Its seeds, young pods and, in Mesoamerica, starchy roots are eaten; the beans contain a toxic protein and must be cooked thoroughly.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten fresh or dried, young pods whole, and roots in Mesoamerica; beans must be cooked thoroughly because they contain a toxic protein.

stories.summary: A cultivated squash originating in South America, particularly northern Argentina near the Andes or in some Andean valleys. Its many forms include all giant pumpkins, while edible cultivars may be roasted, baked or mashed into soup.
stories.edibilityNote: Cultivars are roasted, baked or mashed into soup; the skin, flesh and seeds of JAP/Kent pumpkin are all edible.

stories.summary: A squash plant originating in the tropical Americas. Its flesh, flowers, greens and seeds are eaten, and its cultivars generally tolerate hot, humid weather better than squash from other domesticated species.
stories.edibilityNote: Cultivated flesh, flowers, greens and seeds are eaten; some cultivars are called squash or pumpkin.

stories.summary: An annual, erect or climbing legume of uncertain origin; West Africa is its centre of cultivated diversity, while its domestication remains debated. It has smooth cylindrical pods containing many seeds, whose colours and pod lengths vary among cultivated forms. Edible-seeded varieties are grown for food, including mature or green beans in northeastern Brazil and grain for human consumption in Portugal.
stories.edibilityNote: Cultivated varieties have edible seeds; beans are eaten mature or green in Brazil, while Portugal grows the grain for human consumption.

stories.summary: Large tree native to coastal New Zealand. It is widely planted for ornament and shelter in temperate coastal areas, but can occasionally become invasive, including around the Cape in South Africa and in the Azores.
Fern endemic to New Zealand, with edible fronds eaten as a vegetable. It produces small bulbils on top of its fronds that fall off and grow into new ferns in moist soil.
stories.edibilityNote: The fronds are eaten as a vegetable.

stories.summary: An onion relative native to southern Europe, southwestern Asia and North Africa, wild leek produces a round flower stalk topped by many white, pink or red flowers. Cultivated forms include leek, elephant garlic, pearl onion, kurrat and Persian leek; kurrat and Persian leek leaves are eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Cultivated forms are vegetables; kurrat is grown mainly for edible leaves, while Persian leek leaves are eaten raw alone or with other foods.

stories.summary: A flowering plant native to North America, Jerusalem artichoke has rough, toothed leaves and golden-yellow flowers. It is cultivated for its edible tubers, which store inulin rather than starch and have been grown by Indigenous American peoples since before Europeans arrived.
stories.edibilityNote: Its edible tubers were cultivated by Indigenous American peoples before European arrival; cooking breaks their stored inulin down into fructose.

stories.summary: A deciduous hazel shrub native to southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia, from the Balkans to Ordu in Turkey, the filbert has pale yellow male flowers and tiny bright red female flowers in late winter. Its edible nuts grow in small clusters and are fully enclosed by tubular husks.
stories.edibilityNote: The nuts are edible and are sometimes orchard-grown or used in mixed-nut products in the United States.

stories.summary: A giant timber bamboo native to China and Taiwan and naturalized elsewhere, including Japan. It spreads through underground rhizomes and produces exceptionally fast-growing canes. Its shoots are edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The shoots are edible.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub or small tree native to southern Europe and western Asia, tanner's sumac bears sour fruit. The dried, crushed fruit is widely used as a Middle Eastern spice, while immature fruits and seeds are also eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Dried, crushed fruit is used as a spice; immature fruits and seeds are eaten, and Romans used mature fruit in vinaigrettes.

stories.summary: Evergreen tree native to South China and northeast Vietnam. Its star-shaped fruits, harvested just before ripening, are used as an anise-flavoured spice.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits harvested just before ripening are used as a spice in foods and drinks.

stories.summary: An evergreen shrub from East Asia, although its exact natural range is unknown and debated. Its leaves, buds and stems are harvested to make differently processed teas, while its seeds can yield a sweetish seasoning and cooking oil.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves, buds and stems make tea; pressed seeds yield a sweetish seasoning and cooking oil distinct from tea tree oil.

stories.summary: A moss occurring worldwide, though closely related plants may replace it in tropical latitudes. It forms dense tufts or cushions, with leaves that spread when moist and twist when dry, and readily colonizes polluted or recently disturbed ground.

Evergreen shrub native to Texas and the northern Mexican states of Coahuila, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas. It grows in rocky, limestone-rich soils and produces abundant purple, bell- or funnel-shaped flowers.
A moss native to most of the Northern Hemisphere and Oceania. It forms rounded clumps or mats on soil in dry to moist forests and is especially recognizable by leaves that curve strongly to one side.

A perennial bulb native to the Mediterranean region from Greece to Portugal, as well as Morocco and Algeria, it bears bunches of strongly fragrant white flowers. It is often grown indoors and forced to bloom at Christmas without chilling.
Parasitic tree or shrub native to Western Australia. It has rough grey-brown bark and parasitic roots, and bears yellow-orange flowers mainly from October to January.

An evergreen clumping plant native to Southwest Australia, the tall kangaroo paw has long, strap-like leaves growing from an underground rhizome. In the region’s summer, it may produce more than 350 flowers on tall stems; they are often yellow and green but can also be red, pink, orange or brown.

A grass-like evergreen perennial native to the southern coast of Western Australia. Its flat green-grey leaves accompany dense heads of velvety tubular flowers in shades of red, purple and yellow during spring and early summer.

A strappy perennial herb found in southeastern Australia, including Tasmania, it grows in shady parts of wet forests. Blue spring and summer flowers are followed by violet fruits that are toxic and should not be eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits are toxic to an unknown degree, cause an irritating mouth tingling, and should not be eaten.

stories.summary: A flax lily native to Hawaii and New Caledonia. Its blue to purple flowers have orange anthers and are described as sweet-scented. Hawaiians historically used its berries for blue dye and its leaves for thatching house walls.
Tropical pitcher plant native only to the Philippines. It is carnivorous, attracting insects with nectar before they drown in its pitchers and are digested, and it varies greatly in colour and form.

A perennial insect-eating plant endemic to the Iberian Peninsula and northern Morocco. Unlike many carnivorous plants, it inhabits dry sites, often in acidic scrub, woodland clearings and isolated populations. In mainland Portugal it is classified as Vulnerable, with an estimated national population below 2,500.

stories.summary: A moss common in urban environments worldwide, it has a distinctive silvery-white sheen when dry. It forms dense upright clumps and can survive total drying, with dried shoots documented surviving brief extreme heat.

A deciduous shrub or small tree native to Mexico, Central America, Colombia and Venezuela, it has a thick succulent trunk and blunt, brittle branches. Its strongly fragrant pink, white or yellow flowers appear at branch tips, while broken branches release white latex that can irritate skin and mucous membranes.
stories.edibilityNote: Despite a general poison warning, flowers are reported boiled in water or juice or made into salad for traditional therapeutic uses.

stories.summary: A palm native to the southeastern United States Coastal Plain, Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula and the West Indies. It has a rounded crown of fan-like leaves, black single-seeded fruit and strong tolerance of coastal conditions. Its terminal bud is eaten as heart of palm, but harvesting it kills the tree; the raw fruit and ground seeds are also food.
stories.edibilityNote: The terminal bud is eaten as heart of palm, historically by Native Americans, but harvesting kills the palm; fruit is eaten raw and seeds ground into flour.

stories.summary: A moss found worldwide, commonly growing on urban concrete, brick walls, soil, rocks and trees. It forms low grey-green cushions and is recognizable by its hair-pointed leaves and upright cylindrical capsules.

Moss with an almost worldwide distribution, growing on lime-free or lime-poor silicate rocks in sunny, dry, warm sites. It forms low, grey-green cushions that break apart easily, and its upper leaves end in long, toothed, glass-like tips.

A large, vigorous pitcher plant native to Peninsular Malaysia and southernmost Thailand. It usually grows on the ground in wet mountain forests but can also grow on other plants. Its pitchers vary from green and yellow to orange and red, with usually speckled interiors.

An evergreen flowering plant of unknown original range, ti is believed native from Bangladesh through Southeast Asia, southern China and Taiwan to New Guinea and northern Australia. Its palm-like form carries fan-like clusters of green, red or variegated leaves. Roots and young leaves can be cooked as survival food, while Polynesian green forms supply processed sweet rhizomes and Hawaiian roots can be fermented and distilled.
stories.edibilityNote: Roots and young leaves are cooked as survival food; Polynesian green forms yield processed sweet rhizomes, and Hawaiian fermented roots are distilled into alcohol.

stories.summary: Leafy moss with no explicitly stated native origin, found in temperate North America and oceanic Europe east to Asia Minor. Its glossy whitish-green shoots look flattened and wormlike, with distinctly rippled leaves, and it rarely produces capsules.

sources.attribution: GBIF Secretariat (2023). GBIF Backbone Taxonomy. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/39omei accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.

stories.summary: A calcareous red seaweed found on rocky shores, with no native origin specified. Calcium carbonate in its tissues gives it a pink colour with white patches, especially at the growing tips, and its dense tufts shelter small animals.

A tropical, spiny evergreen shrub or small tree believed native to South Asia, southern China, Southeast Asia, and Central and West Africa. Its drooping branches may bear straight or hooked thorns, although some varieties are thornless. The fruit ripens from light green to reddish brown and is eaten raw, cooked, candied, dried, made into drinks or preserves, depending on ripeness and location.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten raw or prepared in several ways; seed kernels are famine food, and Indonesian leaves are used for an infusion.

stories.summary: A moss native to Europe, the Caucasus, Turkey, China, the Faeroe Islands and western North America. Shining hookeria forms creeping mats and looks transparent or glass-like when wet. Its broad leaves unusually lack a central rib, and the pale green plant becomes somewhat twisted when dry.

A tropical grass native to South Asia and Maritime Southeast Asia, now naturalised widely in the tropics and subtropics. Its fragrant leaves are traditionally used in cooking and can be dried for a mildly sweet, lemon-flavoured tea. It can grow in warmer temperate regions but is not frost-hardy.
stories.edibilityNote: Fragrant leaves are used in cooking; dried leaves are brewed alone or added to other teas for lemon-like flavour.

stories.summary: A tree-like moss found across parts of the Northern Hemisphere and on New Zealand’s South Island, it usually inhabits damp places such as swamps, peatlands, lake edges and moist woods. Its upright stems form miniature palm-like patches, while its reddish-brown spore-bearing shoots are mainly abundant in late winter and early spring.
A moss native across much of the Northern Hemisphere, it forms broad mats of branching stems with leaves bent sharply outward. It rarely produces capsules and reproduces mostly without spores.

A tall tree native to the Philippines, Indonesia and Papua New Guinea, it is the only eucalyptus that usually lives in rainforest and its natural range enters the Northern Hemisphere. Its smooth bark peels away in strips, exposing pale green, red, orange, grey and purplish-brown streaks.

Slender liverwort with a cosmopolitan distribution, though no native origin is explicitly stated. It forms creeping, pale- to bright-green patches, and its distinctive leaves curl inward, especially when dry. It often grows on rotting wood and stumps in sheltered, damp woodland.

Lime-loving moss with no explicitly stated native origin, widespread in Europe and extending to East Asia, tropical Africa and parts of North America. Its green to golden branches shine like silk when moist and curve upward when dry; it commonly grows on limestone, rocks and walls.

sources.attribution: Döring M (2022). German Wikipedia - Species Pages. Wikimedia Foundation. Checklist dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/4wn9dt accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-09-15.
