Their small fruits form conspicuous pink to purple clusters with a metallic sheen, often remaining on bare branches after the leaves fall. The highly astringent berries are made into wine and jelly.
stories.edibilityNote: The highly astringent berries are used to make wine and jelly.

stories.summary: Cactuses native from the Caribbean and western Mexico through Central America to northern South America, extending along the Andes to southern Peru and concentrated in northeastern Brazil. Mature plants develop a distinctive woolly, bristly crown where small flowers grow. Their pink, pepper-shaped fruits are edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The pink, pepper-shaped fruits are edible.

stories.summary: Deciduous shrubs and small trees native to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, with greatest diversity in North America. They bear mostly white spring flowers followed by red, purple or nearly black berry-like summer fruits. The fruits are edible raw and are also used in baked goods, jams and wine.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits are eaten raw and used in pies, muffins, jams and wine; Indigenous people and early western Canadian settlers harvested them.

stories.summary: An evergreen tree endemic to Madagascar, it bears red to purple flowers that fall before withering. Its bark provides fibre for cordage and woven cloth and was formerly made into barkcloth.

sources.title: Dombeya cacuminum — PROTA
sources.attribution: Plant Resources of Tropical Africa; PROTA account on Pl@ntUse

stories.summary: A creeping perennial plant native to Asia, it has thin, yellowish-green leaves. Its fruiting receptacles are matte white or pink, with matte red to brown, rough-textured achenes.

sources.title: Potentilla hebiichigo — first reports outside Asia

stories.summary: A herb endemic to Taiwan, it grows in thickets and along roadsides from medium to high altitudes. It is densely hairy, with coarsely sharp-toothed leaflets, white flowers and small achenes set on an enlarged, fleshy, globe-shaped base.

sources.title: Fragaria hayatai — Flora of Taiwan, second edition 3:79
sources.attribution: Hiroyoshi Ohashi (1993); Plants of Taiwan, National Taiwan University

stories.summary: Flowering plants native to southern Africa, Mesembryanthemum has long-lasting flower heads. Many species have glistening, rounded cells covering their stems, fruit and leaves that sparkle like ice crystals, inspiring the name ice plants.

Cacti native to northern Mexico and the southwestern United States, chollas have barbed spines that cling tenaciously to skin, fur and clothing. Their stems are cylindrical, and their spines carry papery outer sheaths.

Grass-like perennial herbs found nearly worldwide except Africa and Antarctica, Scirpus mostly grows in wetlands and damp places. These plants spread by underground stems and have three-angled stems, flat leaves and clusters of small brown or greenish-brown flower spikes.

Woody shrubs and trees, rhododendrons are native mainly to eastern Asia and the Himalayan region, with smaller numbers native elsewhere in Asia, North America, Europe and Australia. They may be evergreen or deciduous and often bear clusters of brightly coloured flowers. In Nepal, the flowers are considered edible and are pickled, juiced, or added fresh or dried to fish curry.
stories.edibilityNote: In Nepal, flowers are eaten pickled, juiced, or fresh or dried in fish curry; flower squash is also made in Uttarakhand.

stories.summary: Leguminous plants native to the tropical Americas, tropical Africa and Madagascar, Lonchocarpus species bear fruits likened to ornate lance tips or beads on a string.

Evergreen perennial flowering plants native to the Neotropics, Tillandsia ranges from northern Mexico and the southeastern United States through the Caribbean to central Argentina. Often called air plants, most cling to branches, bark or rocks instead of growing in soil, while silvery leaf cells rapidly absorb collected water. Their light seeds have silky parachutes that aid dispersal.

Large deciduous trees native to Southeast and East Asia, the eastern Mediterranean and North America, sweetgums have aromatic lobed leaves and prickly woody fruits called gumballs. Their trunks exude sweet resinous sap; hardened sap, including that of American sweetgum, has long been chewed in the southern United States.
stories.edibilityNote: Hardened sap can be chewed like gum; American sweetgum sap has long been used this way in the southern United States.

stories.summary: Flood-tolerant conifer trees occurring in southern North America, Taxodium species are deciduous in the north but semi-evergreen to evergreen in the south. When growing in or beside water, they form woody projections called cypress knees, whose function remains under study.

A North American genus of nitrogen-fixing shrubs and small trees, native from Canada through the United States and Mexico to Panama. Members may be evergreen or deciduous, thorny or unarmed, with flowers ranging from cream and deep blue to pink; some regrow from roots after fire, while others reproduce only from seed.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Americans brewed dried leaves as herbal tea, and early pioneers used the plant as a black-tea substitute.

stories.summary: Mostly vigorous woody climbing vines, Clematis species occur chiefly in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere and rarely in the tropics. Their divided leaves have stalks that twist around supports, though some species are shrubs or herbaceous perennials. Depending on the type, flowers appear on last year's side shoots, new stem tips, or both.
stories.edibilityNote: The genus can cause internal bleeding if eaten in large amounts; C. ligusticifolia seeds and acrid leaves were historically used as a pepper substitute.

stories.summary: Annual or perennial flowering plants native to the New World, Sisyrinchium species are irises rather than true grasses. They often resemble low grasses with long, thin leaves, while their clustered flowers may be blue, white, yellow or purple, often with a contrasting centre.
Grasses in the genus Setaria occur widely across tropical and temperate regions worldwide. Their cylindrical, bristly flower heads tend to droop when ripe.
stories.edibilityNote: The grains can be eaten raw but may be hard and bitter; boiling reduces both. Several species have historically served as staple crops.

stories.summary: Perennial herbs, shrubs and subshrubs, Justicia species inhabit tropical and subtropical regions, with some adapting to temperate climates.
Tendril-climbing plants in the grape family, Parthenocissus species are native to the Himalaya, eastern Asia and North America. Several species are grown ornamentally.

Flowering plants in the arum family, Arisaema species are native across southern Asia, eastern and central Africa, Mexico and eastern North America, with greatest diversity in China and Japan. An upright central flower spike rises from a surrounding hood. Plants are typically male when small and female or bisexual when larger, and may change sex repeatedly.

Perennial flowering herbs and shrubs native to tropical regions of the Americas, lantanas bear aromatic clusters mixing red, orange, yellow, blue or white flowers. Individual flowers typically change colour as they mature, making a cluster appear two- or three-coloured.
stories.edibilityNote: Reports conflict on whether ripe berries are edible; green berries are described as poisonous, while another source calls all lantana berries toxic to humans.

stories.summary: Aquatic flowering plants found worldwide and primarily in the tropics, Hydrocharitaceae includes both freshwater and marine species. Its leaves may be submerged, floating or partly above water, varying from narrow ribbons to rounded blades.

Bulbous herbaceous perennials native to temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere, from the Mediterranean and North Africa across Eurasia to western North America. They die back after flowering and regrow from underground bulbs, typically bearing nodding, bell-shaped flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: Bulbs of a few species are edible if carefully prepared and were commonly eaten by Indigenous Pacific Northwest peoples; most fritillaries have poisonous bulbs.

stories.summary: Annual or perennial herbs and subshrubs native to temperate Eurasia, North Africa, Macaronesia and North America south to Costa Rica. Wallflowers have distinctive star-shaped or forked hairs, warm-coloured flowers and pods containing many seeds.

Terrestrial orchids of temperate and subtropical America, Asia and Europe; giant helleborine is the only species native to the Americas. Creeping fleshy underground stems send up new shoots in spring, bearing terminal clusters of flowers ranging from greenish-white to violet and purple.

Annual and perennial herbs native to temperate Europe, northern Africa and Asia, with greatest diversity around the Mediterranean. Several species are garden plants, while some spread readily or become troublesome weeds.

Mostly summer annuals, rarely perennials, native to the Americas and found mainly in desert or semi-desert habitats. Most form a basal rosette of divided leaves and produce five-lobed blue, white, pink or yellow flowers.

Mostly deciduous trees native to warm-temperate and subtropical North America, the Caribbean and East Asia. They have large heart-shaped leaves, broad clusters of showy white-to-yellow flowers and long pods filled with flat, winged seeds.

Perennial bulbous plants native to Eurasia, including the Mediterranean basin and parts of Europe, North Africa and Asia. Their spring flower spikes are densely packed with usually blue, urn-shaped blooms resembling bunches of grapes.
Aquatic annual or perennial herbs with a worldwide natural distribution. Most leaves float, while the solitary flowers may float or rise above the water and open during either the day or night.
stories.edibilityNote: Despite general toxicity, some species’ boiled rhizomes and tubers are eaten, sometimes as famine food; seeds and some tubers are exceptions to the stated poison.

stories.summary: Cacti native to the coastal mountains of southeastern Brazil, where they grow on trees or rocks in shady, humid habitats. They are leafless, with green linked stems that are usually flattened into leaf-like pads, and flowers emerge from the joints and tips.

An annual flowering crop reported as native from the eastern Mediterranean to India, common flax is known only as a cultivated plant. Its slender stems yield smooth, strong fibres used for linen, while its seeds are eaten or processed into edible flaxseed oil.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten or ground into meal; flaxseed oil is edible, though solvent-processed oil has also long been used for painting and varnishing.

stories.summary: A genus of green algae with a probably worldwide distribution, Chaetomorpha occurs in marine or brackish water and only very rarely in fresh water. Its visible filaments are unbranched and only one cell thick, with thick-walled cylindrical or barrel-shaped cells.

An order of green algae found mainly in marine habitats, Cladophorales has also made four transitions into fresh water, while only two genera are terrestrial. Its attached filaments are one cell thick, contain many nuclei and range from unbranched to profusely branched.

A herbaceous perennial native to the mountains of southern and central Europe, from the Pyrenees to the Caucasus. Its feathery leaves and softly hairy growth smell strongly of aniseed when crushed. Leaves are sometimes eaten raw or cooked; roots are cooked like parsnips, and seeds are chewed raw.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw or cooked, roots are cooked like parsnips, and seeds are chewed raw.

stories.summary: A grass genus native to tropical and warm-temperate regions, Digitaria comprises slender annual and perennial plants with long, finger-like flower clusters. Seeds of named members—including two fonio species, Digitaria sanguinalis and Digitaria compacta—are eaten in several forms.
stories.edibilityNote: Edible seeds include fonio species, D. sanguinalis and D. compacta; they may be toasted, made into flour or porridge, or fermented into beer.

stories.summary: A perennial nightshade plant originating in Mexico, Physalis philadelphica bears small spherical green or green-purple fruit and is generally farmed as an annual. Its yellow flowers have blue anthers, and each berry fills or bursts a ten-ribbed husk. The fruit is a Mexican staple eaten raw or cooked, notably in salsa verde.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten raw or cooked in Mexican dishes, notably salsa verde.

stories.summary: A mostly annual vine originating in western South America, the tomato bears an edible berry eaten as a vegetable. Its thousands of cultivars differ greatly in size, colour, shape and flavour, while breeding for uniform red ripening has reduced sweetness and flavour.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten as a vegetable and used in sauces, soups, salads, condiments, curries, juice and other drinks.

stories.summary: An herb genus native to Europe and western Asia, Aegopodium has about twelve species. It bears compound flower clusters in spring and summer that attract many kinds of insect pollinators, followed by winged or ribbed nuts that separate when ripe.

A perennial genus of two species, Phormium includes one species endemic to New Zealand and another native to New Zealand and Norfolk Island. Its tough, sword-shaped leaves provide long fibres, while tall stalks bear curved tube-like flowers that turn bright red and produce abundant nectar.

A flowering-plant genus native to North and South America, Gaillardia includes annual or perennial herbs and subshrubs. Its usually solitary flower heads can be yellow, orange, red, purple, brown, white or multicoloured, and many cultivars are grown ornamentally.

A genus of rhizomatous flowering perennials native to mountain ravines and woodlands in Asia and North America. They are remembered for often fern-like foliage and dense, feathery flower plumes, and are well suited to shade and waterlogged ground.

A genus of small deciduous trees native to the mountains of Southern Europe. Spring brings hanging, leafless clusters of yellow pea-like flowers; all parts are poisonous, with spent seedpods the most poisonous.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are poisonous; spent seedpods are the most poisonous part.

stories.summary: A genus of bulbous, herbaceous perennials native to tropical and subtropical America, from Mexico to Argentina and parts of the Caribbean. Most have large fleshy bulbs, broad strap-like leaves, and large red or purple flowers.
A genus of flowering plants native to tropical and warm-temperate regions of the Americas, with one species also native to Fiji. Most are annuals, although a few are herbaceous perennials.

A genus of annual and perennial plants occurring mostly in North America, with one species in Siberia. They inhabit places from alpine tundra to prairie and open woodland, and bear flowers in shades of blue, violet, pink, red or white; many are fragrant.

A genus of flowering plants native to warmer parts of southern Mexico, Central and South America, Florida and the West Indies. Most species have yellow flowers. In species called walking irises, plantlets form at flower-spike tips; after flowering, the spikes fall over and new plants grow.

A fast-growing tropical American tree native from Central America to southern Brazil. It can grow up to three metres per year. Young, often unbranched trees have exceptionally long leaves that can make them resemble ferns or palms.

A genus of aromatic, herbaceous perennials mainly native to North America, with one species native to eastern Asia. Upright summer spikes carry tubular, two-lipped flowers, usually white, pink, mauve or purple. The leaf tips can be eaten or made into tea.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaf tips can be eaten or made into teas.

stories.summary: A genus of carnivorous, mostly climbing plants of the Old World tropics, ranging from South China and Southeast Asia to Madagascar, India, Australia and nearby islands. Pitchers develop at leaf tips and use slippery surfaces and fluid to trap prey, while glands below absorb nutrients.

A family of carnivorous pitcher plants native to North and South America. Their elongated, water-filled tubular leaves lure insects with nectar and trap them for digestion, with bacteria sometimes supplementing or supplying the digestive enzymes.

A genus of carnivorous perennial herbs native to the eastern United States, Texas, the Great Lakes region and southeastern Canada. Their funnel-shaped leaves attract prey with nectar, colour and scent, then use slippery surfaces and downward-pointing hairs to prevent escape.

A carnivorous plant native to the coastal wetlands of North and South Carolina in the United States. Each leaf ends in a jaw-like trap whose two lobes snap shut after trigger hairs register repeated contact, chiefly capturing insects and spiders.

A fern genus naturally distributed across temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, with its greatest diversity in eastern Asia. Many species have stout, slowly creeping rootstocks that support vase-like rings of fronds, and hybridization has produced many species in the group.

A genus of perennial bunchgrasses from the New World, found from North America through South America. Many species produce both cross-pollinating and self-pollinating flowers, while some conceal self-pollinating flower clusters inside their basal leaf sheaths.

A genus of tall biennial and perennial herbs native to temperate and subarctic regions of the Northern Hemisphere. They have large, twice-divided leaves and broad clusters of white or greenish-white flowers whose scents vary by species and even subspecies.
stories.edibilityNote: Some species are foods: candied young A. archangelica stems and leaf midribs are eaten, while A. lucida is eaten like wild celery.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering mayweeds mostly from Europe and temperate Asia, with a few species from North America and North Africa. They typically have deeply divided leaves and distinctive one-celled fruits bearing three ribs and two resin glands at the base.

A genus of trees, shrubs and rhizomatous perennial herbs native to Asia and the Americas, especially mountain woodlands. Their large, twice-divided leaves cluster near stem or branch ends; some species are prickly, and their dark purple berry-like fruits attract birds.
stories.edibilityNote: Some species are edible and cultivated for human consumption, notably Aralia cordata.

stories.summary: A genus of perennial herbs native mainly to temperate western North America, with a few species native to Arctic northern Eurasia and North America. They bear large yellow or orange flower heads, and mature leaves release a strong pine-and-sage scent when rubbed or bruised.

A genus of small biennial or perennial herbs native mainly to temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, especially southern Europe and southwest Asia. Their deeply lobed, dark green leaves form edible cress-like rosettes, while Barbarea verna is used for spicy salads or cooked greens; the plants have four-petalled yellow flowers.
stories.edibilityNote: The cress-like foliage is edible; Barbarea verna adds a spicy taste to salads and mixed greens for cooking.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering plants native to Asia, North America and Central America, Claytonia consists of small, somewhat fleshy plants. Its vitamin-rich leaves are eaten raw or cooked, while its tubers are cooked like potatoes.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw or cooked; tubers are cooked and eaten like potatoes.

stories.summary: A genus of small liverworts, Riccia has flattened bodies rather than distinct roots, stems and leaves. Depending on species, these may form branching ribbons, rosettes or intricate mats, usually with a green upper surface marked by a central groove.

A genus of flowering plants known as cudweeds, Gnaphalium is widespread in temperate regions, with some species on tropical mountains or in subtropical areas. Its species contain plant compounds including flavonoids and diterpenes.

A genus of annual and herbaceous perennial plants native to the Americas, Helenium bears yellow or orange daisy-like flowers. Their flower centres are notably globe-shaped, and each surrounding ray ends in three lobes.

A genus of small annual or perennial flowering plants distributed across Eurasia and parts of Africa, Minuartia grows on rocky ledges and in stony soil where conditions are otherwise inhospitable. It has narrow, bristle-like leaves and five white petals.

Deciduous or semi-deciduous trees native to Europe and distributed across much of the Northern Hemisphere, Ulmus has toothed leaves that are usually uneven at the base and lightweight, round winged fruits. During Norway’s 1812 famine, boiled strips of elm bark sustained much of the rural population; the seeds are also described as especially nutritious.
stories.edibilityNote: Boiled bark strips sustained much of rural Norway during the 1812 famine; elm seeds are described as especially nutritious.

stories.summary: A genus of branching filamentous green algae with a worldwide distribution, found mainly in marine or brackish water and occasionally in freshwater. Its grass-green filaments may attach to underwater surfaces or form dense mats and tufts.
stories.edibilityNote: It is eaten fresh or dried.

stories.summary: Evergreen conifer trees now largely confined to the Southern Hemisphere, including New Caledonia, eastern Australia, New Guinea and southern South America. Many are large, with horizontal branches arranged in whorls and leathery or needle-like leaves; their rounded female cones contain large edible seeds.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds of A. araucana, A. angustifolia and A. bidwillii are eaten, particularly by several Indigenous peoples.

stories.summary: Thorny ornamental vines, bushes and trees native to tropical South America. Their memorable colour comes from large, bright bracts surrounding clusters of three small, generally white flowers.

A perennial flowering hybrid with upright stems and dense branching. Its toothed, grey-haired leaves smell strongly when crushed, while its many cultivars bear flower heads ranging from daisy-like forms to colourful double pompoms.
stories.edibilityNote: In China, chrysanthemum continued to be used for dietary purposes from around the fifth century AD; the part and preparation are unstated.

stories.summary: Perennial flowering herbs or small shrubs native to East Asia and northeastern Europe, with most species originating in East Asia. They bloom in autumn and bear white, yellow or red outer florets around yellow centres; cultivated forms include many additional colours and shapes.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are steamed or boiled as greens; flowers may flavour dishes, while C. morifolium flowers are boiled for tea in parts of East Asia.

stories.summary: A herbaceous perennial native to the Americas, with the cultivated potato originating in present-day southern Peru and extreme northwestern Bolivia. Its edible, starch-rich tubers are underground stems rather than roots; above-ground parts and green or light-exposed tubers can be toxic.
stories.edibilityNote: The starchy tubers are a staple food, usually cooked; green, sprouted or light-exposed tubers may contain dangerous glycoalkaloids.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering herbs, shrubs and trees distributed through tropical and subtropical parts of the Americas, Africa, Asia and Australia. The plants are generally hairy or woolly, with five-petalled flowers that are usually bell-shaped and often yellow or orange.
A flowering-plant genus native to New Zealand and some Pacific islands, comprising 13 species.

Small trees and shrubs native to China and the Americas, from the southern United States to Colombia. They have deciduous leaves divided into many leaflets and hanging clusters of flowers resembling those of black locust.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds of S. affine are believed poisonous, but this member-level claim does not establish the genus as inedible.

stories.summary: Biennial or perennial flowering herbs mostly native to Europe and Asia. They have strong taproots, milky sap and grass-like leaves, followed by wind-dispersed seed globes resembling oversized dandelion heads.
stories.edibilityNote: Roots, young shoots and young leaves of T. porrifolius are eaten, but food use is not established for the genus as a whole.

stories.summary: A genus of coniferous trees native across much of North America and Eurasia, including Turkey and Syria, and in Morocco and Algeria. Firs bear evergreen needles attached singly by round bases and upright, candle-like cones that break apart at maturity.

A citrus tree native to Southeast Asia, including Malaysia. It bears the largest citrus fruit, a natural non-hybrid with thicker peel and less acidic flesh than grapefruit. The flesh and juice are edible, and the peel may be candied.
stories.edibilityNote: The flesh and juice are edible; the peel may be candied, and the pith is braised in East Asian dishes.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to temperate central and northern Europe and northern Asia. Every part is strongly aromatic, while its summer berries ripen glossy, dark purple to almost black. The tart fruit can be eaten raw but is usually cooked for jams, preserves, syrups and juice.
stories.edibilityNote: The berries are edible raw but usually cooked; they are used in jams, preserves, syrups, juice and alcoholic drinks.

stories.summary: A deciduous shrub native to western Europe. Its hanging flower clusters mature into bright red, translucent, tart berries; white currant is a sweeter, less-pigmented cultivar of the same species. The fruit is eaten raw or made into syrups, drinks, jams and other cooked dishes.
stories.edibilityNote: The edible berries are served raw or used in syrups, drinks, jams and cooked preparations.

stories.summary: A genus of grasses from Asia, Africa, Australia and tropical islands. Some species are cultivated as culinary and medicinal herbs for their lemon-like scent, especially C. citratus. C. nardus and C. winterianus have reddish bases and yield citronella oil used in soaps and insect repellents.
stories.edibilityNote: Some species are culinary herbs; C. citratus is especially suitable for cooking, while citronella grasses are also used as flavouring.

stories.summary: An annual climbing legume originating in southern and central Europe. Its leaves end in coiling tendrils, and each pod holds several green or yellow seeds. Immature seeds are eaten fresh, frozen or canned; mature seeds are dried, while snow and snap pea varieties also have edible tender pods.
stories.edibilityNote: Immature seeds are eaten fresh, frozen or canned; mature seeds are dried, and snow and snap pea varieties have edible young pods.

stories.summary: A possible genus of flowering legumes native to southwest Asia and northeast Africa. Its status is disputed: one major database treats it as part of Lathyrus, while another accepts three species.

A naturally cosmopolitan genus of mosses, most common in temperate and cold wetlands of both hemispheres. Living and dead plants can retain 16–26 times their dry weight in water, while their resistance to decay helps form extensive, deep peat bogs.
stories.edibilityNote: In Finland, peat mosses were used to make bread during famines.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering shrubs or small trees native mainly to South America, with a few species in Central America, Mexico, New Zealand and Tahiti. It is remembered for abundant hanging flowers whose colours range from white through red and purple to orange. Its small berries are edible, though flavour varies greatly among species.
stories.edibilityNote: The small berries are edible; depending on species, they may taste pleasant, bland or leave a bad aftertaste.

stories.summary: A genus of shrubs and small trees occurring in temperate and subtropical regions worldwide, with high diversity in southern Africa. Their reddish fruits form dense clusters; poison sumac belongs to Toxicodendron and instead bears white drupes. Dried fruits of some Rhus species are ground as a tangy spice or steeped in water for drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits of some species are ground as a tangy spice or steeped for drinks; R. coriaria is the principal culinary species.

stories.summary: Small, slow-growing deciduous hardwood trees native across much of the temperate Northern Hemisphere. Their serrated dark-green leaves turn yellow, orange or red in autumn, while mature trunks develop distinctive smooth, grey, muscle-like fluting. Their winged nuts spin as they fall.

Deciduous or evergreen trees, shrubs and woody climbers native to warm-temperate and subtropical areas worldwide. They are typically armed and have alternate divided leaves. Several species provide spices, notably Sichuan pepper, whose compounds produce characteristic numbness.
stories.edibilityNote: Several species provide spices; examples include the fruit husks of Z. armatum and Z. bungeanum, ground to make Sichuan pepper.

stories.summary: Mostly large deciduous trees native across most of the temperate Northern Hemisphere. They have heart-shaped, usually asymmetrical toothed leaves and strongly scented yellow-green flowers. Flowers are brewed as tea in several regions, while leaf buds and young leaves are edible raw.
stories.edibilityNote: Flowers are brewed as herbal tea in Europe, the Balkans and China; leaf buds and young leaves are eaten raw.

stories.summary: A large genus of orchids native from North Carolina to Argentina in tropical and subtropical America. Species may grow on trees, on the ground or on bare rock across habitats ranging from humid jungle to dry forest and cloud forest. Their clustered flowers are mostly small or medium-sized, and many are fragrant.
Flowering plants in the carrot family. The genus contains 15 species, of which P. sativa, the parsnip, is economically the most important.
Flowering plants in the carrot family, native to Europe, Asia, North America and northern Africa. The genus includes C. bulbosum, which is cultivated as a root vegetable.
stories.edibilityNote: C. bulbosum, a member of the genus, is cultivated as a root vegetable.

stories.summary: Mostly annual or perennial herbs, though some are shrubs or climbers. Their flower heads usually have conspicuous lilac or white outer florets surrounding numerous yellow central florets.
Twining, tendril-bearing plants in the gourd family. Members include cucumber, true melons, horned melon and West Indian gherkin.

An annual creeping vine native to Asia, from the Indian subcontinent through parts of China and northern Thailand. It climbs with spiralling tendrils and bears roughly cylindrical fruits that are about 95% water. The fruit is eaten fresh or pickled, and shoots are also cooked as vegetables.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits are eaten fresh, cooked or pickled; shoots are stir-fried or used in soups, especially in rural areas.

stories.summary: A unicellular green-alga genus found across polar, tropical and temperate regions. Its spherical cells contain a star-like or clustered chloroplast, and it commonly lives with fungi in lichens, though it can also live independently.
A flowering-plant genus native to the western Cape Province of South Africa. Its eight known species are cultivated as garden ornamentals in Australia.
A liverwort genus widely distributed through temperate regions. It commonly grows attached to tree bark and has leaves divided into a large upper lobe and a small lower lobe.
An order of non-vascular liverworts with no native origin specified. It is the largest liverwort order and is distinguished by thin, overlapping, leaf-like flaps along both sides of the stem.

A genus of slender evergreen palms native to Tanzania, Madagascar, Mauritius, the Comoros and other Indian Ocean islands. They bear yellow flowers among feather-like leaves, and many species branch above the main trunk, an unusual habit among palms. Some retain dead leaves that trap nutrient-rich litter.
A liverwort genus with no native origin specified. It contains only one recognized species, Reboulia hemisphaerica.
A cosmopolitan genus of mosses in the family Polytrichaceae.
A genus of more than 480 moss species, with no native origin specified. Its leaves have paired flaps that clasp the central strand, creating the pocket-like form reflected in its common name.

An orchid genus native across tropical and subtropical America, from Mexico and the West Indies to northern Argentina; one species reaches Florida. These plants grow in clumps on trees, rocks or soil, and their flowers have a broad, fiddle-shaped lower petal with a prominent warty fringe.
A genus of tender perennial flowering plants of South American origin. Most petunias seen in gardens are hybrids, valued for their wide variety of flower colours, sizes and plant forms.

A genus of herbaceous perennial plants, mostly native to cool temperate and subarctic Europe and Asia, with a few species native to mountains in Africa and the Americas. Most form clumps with water-resistant, often fan-shaped leaves and small, petal-free green or yellow-green flowers.

A genus of annual or perennial flowering vines, half of whose species are native only to California, with the group distributed across temperate and subtropical regions worldwide. They twine around supports and bear white or pink trumpet-shaped flowers.

A genus of perennial flowering plants native to Africa. They produce upright spikes of bright red, orange or yellow flowers above grass-like or strap-shaped leaves, and their abundant nectar attracts bees and nectar-feeding birds.

A genus of annual and perennial herbs native throughout the Americas, with one species also native to eastern Eurasia. Their outer florets are white, pink, blue or purple, while the centres mature from yellow or white to pinkish, reddish-purple or brown.
A genus of evergreen perennial flowering plants and subshrubs native to temperate regions, with its greatest diversity around the Mediterranean. It occurs on rocky and waste ground.

A genus of perennial flowering herbs represented by native species on every continent except Antarctica, with centres of diversity in Eurasia and South America, especially the Andes. They have woody roots, hairy stems and divided, toothed leaves; dried plant material develops a strong musky smell likened to male cats.

A genus of flowering plants native to Europe and Asia and naturalized in New Zealand, several Pacific islands, and much of the Americas. One member, Leonurus japonicus, is among the fundamental herbs of traditional Chinese medicine.

A genus of evergreen shrubs and small trees native to eastern Asia, from the eastern Himalayas through China and Korea to Japan. They have glossy, leathery, toothed leaves, separate male and female plants, small purplish-brown flowers and red fruits.

A phylum of non-vascular land plants naturally distributed almost worldwide, generally in damp or humid places. Their flat green body is the long-lived dominant stage, while a slender horn-like spore-producing structure rises from it.

A class of hornworts comprising the phylum's species except those in Leiosporoceros. Young and adult plants usually have slime pores underneath, except in Notothylas, and support round colonies of Nostoc cyanobacteria; most also have a central column in the spore-producing structure.

A worldwide genus of hornworts with small to medium green, irregularly lobed bodies. Its dark grey, brown or black spores distinguish it from yellow-spored Phaeoceros, while the plant body lacks scales and a clear midrib.
A worldwide genus of hornworts. Its yellow spores are the easiest distinction from Anthoceros when plants are mature and fertile; sterile plants are identified by the lack of gaps in the flat body.

A cosmopolitan genus of flowering plants, especially of alpine habitats in temperate Asia, Europe and the Americas. Gentians are remembered for mostly large, trumpet-shaped flowers, often intense blue but also yellow and other colours. Gentian root flavours bitters and other alcoholic or soft drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: Gentian root flavours bitters, aperitifs, liqueurs and tonics; cooked Gentiana scabra was historically used as famine food.

stories.summary: A genus of liverworts. Its flat body has an upper photosynthetic layer with barrel-shaped pores and a lower storage layer. Circular cups hold tiny tissue packets that rain splashes away to grow into new plants.
A liverwort species and the sole accepted species in its genus.
A temperate-region genus of bottle liverworts. It contains eight or nine species and is one of two living genera in its family.
A genus of liverworts in the family Aneuraceae, with 239 species described.
A cosmopolitan genus of liverworts in the family Fossombroniaceae.
A genus of flat-bodied liverworts. Its species may have both sexes on one plant or on separate plants, and roughly 120–200 species have been described.

A globally distributed genus of liverworts, found mostly in tropical, subtropical and temperate regions. Its small dark-green body has a strong hairlike midrib and is otherwise only one cell thick; female lobes carry cup-shaped, fringed structures.

A family of tropical flowering plants from areas including the Seychelles, Madagascar, India, Southeast Asian islands, Australia and New Caledonia. It contains at least 86 species in one genus; most are vines, sometimes growing on other plants, with passive traps.

A liverwort species, Rock Veilwort favors damp hollows and woodlands, particularly on limestone-rich surfaces. It sometimes grows on tree bark, including ash in humid wooded valleys, but is threatened by the loss of cool, moist habitats.

A family of liverworts whose included genera have occupied separate regions: Pellia in the temperate Northern Hemisphere and Noteroclada in the Southern Hemisphere, though the latter is now placed in another family. Noteroclada looks leafy, while Pellia has a flatter, less leafy form; the uncommon Androcryphia resembles leafy liverworts of another order.
A genus of liverworts in the family Lepidoziaceae, Bazzania had 258 accepted species as of November 2024.
A genus of liverworts with a cosmopolitan distribution, Calypogeia belongs to the family Calypogeiaceae.

A liverwort species native to Europe, Africa, Asia and North America, Common Pouchwort forms pale-green patches on loamy soil in woodland ravines and banks. Its loosely overlapping, egg-shaped leaves usually have bent, two-toothed tips; it rarely produces spores but often forms small asexual reproductive bodies.
A genus of liverworts, Cephaloziella includes C. varians, the only liverwort occurring in continental Antarctica.

A low-growing liverwort found across Europe to Iceland and western Russia, and in parts of Asia, North Africa and North America, Pale Liverwort occupies moist or wet ground rich in lime. It forms pale, translucent yellow-green to brown-green patches and has lower leaves deeply split into two long, narrow lobes.
A genus of liverworts and the sole genus in the family Frullaniaceae, Frullania includes living species and four named extinct species documented from Cenomanian Burmese amber in Myanmar.

A genus of prostrate perennial aquatic or semi-aquatic plants occurring across tropical and temperate regions worldwide. Its creeping stems often root at the nodes and form dense mats around water, carrying round or kidney-shaped leaves with scalloped edges.

A genus of annual and perennial flowering plants native to the Americas, chiefly North America. Its broad heads comprise many tiny flowers, while young heads track the sun by day and return east overnight; mature flowering heads generally remain east-facing.
stories.edibilityNote: Documented foods come from particular species: H. annuus seeds and oil, and H. tuberosus tubers.

stories.summary: A cosmopolitan genus of mostly aquatic or moisture-loving sedges. Its green stems perform photosynthesis while its leaves are reduced to basal sheaths, and every species bears flowers in a single unbranched spikelet at each stem tip.
stories.edibilityNote: Within the genus, Chinese water chestnut has rhizome tubers eaten peeled, raw or boiled.

stories.summary: A genus of annual, biennial or perennial legumes native to Europe, Asia and Africa. Melilots bear narrow three-part leaves and loose clusters of mostly white or yellow flowers; their sweet-smelling tissues contain coumarin, which molds can convert into toxic dicoumarol in decaying plants.

A mint-family genus occurring in Central and South America, Mexico, California, Hispaniola and Hawaii; the Hawaiian species is probably a human introduction. Many species bear attractive pitcher-shaped flowers, often in shades of purple.

An annual cereal grass descended from wild Avena sterilis whose ancestral forms grew in the Fertile Crescent. Common oat thrives in cool, wet summers and produces edible grain commonly rolled or crushed into oatmeal or ground into flour.
stories.edibilityNote: The grain is eaten as oatmeal, porridge, flour, baked goods, breakfast cereals and oat-milk products.

stories.summary: A grass genus widespread across much of Africa, Eurasia and Latin America. Its flimsy upright stems form tussocks, with flat or curved leaves and compact summer flower clusters composed of short-stalked spikelets.

A large grass genus occurring across all inhabited continents and many islands. Lovegrasses commonly serve as livestock fodder; their seeds are tiny and cumbersome to gather, although teff is a commercially important crop used for traditional breads in the Horn of Africa.
stories.edibilityNote: Documented edible members include teff for breads; E. clelandii and E. tremula are recorded as famine foods.

stories.summary: A cereal grass whose wild form ranges from North Africa and Crete to Tibet, common barley was first domesticated in the Fertile Crescent. Its spikelets form a herringbone-patterned, bristly ear, and its edible grain is used in soups, breads, malt, beer and whisky.
stories.edibilityNote: After the inedible outer hull is removed, grain is eaten in breads, soups, stews and porridge, or malted for beer and whisky.

stories.summary: A grass genus widespread across Europe, Asia and the Americas. Its plants feed some butterfly caterpillars, including the Zabulon skipper.
A widespread grass genus found on every continent except Antarctica and on various oceanic islands. Its species are generally known as Junegrasses.

A grass native to the Mediterranean region, canary grass is widely grown for birdseed. Its erect, hairless stems carry compact heads resembling club wheat. The seed is eaten in the Canary Islands, Italy and North Africa and prepared as atole in parts of Mexico; its hulls appear to contain silica fibres linked to esophageal cancer, while a hull-less variety was announced for human food.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds are eaten regionally and prepared as atole in parts of Mexico; hulls may contain silica fibres, while a hull-less food variety was announced.

stories.summary: A genus of annual and perennial grasses native to Europe, Asia and North Africa, with one species also occurring in the Americas. These tufted grasses have dense, cylindrical flower heads, and several species are used for livestock feed and hay.

A genus of deciduous flowering shrubs native mainly to North America, with two species native to northeastern Asia. Mature branches shed bark in strips, while the plants bear lobed leaves and clusters of white or pink bell-shaped flowers.

A genus of flowering trees and tall shrubs native to South America, from Peru and northeastern Brazil southward. Commonly called pepper trees, some species have become invasive beyond their natural habitats, and one member, Schinus molle, supplies pink peppercorn.
stories.edibilityNote: Only Schinus molle is identified as a pink-peppercorn source; human food use is not established for the genus as a whole.

stories.summary: A genus in the pea family whose species are all native to North America, from southern Canada through most of the United States to northern Mexico. Unlike typical pea flowers, its flowers have just one petal.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Americans used dried Amorpha canescens leaves for tea, but human food use is not established for the genus as a whole.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering plants native to western North America, from California north to Alaska and the Aleutian Islands. Depending on the species, mistmaidens range from low annual or perennial herbs to small bushes and bear attractive, bell-shaped white flowers.

Carnivorous aquatic or terrestrial plants native across every continent except Antarctica. They lack true roots and capture small organisms with fast, bladder-like suction traps, while their often showy flowers rise above the soil or water.

Annual and perennial sedges with a cosmopolitan distribution, occurring on every continent except Antarctica. They usually have upright three-sided stems and beaked fruits; mature fruits are often needed to distinguish similar-looking species.
Annual or perennial flowering herbs and subshrubs native to Europe, Asia and Africa. They bear yellow, daisy-like flower heads, and larger species often have coarse foliage.

A large annual herb considered native to the central and western United States, southern Canada and northern Mexico. Young buds follow the sun, but mature flower heads remain fixed, typically facing east. Domesticated forms are harvested for edible snack or baking seeds and cooking oil.
stories.edibilityNote: Domesticated seeds are eaten as snacks or in baking, and oilseed cultivars provide cooking oil.

stories.summary: Annual or perennial flowering herbs whose native origin is not supplied. Usually densely hairy, they bear small white four-petalled flowers and long, slender seed capsules, and naturally occupy rocky cliffs, mountainsides or dry ground.

Mustard-like flowering plants found throughout temperate regions worldwide. They produce long upright stems with small yellow or whitish flowers; many species are troublesome weeds, and some are toxic to livestock.
Flat, mat-forming annual flowering herbs native to Eurasia and Africa. Several species have also been widely introduced elsewhere.

Annual herbs or perennial subshrubs native within a range from the western Mediterranean to eastern Asia, with some introduced elsewhere. They mainly inhabit steppes and deserts and have inconspicuous flowers; their fruits may develop five wings.
Flowering plants native to North America. The genus contains about twelve accepted species.
A flowering-plant family whose native origin is not supplied, containing only the genus Paeonia.

Flowering-plant genus native across temperate Northern Hemisphere regions of Eurasia, North Africa and western North America. Most peonies are herbaceous perennials, though some are shrubs; they are popular garden plants, and herbaceous kinds are widely sold as late-spring and early-summer cut flowers.

Fruit-bearing deciduous shrub native to the Caucasus and Iranian plateau, including modern Iran, Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Its spiny branches bear bright red or white flowers and thick reddish fruits divided into seed-filled chambers. The fleshy seed coats and pulp are edible; the fruit and juice are used in drinks, baking, cooking and garnishes.
stories.edibilityNote: The seeds and pulp are edible; the fruit and juice are used in drinks, cooking, baking and garnishes.

stories.summary: Flowering-shrub genus distributed across temperate and subtropical regions on most continents, especially South America, North America and southern Africa. Plants are often thorny, with small fleshy leaves, white, green or purple bell-shaped flowers, and berries that may be red, orange, yellow or black.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruits of L. barbarum and L. chinense are eaten dried, but this does not establish edibility for the whole genus.

stories.summary: Herb and shrub genus indigenous to the Americas, Australia, southwestern Africa and the South Pacific. Species vary in nicotine and related defensive chemicals, which deter most herbivores, while several species are cultivated as tobacco plants.

Small flowering-plant genus native to Mexico and the southwestern United States. Its thick flower stalk bears downward-bent bracts, and its sticky pollen is released as a mass rather than as separate grains.

Annual or perennial grass genus widespread across temperate and subtropical Eurasia, northern Africa and the Americas, and naturalized in Australia and various islands. Plants grow in tufts with flat leaves and dense flower heads; some are weeds, while others are valued in dried-flower bouquets.

Widespread grass genus found across Europe, Africa, Asia, Australasia, the Pacific and the Americas. Some species are cereal or fodder millets, while others become troublesome farm weeds; early barnyard grass can resemble rice closely enough to escape weeding.
stories.edibilityNote: Some species are cereal crops, including Japanese, Indian barnyard, burgu and channel millets; this does not apply to every species.

stories.summary: Grass genus closely related to maize and millets. Some wild Sorghum species are perennial.
stories.edibilityNote: Food use is stated for Australian S. intrans and S. plumosum, not for the genus as a whole.

stories.summary: Usually annual, clump-forming grass native to Africa and the Indian subcontinent, with its origin and first domestication in Sudan. Its large bushy flower heads produce edible starchy grain. Young milky grain can be eaten raw, while mature grain must be boiled or ground into flour.
stories.edibilityNote: Young milky grain may be eaten raw; mature grain must be boiled or ground into flour.

stories.summary: A genus of wild and domesticated grasses whose wild forms were harvested in West Asia before cultivation began in the Fertile Crescent around 9600 BC. Wheat has hollow, jointed stems topped by ears of grain. Its grains are staple foods worldwide and are commonly processed into flour, bread, pasta and other foods.
stories.edibilityNote: The grains are worldwide staples, commonly milled into flour or processed into bread, pasta, cereals and drinks.

stories.summary: A genus of aromatic annual or perennial herbs and low shrubs native to southern and southeastern Europe, North Africa, the Middle East and Central Asia. Its small white to pale pink-violet flowers form rings around the stems. Several species are cultivated as culinary herbs called savory.
stories.edibilityNote: Several species are culinary herbs; summer and winter savory are used to flavour foods.

stories.summary: A genus of bushy, tuberous herbaceous perennials native to Mexico and Central America. Each colourful, usually unscented flower head consists of many small flowers, with surrounding petal-like rays; nearly every hue occurs except blue. Some stems remain soft, while others become woody and resprout after winter dormancy.
stories.edibilityNote: Tubers of some varieties have dietary value; several cultivars are grown in Oaxaca for their large, sweet-potato-like tubers.

stories.summary: A genus of deciduous and evergreen shrubs distributed through temperate and subtropical regions worldwide except Australia, with greatest diversity in South America and Asia. Many have spiny shoots or leaf margins, while their flowers are yellow or orange. The berries ripen red or dark blue, sometimes with a pink or violet waxy coating.

A genus of rhizomatous perennial ferns occurring across temperate regions worldwide, usually on rocks or in soil. Individuals can vary greatly under harsh conditions, and frequent hybridisation makes identification difficult. Their leaves are divided several times, and their usually round spore clusters have inflated, bladder-like coverings.

A genus of annual, biennial or perennial herbs with a strikingly divided distribution across temperate parts of the Western Palaearctic and Southern Hemisphere. They favour wet ground, often marshes and salt marshes, and bear divided leaves with small white flowers in branching clusters. Some species are edible, notably wild celery, the ancestor of celery, celeriac and leaf celery.
stories.edibilityNote: Some species are edible; wild celery is the ancestor of celery, celeriac and leaf celery.

stories.summary: A cosmopolitan genus of perennial aquatic or semi-aquatic herbs. Its usually opposite leaves accompany branching clusters of small white flowers. Water parsnips can be confused with the highly toxic water hemlock.
A small genus of annual wildflowers native to western North America, especially California. Known as bluecups, they have small white or purple blooms with white throats.

A genus of evergreen, short-lived perennial herbs and low shrubs from South America, ranging from southern Brazil to Peru and Chile. These sprawling plants inhabit scrub and open grassland and bear small, petunia-like flowers. Their funnel-shaped blooms may be purple, red, pink or whitish.
A genus of grasses with the greatest number of species native to the southwestern United States and Mexico. Other native species occur in Canada, Central and South America, and Asia.
Genus of flowering plants in the coffee family, comprising 91 species distributed from Europe and northern Africa through temperate and subtropical Asia to Australasia.

Perennial herb native to Afghanistan and Iran. Its shiny green leaves and stems smell strongly of celery when crushed. The leaves are used as an herb, roots as a vegetable and seeds as a spice, especially in southern European cuisine.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are used as an herb, roots as a vegetable and seeds as a spice, especially in southern European cuisine.

stories.summary: Genus of mostly herbaceous perennials native to cool temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere, with greatest diversity in Asia. Flowers may be bright yellow, orange or lilac; the globe shape occurs in T. europaeus and T. × cultorum, while other species have flatter or open flowers.
Class of green algae made up mostly of freshwater and terrestrial organisms. Members range from single cells to colonies and filaments, and nearly all are photosynthetic, although exceptions occur.

Perennial herb native to south-central Europe, the Mediterranean, Central Asia and Iran. It has soft, hairy, heart-shaped leaves with a mild lemon scent and small white or pale pink flowers. It is used raw or cooked in foods and teas, including fish dishes and pesto.
stories.edibilityNote: Used raw or cooked in foods and teas, including ice cream, fish dishes and pesto.

stories.summary: Genus of North American flowering plants in the daisy family, commonly known as little sunflowers.

Perennial herb native from Bulgaria to Turkey. Its early blue-violet flowers and large leaves form a dense groundcover as the plant spreads. In Turkey, the leaves are traditionally eaten as a spinach-like vegetable.
stories.edibilityNote: In Turkey, the leaves are traditionally eaten as a spinach-like vegetable.

stories.summary: A genus of herbaceous or evergreen perennials native to South America, Australia, New Guinea and New Zealand. They grow from short rhizomes, with narrow basal leaves that may turn red, orange or yellow in direct sunlight, and showy white or blue spring flowers.

A cosmopolitan genus of spore-producing lycopods, mostly living in clear ponds, slow streams or other aquatic and semi-aquatic habitats. Their hollow, quill-like leaves arise from a central underground stem, and species often require microscopic examination of their spores for identification.

A genus of perennial herbs native to temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere, especially North America and Europe, usually in wet or marshy places. Their small green or white flowers form umbrella-shaped clusters, but they resemble several edible plants. All parts are highly poisonous, with cicutoxin most concentrated in the roots, especially in early spring.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts contain cicutoxin; roots are most toxic, especially in early spring, and ingestion can be fatal.

stories.summary: A widely distributed genus of roughly a dozen water-loving herbs and amphibious flowering plants.

A genus of small annual grasses native mainly to Eurasia and North Africa, with one species native to South America. The plants form loose tufts and have softly hairy leaves, with flowers carried in branching clusters.
A genus of flowering grasses from Eurasia and North Africa.

A genus of grasses native to temperate and Arctic regions of both hemispheres, Puccinellia is commonly called salt grass or alkali grass. These grasses grow in wet habitats, often under saline or alkaline conditions.

A genus of succulents native to the drier parts of southern Africa, Ruschia has grey or blue-green, often spotted, triangular leaves and small pink or white flower clusters throughout the year. Its seed capsules open and close as humidity changes, while a membrane helps prevent all the seeds from washing away immediately.

A genus of succulents native to rocky, semi-arid habitats in South Africa's Western Cape, Oscularia is restricted to winter-rainfall areas. Its waxy grey-green leaves have triangular cross-sections and varied shapes, while drought can redden the leaves and often-red stems. Abundant almond-scented pink or white flowers appear through summer.
A biennial flowering plant native to Madeira, Geranium yeoi grows mainly in the subtropical biome.

sources.title: Geranium yeoi Aedo & Muñoz Garm. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

stories.summary: A genus of trees, shrubs and vines chiefly originating on Pacific islands, Metrosideros includes small tree forms as well as some exceptionally large ones. Its lightweight, wind-carried seeds can still germinate after freezing or prolonged immersion in salt water. The plants are often cultivated for showy flowers, generally red but sometimes orange, yellow or white.

A genus of deciduous shrubs, Forsythia is mostly native to eastern Asia, with one species native to southeastern Europe. Bright yellow flowers open in early spring before the leaves and hang downward in rainy weather, shielding their reproductive parts. The fruit is a dry capsule containing several winged seeds.

A genus of flowering plants native to North and South America, Gamochaeta also includes one species confined to Tristan da Cunha. These cudweeds or everlastings have small flower heads arranged in spikes and tiny fruits with mucilage-producing hairs; their bristles are joined into rings that detach as single units.

A widespread genus of perennial, spreading grasses, Glyceria occurs in wet temperate habitats across Eurasia, Australia, North Africa and the Americas; no native origin is specified. Its ground-hugging bases may root at several points before producing upright growth, and its branched flower clusters nod when heavy.

An aquatic plant genus widespread over much of the world outside frigid zones and the tropics. Widgeonweeds root in submerged ground and are adapted to brackish estuaries; most are annuals, though some are perennial.

A genus of perennial flowering herbs native to tropical and cool-temperate regions worldwide. Their creeping stems readily root where the leaf nodes touch the ground, and they bear tiny white, greenish or yellowish flowers.
A genus of herbaceous perennial legumes native to temperate North America and eastern Asia. They are commonly called goldenbanners or false lupines.

A genus of flowering perennials native to grasslands of southern and eastern Africa, from South Africa to Sudan; one species is endemic to Madagascar. They grow from vertical chains of underground corms and bear vivid red or orange flowers on arching, zigzag spikes.
A temperate tree whose native range is described as naturally occurring between its native and naturalised parents. It is reported as the hybrid Malus domestica × Malus sylvestris.

sources.title: Malus × dasyphylla Borkh. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

stories.summary: A tender culinary herb native to tropical regions from Central Africa to Southeast Asia. It has glossy green or purple leaves on square stems, and sweet basil's clove-like scent comes from eugenol. It is commonly used fresh in recipes and is a main ingredient in pesto.
stories.edibilityNote: Used fresh in recipes and added late because cooking quickly destroys its flavour; basil is a main ingredient in pesto.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering plants native to southern and eastern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Their daisy-like flower heads can have blue, yellow or purple centres and rays in colours from white and cream to pink, purple and yellow; some cultivars have spoon-shaped petals.
A genus of flowering plants in the carrot family, native to north-western Europe and the Mediterranean.
A bulbous perennial hybrid, honeybells is a cross between Nothoscordum entrerianum and Nothoscordum gracile and has become a nearly cosmopolitan weed. Its whitish flowers are sweetly scented.
A genus of flowering plants found only in the north temperate zone, Moehringia belongs to the carnation family. Its members are among the plants commonly called sandworts.
A genus of herbaceous plants native to Europe, Siberia, western Asia, northern Africa, Ethiopia, New Guinea and Australia, Scleranthus comprises 12 species known as knawels.

A genus of flowering plants native to Asia and Europe, hollyhocks may be annuals, biennials or perennials and are usually upright and unbranched. Their often lobed or toothed leaves usually bear star-shaped hairs, while their notched flowers may be pink, white, purple or yellow.

A genus of succulent perennials of subtropical origin, houseleeks occur from Morocco to Iran across mountain ranges and parts of the Sahara and Caucasus. They form mats of thick-leaved rosettes and spread by offsets; each rosette dies after flowering, usually leaving many offsets behind.
stories.edibilityNote: Houseleek juice was used in medieval Arabic cooking to colour food pink, or mixed with saffron for a deeper yellow.

stories.summary: A perennial herb native to Europe and southern temperate Asia, spearmint has pointed, serrated leaves on square stems and spreads through fleshy underground stems. Its leaves flavour foods and teas, including Maghrebi mint tea.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are used to flavour food and are infused for spearmint tea, including Maghrebi mint tea.

stories.summary: A genus of mostly perennial herbs native to North America, Rudbeckia has daisy-like yellow or orange flower heads surrounding a prominent raised central disc. The outer florets tend to spread outward and downward as the flower opens, creating a cone-shaped head.

A genus of trees native to tropical and subtropical parts of the Americas and tropical West Africa, Ceiba includes species with tall, largely branchless trunks, huge spreading canopies and buttress roots taller than a person. Some species can exceed 70 metres in height.

A genus of shrubs and small trees native to warm-temperate and tropical regions worldwide, Sapindus includes both deciduous and evergreen species. Its fruit pulp contains natural cleaning compounds and is used to make soap and shampoo.

A genus of flowering shrubs and small trees native to semidesert regions of Africa and the Americas. Its members have open, thorny crowns and green bark, bear leaves briefly after rain, and rely largely on green twigs and branches for photosynthesis.

A leguminous tree indigenous to tropical Africa and naturalized in Asia. It bears hard brown pods filled with sweet-sour pulp used widely in cooking, while young leaves are also eaten; seeds must be soaked and boiled before eating.
stories.edibilityNote: Sweet-sour fruit pulp and young leaves are eaten; seeds require soaking and boiling before consumption.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering trees native to Madagascar and East Africa. In Madagascar, the plants release brown resin that is dissolved for glue or sucked as a sweet, and their roasted seeds are eaten as a snack.
stories.edibilityNote: Among the Malagasy, resin is sucked as a sweet and roasted seeds are eaten as snacks, especially in the south.

stories.summary: A mangrove tree native to western African coasts and the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the Americas. It has leathery yellow-green leaves with sugar-exuding glands, rough fissured bark and, depending on conditions, breathing or prop roots. It usually grows inland of other mangroves, above the high-tide line.

A genus of bulb-forming perennial herbs found in seasonally wet tropical and subtropical habitats worldwide. Members have large, showy flowers on leafless stems, and most species lose their leaves during the dry season.

A perennial vine native to tropical South America, in what is now Ecuador. Its creeping stems root at their joints, while cultivars produce sweet, starchy storage roots in many skin and flesh colours. The roots are a major food, usually cooked, and young shoots and leaves are also eaten as greens.
stories.edibilityNote: The starchy storage roots are staple food, usually cooked; young shoots and leaves are also eaten as greens.

stories.summary: A genus of mainly herbaceous vines native to the American, Indian and African tropics. Often called balloon vines or heartseeds, they are cultivated as ornamentals in warm regions and are invasive in parts of the southern United States and South Africa.

A deciduous fern native to eastern North America, from Newfoundland west to Wisconsin and Arkansas and south through the Appalachians to northern Alabama. It grows in acidic soil in both damp and dry woods, and crushed fronds smell like fresh hay.

A delicate tropical perennial crop whose native origin is unresolved, with South Asia and Africa both proposed. Its fruit is botanically a berry, usually purple, with glossy skin, spongy flesh and many soft edible seeds; it readily absorbs oils and flavours during cooking.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit, skin and soft seeds are edible; it is usually cooked, and the green calyx is removed.

stories.summary: An annual herbaceous legume native to South America. After its yellow-orange flowers are fertilized, a peg grows into the soil and the pods develop underground, usually holding one to four seeds.
stories.edibilityNote: Its seeds are eaten in products including oil, peanut butter, sauces and sweets; some people can have a fatal allergic reaction.

stories.summary: A genus of cacti native to South America, ranging from large tree-like forms to small rounded plants. Dense spines and large, long-tubed flowers are memorable features, often carried on small, squat stems.

A genus of flowering plants distributed across Europe, Asia, Africa, North America and Australia. Most are herbaceous perennials that often thrive in salty soils; most leaves form a dense cluster at ground level, and the lasting outer flower cups make several species popular as “everlasting” garden flowers.
A genus of evergreen conifer trees of the northern temperate and boreal Northern Hemisphere. Their four-sided needles attach singly to persistent pegs, leaving the twigs rough after the needles fall.
stories.edibilityNote: Fresh shoots of many spruces provide vitamin C; in Finland, young buds are used as spice or boiled with sugar for syrup.

stories.summary: A genus of marine green algae widely distributed along tropical, subtropical and temperate coasts. Each visible organism is essentially one branched tubular cell without internal cross-walls, often forming dense, feather-like tufts; blooms can create green tides, and aquarium growth is difficult to control.

A genus of aromatic, deciduous flowering shrubs with native species in eastern and western North America and eastern China. Their opposite, undivided leaves and flowers made of spiralling petal-like parts, rather than separate sepals and petals, are distinctive.
A genus of tropical ferns. It grows from rhizomes rather than roots, and some species cling to rocks in flowing water.
A family of mosses. Many species grow on other plants rather than on the ground.
A flowering shrub found in moist canyons and wooded slopes of southern California and Baja California. It usually has several slightly hairy stems, simple toothed leaves and yellow flower heads.

A plant genus whose species are mostly native to Europe, Central Asia and Africa. Commonly called cancerworts or fluellins, the genus includes two species, K. elatine and K. spuria, that are well established as invasive plants elsewhere.
A grass genus found widely in temperate, subarctic and alpine habitats across much of the world. Its members are commonly called oatgrasses.

A genus of flowering trees and woody shrubs native to Australia, with tropical banksia also occurring in New Guinea and the Aru Islands. Banksias are known for densely packed flower spikes or heads and massive woody fruiting structures often called cones; their abundant nectar feeds many birds and mammals.
stories.edibilityNote: Indigenous people of southwestern Australia sucked flower spikes for nectar or soaked them in water to make a sweet drink.

stories.summary: A family of scaly tree ferns found in tropical wet mountain and cloud forests in both the New and Old Worlds, with some species reaching southern temperate regions. It includes the world's tallest tree ferns, while its large leaves bear scales, hairs and spore clusters underneath.

A genus of shrubs and small trees, mostly native to temperate and subtropical Asia; E. triflora reaches northeastern Australia, while E. commutata is native to North America. Tiny silvery or brownish scales often give the foliage a pale cast, and the small, petal-free flowers are often fragrant.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit is edible in many species; E. angustifolia, E. umbellata and E. multiflora are cultivated for it.

stories.summary: A small family of red algae containing several genera. Many species are processed into agar, a cell-wall substance used in foods and several other industries.
stories.edibilityNote: Many species are used to produce agar, which is used in food products.

stories.summary: A red-algae genus distributed through the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian oceans, with the Atlantic holding the most species. Its upright or spreading bodies vary greatly in colour and branching, making species difficult to distinguish by appearance, and are a source of kappa-carrageenan.
stories.edibilityNote: Cultivated experimentally, not commercially, in several tropical countries for food and kappa-carrageenan, mostly using H. musciformis.

stories.summary: A red-algae genus found mainly in warm waters worldwide and seasonally in temperate waters, in every ocean except the Arctic. It supplies more than 90% of the world's agar and is eaten in several Asian, Pacific and Caribbean cuisines.
stories.edibilityNote: Used in Filipino, Hawaiian, Japanese, Korean and Sri Lankan cuisines; in the Philippines it is eaten fresh or sun-dried and made into jellies.

stories.summary: A semi-succulent species native to tropical Africa from West Africa through Nigeria to the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It forms upright basal rosettes of stiff, pointed leaves, commonly dark green with paler cross-bands; some varieties have yellow margins.

A historically recognized genus of herbaceous, perennial plants with spreading underground stems, native to Africa, notably Madagascar, and southern Asia; it is now included in Dracaena. Species often form dense clumps, with leaves ranging from thick, hard and cylindrical in dry climates to broad and strap-like in tropical regions.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaves are described as potentially poisonous if ingested.

stories.summary: A perennial shrub reported as native across most circum-Mediterranean countries, although whether it is indigenous there is uncertain. It has rounded, fleshy leaves and large white to pinkish-white flowers with long violet stamens. Its flower buds and fruits are usually eaten salted or pickled as capers and caper berries.
stories.edibilityNote: Flower buds and fruits are generally eaten salted or pickled as capers and caper berries.

stories.summary: A very large genus of mostly tree- or rock-growing orchids found across much of southern, eastern and southeastern Asia, Australia, New Guinea and Pacific islands. Their roots creep over trees or rocks, while white, green, yellow, pink or purple flowers line unbranched stems.

An annual herb native to the Mediterranean Basin. Most people find its leaves fresh and slightly citrus-like, while some perceive them as soapy or rotten. All parts are edible, though fresh leaves and dried seeds are most traditionally used in cooking.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts are edible; fresh leaves and dried seeds are most traditionally used in cooking.

stories.summary: A liverwort species widespread across Ukraine, where it grows on the bark of many trees and on rocks. It forms flattened green mats with overlapping, flat leaves, and numerous buds develop along the leaf edges.
A liverwort genus with a worldwide distribution, concentrated mainly in the Northern Hemisphere. Its species typically occupy moist habitats on non-calcareous rocks.
A moss genus with a worldwide distribution.

A highly variable moss genus whose classification has been substantially reshaped by DNA studies. Its species can be distinguished by their patterns of reproduction without spores, stem and leaf-base colour, and the strength of the leaf border.
A family of mosses whose male and female reproductive structures occur on separate plants. Its genera include Dicranum, Dicranoloma and Mitrobryum.
A moss genus distributed throughout the world, with about 125 species.
A large genus of mosses with a cosmopolitan distribution; 114 species were accepted as of 2020.
A family of mosses found almost worldwide, including Antarctica. It occurs mainly in temperate regions and at higher tropical elevations.
A genus of mosses with a cosmopolitan distribution.

A family of perennial flowering herbs found in tropical and subtropical America, Africa and Asia, especially the American tropics. Its flowers have a distinctive, one-time rapid movement that transfers pollen when triggered by a pollinator.
stories.edibilityNote: Maranta arundinacea provides arrowroot starch; flowers of two Calathea species are cooked, and C. allouia has an edible tuber.

stories.summary: A genus of perennial flowering herbs native to tropical America. Its often large, brightly patterned leaves fold upward at night and unfurl in the morning; young leaves and bracts may also hold pools that shelter invertebrates.
A genus of mosses with an almost cosmopolitan distribution.

A genus of cactuses, mostly native to Mexico, with others native to the southwestern United States, the Caribbean and parts of Central and northern South America. Each stem bump has a spiny point at its tip and a separate spineless, often woolly base where flowers and fruits form.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit from several species is edible and is best harvested when fully exposed and easily detached.

stories.summary: A genus of mosses with an almost cosmopolitan distribution.

A genus of mainly tropical trees native to western Africa, the Indian subcontinent, Southeast Asia, subtropical East Asia and northern Australia. These large trees shed their leaves during the dry season and produce red flowers; their buoyant, water-resistant fibres are used for insulation and stuffing.

A genus of evergreen flowering shrubs and vines native to Old World tropical regions from Africa through Southeast Asia to Australia and the western Pacific. Its white, pink, red or orange flowers appear singly or in large branched clusters.

A widespread genus of filamentous green algae found on almost all continents, Trentepohlia grows on moist terrestrial surfaces or in lichens. Its often orange, felt-like patches contain carotenoid pigments that mask the green chlorophyll.

A genus of small red algae, Ceramium includes at least 15 species in the British Isles. Its irregularly branching bodies have pincer-like growing tips and attach by simple or branched root-like structures.
A genus of slow-growing red algae, Hildenbrandia forms non-mineralized crusts. It expands around the margins, rapidly repairs gaps from a basal cell layer and seasonally sheds its outer layer.

A pantropical genus of trees in the pea family, Pterocarpus is notable for unusually winged seed pods. Most species yield valuable padauk timber, which is generally tough, stable and reddish, and many woods can also provide dyes.
stories.edibilityNote: Wood from several Pterocarpus species is called padauk; padauk wood is used as a spice, including in Swedish soused herring.

stories.summary: A tropical Asian genus of giant clumping bamboos, Dendrocalamus occurs across the Indian subcontinent, China and Southeast Asia. One member, D. giganteus, can reach about 46 metres and is among the tallest bamboos.

A large genus of flowering plants in the mallow family, Grewia includes several species whose astringent, refreshing edible drupes have local commercial importance and are especially popular in summer.
stories.edibilityNote: Several Grewia species have edible drupes of local commercial importance; the fruits are especially popular in summer.

stories.summary: A large genus of mainly shade-loving herbs and shrubs, Pilea occurs through tropical, subtropical and warm-temperate regions, except Australia and New Zealand. Most have opposite leaves, while some cultivated kinds are valued for lily-pad-shaped ornamental foliage.

A genus of broad-leaved flowering perennials native to tropical and subtropical Asia and eastern Australia, Alocasia grows from rhizomes or tubers. Its large heart- or arrow-shaped leaves often hide the inconspicuous flowers. Corms of some species can be processed for food, but raw plants contain irritants and ingestion may remain dangerous despite precautions.
stories.edibilityNote: Corms of some species can be processed as food; raw plants irritate the mouth and throat, and ingestion may remain dangerous despite prolonged boiling.

stories.summary: A genus of medium-sized to large conifer trees native to eastern Asia and the western and eastern margins of the United States, Chamaecyparis has foliage arranged in flat sprays. Seedlings bear needle-like leaves, while adults have scale-like leaves; the scented wood is especially valued in Japan for temple construction.

A genus of herbaceous or evergreen flowering perennials native to southern Africa, Clivia has green strap-like leaves and bell-shaped yellow, orange or red flowers held above the foliage. Unlike most close relatives, it forms no bulbs; its leaves arise from thick branching roots or rhizomes.

A genus of evergreen coniferous trees native to high mountains in the western Himalayas and Mediterranean region. Cedars have clustered green or blue-green needles and upright cones that break apart when mature, releasing winged seeds.

A genus of mosses with a worldwide distribution. These often-shiny, green or yellowish mosses form shelf-like growths, with creeping, irregularly branched stems and leaves that may be flat or strongly wavy.
