A genus of tropical plants ranging from short shrubs to tall upright forms, native to tropical Africa, southern and eastern Asia, Australia and various oceanic islands. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants. Its fleshy, juicy fruits are edible and change from white through red to black as they ripen.
stories.edibilityNote: Fleshy, juicy fruits are edible and taste sour to bittersweet; some people find Antidesma bunius berries bitter.

stories.summary: A genus of evergreen, rhizomatous flowering perennials native to Africa, including Madagascar. Its mostly blue, star-shaped flowers generally last only a morning, while clusters open in sequence over several weeks.

A family of tiny liverworts that recent molecular studies treat as containing only Arnellia fennica. Its overlapping, opposite leaf-like structures are joined at the back of their bases; underleaves are absent and root-like rhizoids are rare.
A genus of mosses in the family Grimmiaceae.

A genus of shrubs and small trees native to southern and eastern Asia and northeastern Africa. Its small green leaves contrast with a leathery, multicoloured trunk, while the flowers are small and inconspicuous.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is edible but not an important crop; leaves are sometimes used as a tea substitute in China.

stories.summary: A genus of large herbs and subshrubs native to the southwestern United States, Mexico and Central America; some members are naturalized elsewhere. It belongs to the groundsel tribe of the sunflower family.
A genus of mosses with a cosmopolitan distribution, belonging to the Bryaceae family.

A cosmopolitan genus of mosses that grows on damp to wet silicate rock. Its lance-like leaves have browned bases and distinctive swollen orange-brown cells at their lower corners; its oval to pear-shaped spore capsules may lack teeth.
A genus of mosses in the Pottiaceae family with a cosmopolitan distribution.
A genus of mosses in the Pottiaceae family with a cosmopolitan distribution.
A genus of flowering plants native to North and South America, belonging to the sunflower family.

A genus of fan palms found on tropical Pacific islands, including Fiji, Samoa, Tonga, the Tuamotus and especially Hawaii. They have fan-shaped leaves and column-like trunks, with flowers and fruit borne in arching or hanging terminal clusters. Native Hawaiians often eat their seeds raw.
stories.edibilityNote: Native Hawaiians often consume the palms' seeds, called hāwane or wāhane, raw.

stories.summary: A genus of mosses found in Eurasia and northern North America.
A North American genus of plants in the aster family. Its species are commonly known as silkgrasses, golden asters or grass-leaved goldenasters.

An arum-family plant genus native to East Asia—China, Korea and Japan. Its green, hooded flower structure bears a long tongue-like projection, inspiring the common name green dragons. Leaves range from simple and heart-shaped to divided into several leaflets, and many species form small bulbs on their leaves.

A cactus genus native to the Neotropics. Its species are column-shaped shrubs or trees, sometimes densely branched; their usually night-opening flowers may smell strongly of garlic. Ripe fruits can have white, red-purple or other-coloured pulp.
A genus of deciduous trees native to eastern and northeastern Asia. They have leathery, feather-like leaves and clustered yellow flowers; some, but not all, species develop thick corky bark.
A genus of evergreen flowering vines native to the tropical Americas, from Florida and northeastern Mexico south to Bolivia, Paraguay and southern Brazil.
A genus of plants native to Europe, Asia and Africa.

A genus of flowering plants in the sunflower family, native to southern and northwestern Africa, Chad, Somalia and the southern Arabian Peninsula. One member, Pentzia incana, is naturalized in Australia and the southwestern United States.
A genus of large cacti native to Central America and Mexico. They form massive shrubs or small trees with stout stems; one member, Pachycereus pringlei, is the tallest recorded cactus species.
A genus of flowering plants native to Europe and western Asia. They produce blue or white, forget-me-not-like flowers in spring, and their seeds have a distinctive navel-like shape.

A genus of creeping, mat-forming perennial herbs native mainly to Southern Hemisphere parts of South America and Australasia, although one species extends into the Northern Hemisphere. Its flowers are inconspicuous, while the fruit is usually a bright orange berry but may be a dry capsule in some species.
A genus of flowering plants in the myrtle family, native to Central and South America, the West Indies and southern Florida.
A genus of flowering plants in the cabbage family, with three accepted species ranging from the Mediterranean through central and Eastern Europe and Western Asia to Siberia and northern China.

A one-species genus of flowering plants native to China and Korea. Its sole species is an annual or biennial with an upright, mostly unbranched stem and a large solitary flower head. Wild flowers are purple, while cultivated varieties offer many colours and single or double heads.

A genus of perennial flowering herbs whose sole species is native to the Canary Islands, the Azores and Madeira. Its compound leaves have three leaflets, an unusual form in its family, and its leafy stems end in dense spikes of white or pink flowers.
A flowering-plant genus whose sole species is native to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East eastward to Iran. This annual has trailing stems and oblong fruits covered with hooked spines.

A genus of flowering shrubs native to eastern and central Asia, Central America and Europe, with its greatest diversity in China. Most are deciduous and bear clustered white flowers, sometimes pink or reddish. Species can be difficult to distinguish without microscopic examination of leaf hairs and seed capsules.
A genus of flowering plants in the cucumber family. In some species, the stamens are fused into a ring around the flower’s female structures.
A genus of liverworts with a worldwide distribution.
A genus of flowering plants native to Eurasia and North America.

A genus of flowering subshrubs and small trees distributed across paleotropical regions from Madagascar through southern and southeastern Asia to Melanesia, Hawaii and Australia. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, and half of its species are found in Malesia.

A genus of aromatic evergreen shrubs native to southern North America, from Arizona, New Mexico and Texas through most of Mexico. Its white, star-shaped flowers resemble orange blossoms in both shape and scent, while the glossy compound leaves smell of rue when bruised or cut.

A genus of flowering shrubs and small trees native from southern Florida through Mexico to South America. Commonly grown as hedges and ornamentals, it has also become a fast-growing, thorny invasive weed in Australia, spreading from gardens into natural reserves through bird dispersal.
A genus of mosses in the family Funariaceae.

A genus of succulent plants native to tropical Mexico, the Caribbean, Central America and northern South America. Some species have become naturalized in Africa, Florida, Portugal, Thailand, India, Australia and various oceanic islands.
A genus of flowering plants native from Mexico to Colombia.
A genus of leafy liverworts with a worldwide distribution.
A genus of mosses in the family Hypopterygiaceae.
A genus of mosses with a cosmopolitan distribution.

A genus of deciduous flowering shrubs occurring across Europe and Asia. These exceptionally hardy plants develop extensive root systems and are used for erosion control and land reclamation. Their edible berries are naturally astringent, sour and oily, and are made into juice, jams and other foods.
stories.edibilityNote: Berries are edible but astringent, sour and oily; they may be frosted or mixed with sweeter juice and made into various foods.

stories.summary: A genus of leafy liverworts with a worldwide distribution.

A genus of gourd-bearing vines indigenous to tropical Africa. Its six species produce gourds that can be eaten young as vegetables; mature dried gourds are more commonly made into utensils, musical instruments and containers.
stories.edibilityNote: Young gourds from the various species may be eaten as vegetables; mature gourds are generally dried for non-food uses.

stories.summary: A flowering perennial of African origin, although truly wild populations are not known with certainty; it is often grown as an annual in temperate climates. Its white-to-yellow flowers often have a red or purple basal spot, while its many-seeded pods quickly become fibrous and woody. The immature pods are eaten raw, cooked or pickled and release characteristic slime when cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: Immature pods are eaten raw, cooked or pickled; young leaves are edible, roasted seeds substitute for coffee, and seed oil is edible.

stories.summary: A rosette-forming flowering plant of uncertain native origin, though it is thought to come from Chiapas in southern Mexico. Its sword-shaped leaves yield a stiff fibre traditionally used for rope and twine.
stories.edibilityNote: The leaf pith can be fermented and distilled to make mezcal.

stories.summary: A vegetable whose native origin is not supplied. Instead of a rounded bulb, it forms a long cylinder of overlapping leaves; the white underground portion is most commonly cooked, while the green portion is also used.
stories.edibilityNote: The white and green leaf portions are cooked; leeks are also eaten raw in salads.

stories.summary: An annual culinary herb of uncertain native origin, variously placed in the Caucasus alone or across central and southeastern Europe and southwestern Asia. Related to parsley, it has a faint liquorice or aniseed taste and is usually added near the end of cooking.
stories.edibilityNote: Used to season savoury dishes; dried leaves and, in North Africa, seeds are used as spices.

stories.summary: A shrub or small tree native to Mexico and Central America. Its celebrated red structures are modified leaves surrounding tiny, inconspicuous flowers, rather than petals.

A tree native to the US Midwest, Upper South and Appalachia, with small pockets in New York and Ontario. It sheds its leaves early and may look bare for six months, while emerging leaflets change from bright pink to bronze-green. Its roasted seeds were eaten or brewed, but unroasted or partly roasted beans and pods are considered poisonous.
stories.edibilityNote: Roasted seeds were eaten and brewed as a coffee substitute; unroasted or partly roasted beans and pods are considered poisonous.

stories.summary: A woody shrub native to South America, including Brazil, Paraguay and parts of the Andes. Its starchy storage roots are an important food crop, but roots, peels and leaves require correct preparation because raw or poorly processed material can release poisonous cyanide.
stories.edibilityNote: Starchy roots are eaten boiled or processed into flour and tapioca; roots, peels and leaves are dangerous raw and require correct preparation.

stories.summary: A cold-sensitive perennial herb or small shrub native to Cyprus, the Mediterranean, Turkey, western Asia, the Arabian Peninsula and the Levant. Its very smooth, aromatic leaves have sweet pine and citrus flavours and are used fresh or dried in seasoning blends.
stories.edibilityNote: Fresh or dried aromatic leaves season foods and herb blends; marjoram is also used in herbal tea.

stories.summary: A moss common throughout Europe, it favours base-rich rocks, walls and concrete, and occasionally grows at tree bases. It forms dark green cushions, with cylindrical capsules held conspicuously above the leaves.

An evergreen shrub native to southeastern Arizona and the mountains of eastern, western and southern Mexico. Its crushed leaves have a strong scent described as mint-like or resembling blackcurrants, while its flowers range from magenta and red to pink and rose.
stories.edibilityNote: Grown in central Mexico as a medicinal plant and used to make tea.

stories.summary: A perennial, semi-evergreen herb native to warm-temperate southern Europe, the Mediterranean and Africa. It has leathery dark-green leaves and summer flowers ranging from pale lavender or pink to white.
stories.edibilityNote: Used with beans, meats, stuffing, soups and sauces; its strong raw flavour diminishes during prolonged cooking.

stories.summary: A deciduous or semi-evergreen hybrid shrub first raised in Italy in 1886. Its arching branches carry glossy dark-green leaves and clusters of fragrant, pink-tinged white bell-shaped flowers from late summer well into autumn.

A herbaceous plant generally considered a hybrid, it occurs widely but patchily across much of Canada and the central and eastern United States. It has simple alternating leaves on green stems and bears yellow flowers in late summer.

A flowering herbaceous perennial hybrid created in cultivation in 1890 from several daisies originating on three continents. It has the classic daisy form of white petals around a yellow centre, but is larger than the oxeye daisy.

A hybrid vine believed to descend from Lonicera sempervirens and Lonicera × americana. Its twining stems bear opposite simple leaves and fragrant flowers shading from pink to yellow, prized in gardens for their showiness and long flowering season.

A cultivated banana hybrid between Musa acuminata and Musa balbisiana, domesticated very early by humans. Its apparent trunk consists of fused leaf bases; each produces one flowering stem, dies after fruiting and may be replaced by shoots from the base.
stories.edibilityNote: Its cultivars include cooking and dessert bananas; the described banana-da-terra fruit is mainly cooked, fried or baked.

stories.summary: A garden hybrid of unstated native origin, this petunia encompasses hybrids derived from Petunia axillaris and P. integrifolia, with other members of the latter’s complex also involved. Most petunias sold for home gardens are this type, which tolerates hot climates and grows readily in containers.

A vigorous hybrid tree of unstated native origin, grey poplar arose from white poplar and common aspen. Its leaves have a thin grey down and are much less deeply lobed than white poplar leaves, while the tree can grow markedly larger than either parent.

A naturally occurring flowering hybrid native to Europe, polyanthus grows where common cowslip and common primrose overlap. Wild individuals tend to have yellow flowers, while garden cultivars have been developed in many colours.

A tall hybrid shrub of unstated native origin, this rose has been cultivated in Europe since ancient times. It has arching stems, bluish-green leaves and sweet-scented flowers, usually white or pink with many petals, and blooms only in midsummer.

An artificial deciduous shrub hybrid with no native range stated, Van Houtte's spiraea was created from two Asian species. It is vigorous, appears sterile and is typically encountered around old hedges, homesteads and roadsides; it is introduced in Europe and the eastern United States.

A large-flowered garden hybrid of European and Asian origin, the garden pansy was developed from several Viola species. Its flowers come in many colours and usually have a bold central “face”; although perennial, it is normally grown as an annual or biennial.

A genus of evergreen shrubs and small trees native to warm-temperate and subtropical East and Southeast Asia, Rhaphiolepis has glossy, leathery leaves, white or pink flowers and dark purple-to-black fruits. Some varieties have fruit that is edible when cooked for jam, but some ornamental varieties have no culinary value.
stories.edibilityNote: Some varieties have fruit edible when cooked and used for jam; some ornamental varieties produce fruit with no culinary value.

stories.summary: A genus of palms native to Southeast Asia, southern China, New Guinea and northern Australia, Arenga contains small to medium-sized species with long, feather-like leaves. These palms can grow with little sunlight and in relatively infertile soil.

A genus of palms native to Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina, Butia typically has long, feather-like leaves with a distinct downward arch. Many species produce edible fruits, sometimes used to make alcoholic drinks and other foods.
stories.edibilityNote: Many species produce edible fruits, sometimes made into alcoholic drinks and other foods.

stories.summary: A genus of green algae found worldwide in fresh, brackish and marine waters, Rhizoclonium usually forms straight or curved, unbranched threads. Short root-like structures anchor these threads, and the algae commonly inhabit saltmarshes, rock pools, mud and sand.

A genus of multicellular green algae found in freshwater, especially over limestone in temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere. Their stem- and leaf-like structures resemble land plants, while calcium deposits make them rough to the touch and they often have an unpleasant hydrogen-sulfide smell.
A genus of evergreen flowering trees native to southeastern Asia. Its members have leaves divided two or three times and large, bell-shaped flowers that may be white, pink, pale purple or yellow.

A genus of flowering plants native to Africa, with its current species found in tropical and southern regions. Some members bear notably large solitary flowers, although flowers in this family are generally grouped in clusters.

A garden hybrid first bred in France in 1880 from Crocosmia aurea and C. pottsii. It grows from a swollen underground stem and has long, sword-shaped leaves with deep-orange flowers. It is considered invasive in the United Kingdom, Isle of Man and New Zealand, and of limited invasive concern in California.

A perennial herbaceous mint hybrid indigenous to Europe and the Middle East. It usually produces no seed and spreads rapidly through runners, bearing dark-green leaves and purple flowers. Fresh or dried leaves are commonly brewed as tea and used to flavour foods, sweets and drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: Fresh or dried leaves are used in tea and to flavour foods, sweets, preserves, alcoholic drinks and chewing gum.

stories.summary: A rhizome-forming perennial mint hybrid native to temperate and warm-temperate Europe. It occurs in meadows, pastures and disturbed ground, and has wide-spreading fleshy underground stems. In Cuba it is a core ingredient in the mojito cocktail, though other mints may substitute when it is unavailable.
stories.edibilityNote: In Cuba it is a core mojito ingredient; the Cuban mojito-mint variety is also grown for other culinary uses.

stories.summary: A hybrid leguminous tree that originated in Hong Kong around 1880. It has large, thick leaves and fragrant, orchid-like purplish-red flowers that usually bloom from early November through March. It is generally sterile, and apparently all cultivated trees descend from one grown at the Hong Kong Botanical Gardens.

A compact evergreen hybrid shrub that can develop into a medium-sized tree. Its oval leaves emerge crimson red, especially in early spring, before becoming dark green; large clusters of small white flowers appear in late spring.

A deciduous hybrid tree created in cultivation in France soon after 1700 by crossing European and North American poplars. It is vigorous and broadly column-shaped, with separate male and female trees bearing red pollen catkins or green seed catkins. Heavy mistletoe infestation is a useful clue for distinguishing it from European black poplar.

An erect wetland hybrid originating from broad-leaved and narrow-leaved cattails, it is abundant in the upper Midwestern United States, where its parents hybridize. It has long, swordlike leaves and velvety brown flower spikes, and can spread rapidly into dense stands that displace other plants.
stories.edibilityNote: Rhizomes and pollen were eaten historically by Indigenous Americans and Europeans; contaminated water can make them dangerous because the plant accumulates metals and other toxins.

stories.summary: A perennial herb hybrid occurring naturally in the Caucasus region, Russian comfrey grows on waste ground and disturbed soils. It has a deep taproot, hairy above-ground growth, and flowers that turn from pink to blue or remain purple.
stories.edibilityNote: Documented for human consumption; Bocking No. 4 is recommended, but prolonged intake of its alkaloids may damage the liver, prompting food-use restrictions.

stories.summary: A cosmopolitan genus of macroscopic green algae ranging from the Arctic to the Antarctic, Prasiola occurs on land and in fresh and marine water. It forms single-cell-thick blades shaped like fans, ribbons or wedges; marine forms often grow side by side as dense green turf on rocks.
stories.edibilityNote: Species are harvested for food, especially Prasiola japonica in Japan and Myanmar.

stories.summary: A widespread genus of red algae found in marine and freshwater environments, Audouinella grows as small tufts of red, brown or black hairlike threads on solid surfaces. The black-brush form is an aquarium nuisance because most algae-eating fish and invertebrates avoid it.
A nearly worldwide genus of red algae in the family Bonnemaisoniaceae.
A genus of red algae in the family Kallymeniaceae. Several species are harvested as edible seaweeds called carola, especially Callophyllis variegata.
stories.edibilityNote: Several species are used as food under the name carola, most commonly Callophyllis variegata.

stories.summary: A genus of evergreen subtropical and tropical plants found in Asia, Indonesia, New Guinea and the Philippines, Aeschynanthus species are usually trailing plants that grow on other plants. Their brightly coloured flowers are pollinated by sunbirds; some species have thick, waxy leaves while others have softer ones.
A 75-species plant genus native to tropical sub-Saharan Africa, the southern Arabian Peninsula, southern and southeastern Asia, New Guinea and Australia.

A genus of African flowering shrubs found mainly in South Africa and Namibia, Eriocephalus often has silky-grey leaves and a spicy scent when bruised. Its flower heads become strikingly woolly after flowering.
stories.edibilityNote: Various species have been used on a small scale in cooking, similarly to rosemary.

stories.summary: A flowering-plant genus growing chiefly across Africa and Madagascar, Dombeya has its greatest diversity in Madagascar, with about 175 native species there. Its flowers can superficially resemble those of pears or hydrangeas, although those plants are unrelated.
Plant genus in the nettle family, native from northern Africa to China, Southeast Asia and Australia.

Tree genus native from South and Southeast Asia to northern Australia and the western Pacific. Its trees have simple alternating leaves, pale flowers and lens-shaped fruits with a woody stone containing one seed.

Genus of flowering shrubs, small trees and rare vines native to the Neotropics. They typically have simple oval leaves and large, five-lobed, trumpet-like flowers; some flowers are showy and scented at night.
Plant genus native chiefly to South Africa, with a few species elsewhere in southern Africa and on several islands. Most species have densely leafy stems.
Plant genus native from Costa Rica through southern tropical America and Trinidad.
Plant genus native to tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa, Australia and various oceanic islands.

Genus of tropical and subtropical flowering vines native to the southwestern United States, Mexico, Central America, the West Indies and South America. Its often fragrant flowers may be white, pink, yellow or red, and the vines can cover walls or trellises.

Genus of evergreen trees native to northeastern New South Wales and central and southeastern Queensland, Australia. Its round fruits have exceptionally tough woody shells; only M. integrifolia and M. tetraphylla are commercially grown for edible nuts, while the other two species contain cyanogenic glycosides.
stories.edibilityNote: M. integrifolia and M. tetraphylla nuts are cultivated for human food; M. jansenii and M. ternifolia nuts contain cyanogenic glycosides.

stories.summary: Genus of shrubs or small trees native to China, Japan and southeastern Asia. In spring, it produces clustered flowers with slender, strap-shaped petals resembling those of witch-hazel.

Genus of succulent plants native to southern Africa. Their nearly fused leaf pairs are mostly buried, with translucent upper surfaces that admit light, while stone-like colours and patterns camouflage them in rocky ground.

A genus of low-growing evergreen shrubs and subshrubs native to southwestern Europe, southern Greece, Turkey and Algeria. It bears five-lobed blue or white flowers and is often grown in rock gardens or raised beds.
A genus of Eurasian and North African flowering plants.

A genus of perennial stem succulents native to eastern and southern Africa and Arabia. Its five-lobed, often vividly striped flowers can be funnel- or bell-shaped and commonly emit a carrion-like scent that attracts flies. In southern Ethiopia, various Huernia species are boiled and eaten with sorghum as famine food.
stories.edibilityNote: Various Huernia species in southern Ethiopia are boiled and eaten with sorghum as famine food.

stories.summary: A genus of shrubs and small trees whose 17 species are native to Mexico and Central America.
A genus of cacti with no explicitly stated native origin in the supplied information. All listed species occur in Argentina, with some also recorded in Bolivia and Chile.

An evergreen shrub endemic to Madeira Island. Its branched stems bear three-part spines, glossy yellow flowers grow in clusters, and ripe berries are blue-black; this rare plant inhabits laurel forest and high rocky escarpments.

An evergreen shrub or tree native to eastern Africa. Its leaves contain the stimulant cathinone; fresh leaves and tops are chewed, or less often dried for tea, to produce euphoria and stimulation, and the WHO classifies khat as a drug of abuse that can cause psychological dependence.
stories.edibilityNote: Fresh leaves and tops are chewed; less often, dried material is consumed as tea for stimulation.

stories.summary: A perennial climbing shrub endemic to Madeira Island. Its branched stems become woody with age, and its white funnel-shaped flowers have pink stripes; it grows mainly in laurel forest and also on the Desertas Islands.

A tropical tree native to Southeast Asia and southern China. Its edible fruit has translucent, sweet, mildly aromatic flesh around a large black seed that creates an eye-like appearance. The flesh is eaten raw or used fresh, dried, preserved or canned in soups, snacks and desserts; the peel and seed are not eaten.
stories.edibilityNote: The flesh is eaten raw or used fresh, dried, preserved or canned; the peel and seed are not eaten.

stories.summary: An evergreen shrub that matures into a tree, native to South America. Its caffeine-containing leaves are steeped in hot water as mate or brewed cold as tereré, drinks with a typically bitter, herb-like flavour.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are steeped in hot water for mate or brewed cold for tereré; both drinks contain caffeine.

stories.summary: A large shrub or small tree native to northern China and Korea. Unusually for citrus, it has deciduous leaves divided into three leaflets, large thorns and finely downy fruit.
stories.edibilityNote: The very bitter fruit is generally considered inedible fresh, but can be made into marmalade or dried and powdered as a condiment.

stories.summary: A freshwater green-algae genus whose native origin is not stated. Its cylindrical cells join end to end in large colonies resembling pentagonal or hexagonal nets; microscopic daughter nets develop within parent cells.

A freshwater green-algae genus with a more or less worldwide distribution. Its cells form round, hollow colonies linked by extensions of their walls, and new daughter colonies develop inside parent cells.

A filamentous freshwater green-algae genus found in both hemispheres. Its narrow cylindrical cells form unbranched green strands that may attach by a colourless holdfast or float in surface mats; species are difficult to identify because decisive features appear only during uncommon reproductive stages.

A genus of microscopic freshwater green algae found around the world. Each cell has two matching halves, usually separated by a deep central constriction, and many species bear long arm-like projections or walls decorated with granules or spines.
A cactus genus native to the West Indies and Florida. Its members grow as trees and have male and female reproductive functions on separate plants or mostly separate plants.

A summer annual cereal grass whose centre of diversity and suggested domestication area is the Sahel of West Africa. It has unusually large millet grains and tolerates drought, heat, poor soil, salinity and low soil acidity better than many cereal crops.
stories.edibilityNote: The grain or flour is widely prepared as porridges, flatbreads, fermented drinks and local beer in Africa and India.

stories.summary: A filamentous green-algae genus common in freshwater habitats around the world. It usually forms unbranched chains one cell thick, while each long cylindrical cell contains one or two flat ribbon-like chloroplasts that twist in response to light.

A genus of microscopic green algae found in freshwater worldwide, Cosmarium usually consists of single cells. Each cell is pinched in the middle into two lobes, and its wall may be smooth or decorated with spines, granules, pits or pores.

A freshwater green-algae genus with a worldwide distribution, Eudorina forms spherical, swimming colonies. These colonies contain dozens of two-tailed cells embedded in a shared matrix and can reproduce sexually or asexually.
A flowering-plant genus native to temperate Eurasia and northwestern Africa, Pilosella contains approximately 250 species.
A flowering-plant genus native to Europe, the Caucasus and the Middle East as far east as Iran, Atocion has its greatest species diversity in the Balkans.
A Eurasian genus of flowering grasses, Avenula currently contains just one accepted species.

A deciduous hybrid flowering plant first bred near Paris from Magnolia denudata and Magnolia liliiflora, Magnolia × soulangeana grows as a large, many-stemmed shrub or small tree. Its large white, pink or purple flowers open dramatically on bare branches in early spring, shortly before the leaves.

A genus of small, dry-adapted tropical trees native to Mexico and Central America, Beaucarnea has trunks with conspicuously flared bases. Flowers appear only on old trees, in large clusters of numerous tiny greenish-white blooms.
An orchid genus native to Mexico, Central America and Venezuela, Rhynchostele includes both species and hybrids.

An orchid genus from Central and South America, Stanhopea mostly grows on other plants in damp forests. Its complex, usually fragrant flowers hang downward, often emerging through the bottom of containers, but generally last no more than three days.

A small genus of orchids found growing on other plants in wet forests from Mexico and Central America to Colombia, Venezuela and Trinidad, Guarianthe contains four listed species and a natural hybrid.

A genus of evergreen herbaceous flowering perennials native to tropical regions of the Americas and southeastern Asia. Its glossy dark-green leaves form rosettes, while each flowering structure pairs a pale central spike with a prominent white or greenish-white modified leaf.
stories.edibilityNote: At least one species is eaten: the young flower spike of S. matudae is pickled in vinegar or cooked with eggs.

stories.summary: A genus of epiphytic cacti native to Central America, the Caribbean and northern South America. Its tropical species grow on trees or rocks, and some develop stems that begin round before flattening into leaflike forms.
A genus of epiphytic cacti native to Mexico. It grows without parasitizing its host on tree branches, producing drooping or creeping, ribbed stems covered in many small spines.

A genus of succulent plants native to semi-arid Mexico and Central America. Its members are generally large, evergreen, clump-forming perennials with grey-green leaves and tall flower spikes, and may need protection from frost.
A genus of flowering plants native to Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Hispaniola and the Bahamas.

A moss found across temperate Eurasia and widespread in Central Europe. Its unusually large, tongue-shaped leaves become distinctly cross-waved when wet; sterile shoots arch over, while fertile shoots stand upright and branch into rosette-like or tiny tree-like forms.

A genus of bushy cacti with strongly ribbed stems branching from the base. Its tubular summer flowers may be reddish, orange, greenish or yellow, and its red fruits are eaten fresh or dried or made into sauces, ice cream and jams.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruits are eaten fresh or dried and used in sauces, ice cream and jams.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering plants native to dry meadows of the Mediterranean region. Its cornflower-like summer blooms come in blue, yellow and white and are grown for sunny borders and dried arrangements.

A tropical evergreen fruit tree native to eastern Mexico and Central America south to Costa Rica. Its ripe fruit has edible skin and smooth pulp whose flavour varies from bland to banana, peach, pear or vanilla flan, but its large seeds are inedible.
stories.edibilityNote: The ripe fruit's thin skin and pulp are edible; its one to five large seeds are inedible.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering shrubs and occasional small trees native to Australia and New Zealand. Its sometimes-sticky foliage bears alternate leaves and heads of white, cream, yellow or pinkish flowers surrounded by several rows of modified leaves.

An orchid genus native to southern Mexico, Central America, the West Indies and Venezuela, Myrmecophila grows on trees or rocks. Its lightly scented flowers appear on tall, pole-like growths, while large hollow, banana-shaped pseudobulbs commonly house ant colonies.

A perennial herbaceous orchid subfamily occurring across parts of the Americas, Europe and Asia, Cypripedioideae is distinguished by slipper-shaped flower pouches. These trap insects and direct them past the reproductive structures, while the flowers unusually have two fertile anthers.

An orchid genus, Gennaria had two accepted species as of March 2018. Gennaria diphylla occurs in Macaronesia, north-west Africa and south-west Europe, while Gennaria griffithii ranges from Afghanistan to China.

A clump-forming perennial hybrid native to South Africa, Kniphofia × praecox is believed to result from Kniphofia uvaria crossed with K. bruceae. It has narrow, grass-like leaves and upright flower clusters whose buds change from scarlet through reddish-orange to yellow as they mature.

A bulbous hybrid developed from iris species native to Portugal, Spain and North Africa, Iris × hollandica has narrow green leaves and large, unscented flowers ranging from blue to yellow or white. It mainly blooms in May–June in the Northern Hemisphere and September–October in the Southern Hemisphere.

A succulent genus native to South Africa and the far south-west of Namibia, Gasteria has thick, hard, tongue-shaped leaves arranged in opposite rows or spirals. Its curved, hanging flowers have a distinctive swollen, stomach-like base.

A flowering-plant genus in the daisy family, Sphagneticola includes five recognized species. Among them, Sphagneticola trilobata is native to South America and has become widely naturalized across many tropical and subtropical regions.
A moss genus with a cosmopolitan distribution, Microbryum belongs to the family Pottiaceae.
A flowering-plant genus native from Mexico to Colombia, Rogiera contains 15 species. Rogiera amoena, R. cordata and R. gratissima are sometimes grown as ornamentals.

A flowering-plant genus in the daisy family, Chrysanthellum includes members recorded across parts of the Americas. Examples include Chrysanthellum pusillum in the Galápagos and C. integrifolium in Central America and southern Mexico.
A genus of tree-like cacti from Puebla and Oaxaca, Mexico. Its species form dense crowns of repeatedly forked green shoots, and bear juicy red fruits that are edible.
stories.edibilityNote: The juicy red fruits are edible.

stories.summary: A liverwort genus with a cosmopolitan distribution.
A fern genus with furry rhizomes that spread across potting mix and root into it. Its triangular, finely divided fronds and fast-spreading rhizomes make it especially suited to hanging baskets.

A genus of perennial succulents native to eastern and central Mexico, where they grow on rocky, well-drained slopes. They form rosettes of thick leaves, often with a striking blue, teal or lavender coating, and their delicate stems may trail as they age.
A genus of small succulents endemic to southern Africa. They form compact leaf rosettes; some species have translucent panels in their leaves, while water stress can turn the plants red or purple.

A genus of small fan palms native to southeastern Asia, from southern Japan and southern China to Sumatra. Their thin stems branch at the base to form clumps, while bare leaf stalks end in rounded fans of many leaflets; male and female flowers grow on separate plants.
A genus of spiny flowering shrubs native to southern South America. Its five species can fix nitrogen despite not being legumes.
A genus of Mesoamerican plants in the daisy family.

A genus of flowering trees indigenous from Central America to northern Argentina, Paraguay, Brazil and Chile; one species is also native to the Antilles. Its large yellow or magenta flowers often appear on leafless branches near the end of the dry season, and its wood is exceptionally hard and heavy.
A succulent hybrid originating in Mexico. Its short, jelly-bean-like leaves change from green to red in summer, and bright yellow flowers appear in mid-spring.
stories.edibilityNote: Poisonous if ingested; contact may also cause irritation.

stories.summary: A small evergreen tree native to the tropical continental Americas, although its exact origin is unknown. Its prickly green fruit has juicy, aromatic, acidic white flesh that is edible, while the leathery skin is inedible and the black seeds are indigestible.
stories.edibilityNote: The white fruit pulp is eaten or used in drinks and sweets; the leathery skin is inedible and black seeds are indigestible.

stories.summary: A large succulent native to Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit, Michoacán and Aguascalientes in Mexico. It has spiky, fleshy leaves and sends up a tall, yellow-flowered stalk before dying. Only the Weber Azul cultivar supplies tequila: its mature heart is heated, pressed, fermented and distilled.
stories.edibilityNote: The heated heart of the Weber Azul cultivar is pressed, and its sugary liquid is fermented and distilled into tequila.

stories.summary: A genus of about thirteen species of single-celled or colonial green algae, with no native origin stated. Its rounded, non-swimming cells contain green pigments and can multiply rapidly under ideal conditions. Chlorella is consumed as a dietary supplement, but its tough natural cell walls must be pulverized for humans to digest it.
stories.edibilityNote: Consumed as a dietary supplement; its tough natural cell walls must be pulverized for humans to digest it.

stories.summary: A cosmopolitan genus of freshwater red algae, found mainly in rivers and less often in standing water. It forms slippery, gelatin-coated filaments and has a complex life cycle in which some stages grow attached to and depend on others.

A family of freshwater red algae found in rivers and streams, with no narrower native origin supplied. Each thread grows from a single tip cell, and its life cycle passes through several distinct reproductive forms.

A genus of evergreen shrubs native to Zimbabwe and South Africa. Its dense flower heads have prominent, pin-like structures, while ants carry the seeds of all species underground, protecting them from fire.
A genus of evergreen flowering shrubs native to wet slopes and banks in southern Africa. It bears many hanging, tubular flowers over a long summer period, in shades of white, yellow and red.

A tree fern native to Madagascar and widely distributed across sub-Saharan Africa. It usually has a stout trunk, dense crown and large arching fronds, and often grows in open, moist places such as grasslands and stream banks.

An Australian-endemic genus of flowering shrubs, found in every state except the Northern Territory. Its species have simple alternating leaves, usually five-petalled flowers with inward-curving stamens, and capsules that release their seeds explosively.

A genus of perennial flowering herbs native to Africa. Its species form leafy basal rosettes and bear colourful daisy-like heads, while cultivated hybrids are widely grown as garden plants and cut flowers in many colours and forms.

An East Asian genus of evergreen flowering perennials native to stream banks and seashores. Its plants spread through underground stems and have rounded, leathery leaves with bright yellow flowers in autumn and winter.

A genus of flowering herbs and small shrubs, with most species endemic to Australia and a few occurring in New Zealand and New Guinea. They bear white, blue, pink or mauve ray flowers around yellow centres and inhabit environments ranging from rainy coasts and mountains to dry central Australia.

An Australian shrub or small tree native to New South Wales and Queensland. It grows mainly in warm-temperate and subtropical rainforest gullies and along small watercourses, bearing large pointed leaves, yellowish flowers and small black berries containing many seeds.

An Australian-endemic small, rounded shrub with tangled, woolly branchlets that give it a silvery appearance. It grows on exposed southern coastal cliffs and dunes, tolerating wind, sea spray, drought and frost, and produces rounded white-yellow flower heads in summer.

A tree fern native to southeastern mainland Australia, Tasmania and Norfolk Island. Its massive upright trunk supports a crown of long fronds that are dark green above and paler below, while old spiny frond bases often remain around the trunk after withering.
stories.edibilityNote: An 1889 account says Aboriginal Australians ate the starchy pulp from the top of the trunk raw or roasted; it was also boiled.

stories.summary: A cosmopolitan genus of freshwater green algae, with no narrower native origin stated. It forms branching chains of cells enclosed in soft slime, usually growing in cold, well-aerated water attached to sand, rocks or other aquatic plants.

A genus of unicellular freshwater green algae with no native origin stated. Its typically flattened cells have two matching, often intricately lobed halves joined by a narrow bridge containing the nucleus, and the algae occur mainly in nutrient-poor to moderately fertile lakes and bogs.
A genus of succulent plants indigenous to southern Africa.

A family of green algae whose members are common freshwater microalgae, with a few occurring in semi-saline water. Their solitary or colonial cells have distinctive multilayered walls, with fibres in adjoining layers running across one another.

A genus of green algae commonly found in freshwater plankton, especially in nutrient-rich ponds and lakes. It usually forms rows of cells with spiny ends and ornamented walls, although solitary cells also occur.

An evergreen, mat-forming perennial hybrid with no agreed natural origin. Its lemon-scented foliage and pink-to-lavender summer flowers are especially memorable. The leaves are eaten raw or used fresh or dried in cooking and herbal teas.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves are eaten raw in salads or used fresh or dried in cooking and herbal teas.

stories.summary: A perennial coastal flowering plant native to temperate parts of Africa, Asia and Europe, it grows on salt marshes and sea cliffs. It has narrow, fleshy leaves and yellow flower heads that can smell like shoe polish. Young leaves may be eaten raw or cooked.
stories.edibilityNote: Young leaves may be eaten raw or cooked; they were formerly sold in London markets for pickling.

stories.summary: A genus of succulent, drought-adapted plants in the daisy family.
A perennial daisy native to the Andes, yacón is grown for its crisp, sweet-tasting storage roots. Its mature stems are hollow, while branching underground rhizomes continually produce new shoots.
stories.edibilityNote: Tubers are eaten raw, boiled, roasted or processed; South American leaf infusions are medicinal, but oral leaf use is discouraged.

stories.summary: A herbaceous hybrid native to India, giant spider lily is reported as a cross between Crinum asiaticum and Crinum zeylanicum.
A flowering garden hybrid of Bougainvillea glabra and Bougainvillea peruviana. It is an evergreen, thorny vine with tiny white trumpet-shaped flowers surrounded by showy magenta-rose papery bracts.

A thorny, shrubby tree hybrid native to Southeast Asia, the Key lime arose naturally from a wild papeda and citron. Its fruit is smaller, seedier, more acidic and more aromatic than the Persian lime, with a notably thin rind. Usually picked green, it turns yellow when ripe.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit flavours Key lime pie; boiled in brine and dried fruit is used as black lime, a Middle Eastern condiment.

stories.summary: A hybrid citrus tree native to Southeast Asia, bitter orange bears orange fruit with a distinctly bitter or sour taste and has long thorns. Its raw pulp is not usually eaten, but the fruit and peel are widely used in marmalade, sweets, cooking and drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: Raw pulp is not usually eaten; the fruit, juice and peel are used in marmalade, sweets, cooking, condiments and drinks.

stories.summary: A small evergreen citrus hybrid of uncertain origin, possibly arising in northeastern India during the first millennium BC. It produces pointed oval yellow fruit with aromatic rind and notably sour juice; the juice, pulp and rind are widely used in foods and drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: The juice, pulp and rind are used in cooking, baking and drinks; whole lemons are also made into preserves and liqueurs.

stories.summary: A genus of trees occurring from temperate to tropical East Asia. Its members have deciduous, glossy, feather-like leaves.

An order of ferns that includes most tree ferns. Members range from tree-like forms with upright, trunk-like stems to plants with short or horizontally spreading stems, and no single obvious physical feature characterizes the whole order.

A perennial bulb-forming flowering plant native to parts of mainland Portugal. Its leaves emerge in autumn, remain green until spring and die back in summer, while solitary flowers usually appear from September to November. All parts contain toxic colchicine.
stories.edibilityNote: All parts contain toxic colchicine; the bulb has the lowest concentration, but the species is considered unfit for human consumption.

stories.summary: An Old World genus of annual and perennial flowering herbs distributed from the Mediterranean region to Central Asia, with a few species extending to China. A memorable identifying feature is the ring beneath each flower head, whose tube bears eight pits; flowers may be pink, violet-pink or blue.

A genus of red algae distributed widely through temperate, tropical and Antarctic seas, with greatest diversity in the Southern Hemisphere. Its members are bright red, with strongly flattened, delicately branching fronds that divide into small branchlets.

A genus of green algae with no native origin stated in the supplied source. Its larger spore-producing phase and less conspicuous sexual phase were once treated under different names before laboratory culture showed they were stages of the same life cycle.
A genus of flowering plants recorded from Africa and Southeast Asia.
A genus of flowering plants in the nightshade family; its native origin is not supplied.

A rhizome-forming perennial of uncertain native origin, it grows across the Middle East and northern Africa and was traditionally planted on graves in Muslim regions. It has a violet-scented rhizome and fragrant white flowers, sometimes flushed with pale blue or lavender.
stories.edibilityNote: Its violet-scented rhizome is used in sweets, to mature Chianti wine and in gin, although most parts are poisonous if eaten.

stories.summary: A flowering plant found in southern and western Europe; its native origin is not specified. It grows from an underground storage organ, favouring cultivated ground and damp lawns, and flowers from March to June.
A genus of flowering plants native around the Mediterranean and eastward to Iran.
A genus of flowering plants native to the Mediterranean, occurring across parts of North Africa and southern Europe.
A genus of ferns in the polypody family; its native origin is not supplied.

A genus of flowering plants native to mountain habitats in central, eastern and southern Africa, including Madagascar and the Comoro Islands. Its five-petalled tubular flowers arch above the plant, while the pointed fruits twist into spirals.
A semi-evergreen hybrid shrub endemic to China. It has leathery leaves and rose-purple flowers flecked with dark red.

A genus of flowering plants whose species are all endemic to Brazil. These trailing or spreading plants usually grow on other plants and have small, firm, succulent leaves; some species bear pouch-shaped flowers resembling goldfish.

A genus of low-growing cacti from South America. The usually rounded stems often have a chin-like projection below each spine-bearing point, while white, pink, yellow or red flowers open near the top.
A genus of shrubs native to Australia and also found wild on Norfolk Island. Its leaves grow in rings of three or four, and the upper flower petal is split into two lobes.

A genus of slender, often branching cacti native to mountainous parts of South America. Its many tubular flowers barely open at their tips and occur in colours ranging from green and white to yellow, orange, red and violet.
A genus of flowering plants in the carrot family.
An algal genus whose species are found in Europe and North America.

A genus of columnar cacti known from the Andes of southern Ecuador and Peru. Its members have pink-white flowers and columns covered with spines and white hair. Their fruit is edible, sweet and juicy.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is described at genus level as edible, sweet and juicy.

stories.summary: A palm found in Trinidad and Central and South America, especially floodplains and islands of the Brazilian Amazon. Its hanging fruit cluster is enclosed in a tough, flexible fibrous sack. Riverside communities use its fronds for roofing.

A tropical herbaceous perennial genus native to eastern Africa, from Kenya to KwaZulu-Natal and Zimbabwe. Its sole species grows slowly from a large, fleshy, potato-like underground stem and bears upright leaves with glossy foliage.
A genus of red algae found worldwide in intertidal zones and shallow water. Its species have folded, thin blades in red, brown or dark green, and some are farmed to make edible nori.
stories.edibilityNote: Multiple species are used for edible nori, especially Pyropia yezoensis and P. haitanensis.

stories.summary: An ornamental yucca native to the southern United States, from coastal southeastern Virginia through Florida and west to Texas. It often develops a trunk, then branches and sends up suckers to form colonies.

A flowering-plant hybrid native to Ecuador, produced naturally from Brugmansia aurea and B. versicolor. It is a large shrub or small tree with broad, rough, pale-green leaves and large hanging white trumpet-shaped flowers that may be tinged pink.

A genus of annual or perennial herbs and shrubs known from Africa, with most recorded species in South Africa. It typically has alternating leaves with toothed edges and round flower heads, usually held on long stalks.

A genus of robust, upright perennial flowering plants native to eastern Asia, including eastern China and the Russian Far East. They grow from underground stems; some members, such as Japanese knotweed and its hybrid with R. sachalinensis, are highly invasive after introduction to Europe and North America.
A small flowering bush found in Japan and introduced to Australia and New Zealand. It has alternating, tapering leaves and red berries, and is considered a weed in New Zealand.

A large deciduous hybrid tree occurring naturally at scattered sites in Europe where both parent species are native. It often develops burrs and dense brushy growth at the trunk base, while fragrant early-summer flowers attract bees. Raw leaves are edible once the stalks are removed, and the flowers are used for tea.
stories.edibilityNote: Leaves can be eaten raw without their stalks; flowers are used to make tea.

stories.summary: An ornamental deciduous hybrid shrub of garden origin. Its upright form carries arching branches, with bright yellow flowers appearing on one- to two-year-old growth; it is among the earliest shrubs to bloom.

An artificial flowering-plant hybrid created in Nantes, France, in 1912. It combines a shrubby form with five-lobed leaves; its weak branches bend unless tied to a support, when it can grow as a vine. Yellowish-white flowers appear in late autumn or early winter and are usually sterile.

A cultivated citrus hybrid of Key lime and lemon, known only in cultivation. The nearly thornless plant bears seedless, thick-skinned fruit that is sold green but turns yellow when ripe. The fruit is used as seasoning and in drinks, and is also dried for Persian cooking.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is used as seasoning and in drinks, including caipirinha, and is often used dried in Persian cuisine.

stories.summary: A genus of green algae found mainly in stagnant, warm-temperate or tropical fresh water, with some reports from moist soil. It forms floating masses of branched filaments and develops distinctive swollen, dark resting cells that can sprout new branches.

A small, bushy flowering hybrid with dense, dull green, wavy leaves. Its pink flowers have a dark blotch near the centre and appear successively from spring to summer, although each flower lasts only one day.

A fruiting hybrid of a North American blackberry and European raspberry, accidentally bred in Santa Cruz, California, in 1881. The plant and fruit resemble blackberry more than raspberry, but the ripe fruit is dark red rather than black. Its edible berries are eaten fresh or made into juice, preserves, baked dishes, syrups and wine.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten fresh or used for juice, jams, pies, crumbles, syrups and country wines.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering plants in the daisy family, native to temperate Asia, primarily Russia and China.

An orchid subtribe containing about 70 genera and more than 1,000 species. Most species have swollen stem bases and folded leaves, and hybrids can sometimes be formed between different genera within the group.

A genus of flowering orchids occurring from tropical and subtropical Asia to the western Pacific. These plants grow on other plants and have long, sometimes branched hanging stems, leathery leaves in two rows, and dense clusters of many small flowers on drooping stalks.

A small deciduous tree or shrub thought to originate in eastern Asia, though its precise natural range is uncertain because of extensive cultivation. It usually has thorny branches, and its oval fruit changes from smooth green with an apple-like taste to brown or purplish-black and wrinkled. The fruit is eaten fresh, dried or candied.
stories.edibilityNote: The fruit is eaten fresh, dried or candied and is also used in drinks, preserves, pickles and desserts.

stories.summary: A genus of flowering leaf succulents endemic to southern Africa. Its plants are easily propagated from their thick leaves.
A genus of grape-family plants native to the Afrotropics. The leaves of R. tomentosa and R. tridentata are eaten by silver-striped hawkmoth caterpillars.
A formerly recognized genus of cacti native to South America, from Bolivia and Peru to northwestern Argentina and northern Chile.

A dwarf tree fern native to warm, humid subtropical forests of South America. Its new fronds are striking deep red, sometimes pinkish-red, before maturing to glossy green, and its upright underground stem forms a thin trunk.
A genus of bromeliads endemic to the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil. It comprises about 22 recognized species divided between two subgenera.

A shrub or small tree native to southeastern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, Bolivia and northeastern Argentina. Its strong opposite branches form crosses, while its very fragrant pinkish-white flowers are followed by dark, velvety fruit.

An evergreen climbing hybrid whose origin is disputed between cultivation and natural occurrence in Brazil. It has opposite, thick, wrinkled leaves with prominent veins and pink flowers with yellow throats.

A climbing plant native to the Amazon basin and especially common in Brazil. Its split brown-to-red fruit exposes black seeds partly covered by white flesh, creating an eye-like appearance. Its caffeine-rich seeds are processed into soft drinks, while Guaranis prepare them as a sweetened hot drink after shelling, washing, drying and pounding.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds are made into soft drinks, a fermented drink and Guarani tea; preparation may include shelling, washing, drying, pounding, grating and hot water.

stories.summary: A flowering plant in the daisy family, prevalent throughout most of South Africa.
A genus of flowering plants native to eastern, central and southern Africa and Madagascar. It contains three accepted species.

A genus of non-aromatic annual flowering herbs occurring in Europe, Asia, North Africa and the Americas. Its branched stems may be upright or ground-hugging, while its somewhat fleshy leaves vary greatly in shape. Terminal flowers are usually bisexual, whereas side flowers are usually female.
A fern species native to New Zealand and also present in Australia. It is densely covered with black scales, and its new fronds are distinctively pinkish red.
A perennial bulb-forming hybrid of garden origin, produced from Crinum longifolium and Crinum moorei. It bears showy white or pink, lily-like flowers in summer and is cultivated for them.

A flowering hybrid of garden origin between Geranium endressii and Geranium versicolor. It is highly variable, with rounded, hand-shaped leaves and often veined flowers in shades of pink, and it can become invasive.
A shrub hybrid native to the Iberian Peninsula. Its hairy branches bear rough green leaves, often with rolled edges, and solitary flowers or clusters of up to eight. It flowers and fruits in June.

A perennial shrub reported from Madeira and Porto Santo. It has leaves with a densely white, woolly underside and numerous flower heads with bright purple centres and paler outer florets. On Madeira it inhabits laurel forests and high rocky cliffs.
A genus of flowering vines native to Latin America and the Caribbean. Its climbing members have distinctive three-pronged, hooked tendrils.
An order of green algae in Chlorophyta, with no native origin stated in the supplied sources. It is the only order in its class.
A fern species native from the Canary Islands through Europe, northern Africa and western Asia to the western Himalayas. It is the sole species in its genus.
A plant genus in the dogbane family, containing one species listed for Madagascar and another for South Africa.

A freshwater red-alga genus widespread across the Northern Hemisphere, despite being green in colour. Its stiff, coarse-hair-like strands may be branched or unbranched and have small swellings at intervals.

A genus of thread-forming green algae found mostly in soil and on moist surfaces, although aquatic species and one marine species are known. It forms unbranched, one-cell-wide threads of cylindrical or barrel-shaped cells.

A mostly freshwater green-alga genus with a worldwide distribution, found in still or flowing water and most commonly during colder months. Its unbranched, one-cell-wide threads have cells with two overlapping, H-shaped wall halves.

A flowering shrub or small tree native to eastern and western Africa, including Madagascar. Its drooping, angular branches bear spines, and male and female flowers usually grow on separate plants, although they may occur on one plant.

A flowering vine originating in tropical South America and Central America, perennial where the climate is frost-free. It has highly fragrant, multicoloured flowers with distinctive corkscrew-like shapes.
stories.edibilityNote: Seeds could be edible, but parts of the plant might be poisonous.

stories.summary: A cactus tribe found mostly in the tropical forests of Central and northern South America. Most members climb or grow on other plants, and their diverse flowers range from large white night-opening blooms to bright red daytime blooms.
A plant tribe from Southeast Asia and Oceania, with its main centre of diversity in Australia.

A tuberous begonia hybrid group derived primarily from high-altitude Latin American species. The plants die back to dormant tubers in winter and regrow, producing showy flowers in almost every colour except blue on forms ranging from trailing to upright.

A medium-sized artificial hybrid tree of uncertain origin that arose in Germany around 1818. It has dull red flower clusters and coarse, dark leaves, and is fertile enough to produce viable seeds whose offspring closely resemble the parent.
An ornamental flowering plant native to North Africa. It is the sole species in its genus, is cultivated in gardens and also grows as a weed in California.
A genus of red algae with 11 currently accepted species.
A flowering hybrid created from two species native to the Canary Islands. It can be raised from seed and is grown under cool conditions with protection from frost.

A one-species genus of flowering trees whose sole member, Curtisia dentata, is an evergreen native to South Africa. That species has dark glossy foliage and long-lasting white berries; harvesting its medicinal bark has contributed to declines in some areas, and the tree is protected in South Africa.

A genus of annual or perennial herbs and small woody shrubs found from southern and eastern Europe and northwestern Africa across Asia to the Himalayas and Altai Mountains. Its aromatic leaves and preference for open, often dry habitats are characteristic.

A widespread genus of freshwater green algae found floating in ponds and lakes or living on the bottom in mires and swamps. Its cells often form colonies that repeatedly double in number within a conspicuous, sometimes layered jelly-like envelope.

A possibly single-species genus of succulents native to Namaqualand in Namibia and South Africa’s Cape Provinces. Its rounded leaf tips have transparent windows, and wild plants commonly remain buried in sand except for these tips.

A deciduous willow hybrid native to Europe and western Asia, especially riversides and wetlands. Its twigs snap cleanly with an audible crack, while broken branches can root after waterways carry them downstream.

A genus of succulent flowering plants endemic to South Africa’s Cape Provinces. Its species have pairs of thick, grey-green, pitted leaves resembling split pebbles, with disproportionately large flowers emerging between them.

A subfamily of flowering aquatic plants that floats on or just below still or slow-moving fresh water. Duckweeds lack obvious stems and leaves; their simple bodies may have no roots or several rootlets and reproduce mainly by budding.
stories.edibilityNote: Consumed in Laos, Thailand and Myanmar, used in place of salads or vegetables, and cultivated as a vegetable in Israel.

stories.summary: A genus of bromeliads whose species are endemic to humid tropical and subtropical Brazil. Their flower clusters have a distinctive nest-like form.
A genus of flowering bromeliads native only to eastern Brazil. Its species grow on rocky outcrops and are generally giant bromeliads that collect substantial rainwater between their leaf bases.
A genus of orchids native to Costa Rica, Panama, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru. Each swollen stem bears one leaf, and the flowers resemble pansies.

A plant hybrid between Kalanchoe daigremontiana and Kalanchoe delagoensis. Its leaves are relatively narrow, with bases ranging from tapered or wedge-shaped to weakly heart-shaped or eared; of its four forms, only form A is considered invasive.
A flowering-plant hybrid native to mainland Portugal.

A genus of about 57 subtropical succulent species native to South Africa, especially Cape Province and the Karoo. Its plants have thick, soft paired leaves held near the ground and produce narrow-petalled yellow flowers in autumn and winter, sometimes with fragrance.

An intergeneric orchid hybrid group commonly cultivated in greenhouses as ornamentals. Its plants have branched flower stems bearing numerous long-lasting flowers, fleshy pseudobulbs and cultivars in many colours.

A small genus of perennial ginger-family plants native to cool forests from the eastern Himalayas through China and Vietnam. The plants die back in winter and reappear in spring, producing yellow or orange summer flowers surrounded by persistent coloured bracts.

A large deciduous hybrid tree most likely formed in Spain or southern France in the 17th century, though a London origin has also been suggested. It has broad, stiff, maple-like leaves and usually pale grey-green bark that peels away. Its tolerance of pollution and compacted soil makes it a popular urban tree.

A genus of bulbous flowering plants distributed from Zimbabwe to South Africa. Its plants have broad leaves and large bulbs usually partly exposed above ground, followed by star-shaped blue flowers and brownish seeds.
A genus of liverworts found mainly in the Northern Hemisphere.
A small genus of three succulent species endemic to coastal South Africa, Namibia and Angola. Its compact triangular leaves form three vertical or spiralling ranks.

A genus of succulent shrubs native to Southern Africa. Its members typically have many long, slender stems that climb or sprawl from a large woody base, along with soft, narrow triangular leaves that clasp the stem.

An orchid subtribe found across the American tropics, from southern Mexico to northern Argentina and Bolivia. Most members grow in shaded, wet lower-canopy settings, either in soil or on often moss-covered trees, and bear one to several spirally arranged flowers from young shoots.

A perennial herb native from Southern Europe through South Asia to Northeast Asia. Its fruit is enclosed by a large, papery orange-to-red covering resembling a lantern. A spreading root system can make it invasive where cultivated.
A monotypic genus of flowering plants native to Burundi, Gabon, Madagascar, Rwanda, Tanzania and the former Zaïre. It contains only Saintpauliopsis lebrunii.
A monotypic genus of flowering plants in the daisy family. Its sole species, Artemisiopsis villosa, is native to eastern and southern Africa.
A genus of flowering plants native to Africa. It belongs to the figwort family and includes species such as Freylinia crispa, Freylinia longiflora and Freylinia tropica.

A genus of short perennial succulents whose native origin is not supplied. The leaves usually form rosettes or spirals and often carry raised white markings, while small, pale, two-lipped flowers appear on tall stalks.

A genus of mosses whose native origin is not supplied. Its upright plants form loose or moderately dense cushions, with narrow leaves held upright or spreading slightly. Spore capsules may sit among the leaves or rise above them.

An evergreen perennial succulent indigenous to South Africa and Lesotho. It is stemless, with dense rosettes of soft, sawtoothed leaves bearing bristly edges and long threadlike tips. Its nectar-rich tubular orange flowers readily attract birds, bees and wasps.

A flowering plant endemic to South Africa’s Cape Province, Dymondia margaretae forms a flat, slow-growing and drought-tolerant carpet. Its leaves curl when water is needed, exposing their silver undersides.
A moss reported as restricted to wooded areas of open grassland in South Africa. However, the variety Oedipodiella australis var. catalaunica is reported from Spain.
A Neotropical subtribe of orchids comprising about 40 genera, including Cattleya, Laelia and Brassavola. Its members may grow in clumps, creep or climb, and may have one or several leaves.

A naturally occurring horsetail hybrid native to Europe and Asia, produced by Equisetum hyemale and Equisetum ramosissimum. It occurs in forests and damp, disturbed places such as clay banks and stream banks.

A naturally occurring oak hybrid native to central and northern Europe, where the ranges of sessile and pedunculate oaks overlap. It is fertile and variable in appearance, generally combining intermediate traits of both parents.

A flowering-plant subtribe whose genera are chiefly native to Africa, with fewer widespread in Arabia and Asia. Most genera are stem succulents that resemble cacti despite not being close relatives. Many have carrion-like flowers that attract flies, although not all smell unpleasant or use flies as pollinators.
A tribe of flowering plants in the sunflower family, with Helenium as its type genus and Gaillardia among its best-known members.

An annual herb native to Europe, from the Mediterranean north to Northern Ireland and Scotland. Its stems and wavy-edged leaves look white and woolly, while dense clusters of pale yellow flowers appear from July to September.

A perennial red seaweed whose attached form is widely distributed on both sides of the North Atlantic. It occurs in attached and drifting forms and can create dense underwater belts that provide spawning habitat for many fish. It is commercially harvested as a source of carrageenan.
stories.edibilityNote: Furcellaran extracted from this seaweed is used to add texture to foods such as sweets, ice cream and puddings.

stories.summary: A plant genus native to eastern Asia, including China, Japan, the Himalayas and Indochina.

A citrus hybrid native from the Philippines through parts of Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei to Taiwan and tropical southern China. It is a shrub or small tree with winged leaf stalks and white or purplish flowers; its small, round fruit has orange flesh and a very thin ripe peel. The naturally sour fruit is widely used in Philippine condiments, drinks, marinades and preserves.
stories.edibilityNote: The sour fruit and juice are used in condiments, drinks, marinades, preserves and cooked dishes; the peel is sweet.

stories.summary: A perennial flowering hybrid thought to have originated in the Mediterranean region. It grows from underground stems and flowers in mid-to-late spring, with cultivars spanning nearly every colour; some flower again in autumn.

An ornamental hosta of unstated origin, now treated as a cultivar rather than an accepted species. Typical plants have leaves with a broad white centre and green margins, though the centre can narrow or turn greener with time and growing conditions. Tall flower stalks bear pale lavender blossoms attractive to bees.
A genus of flowering succulent plants in the stonecrop family; no native origin is supplied.

A citrus hybrid of unstated native origin, first recorded in Italy in the early 19th century and later widely grown around the Mediterranean. Its sweet fruit is eaten, while oil from the rind flavours food and drinks.
stories.edibilityNote: The sweet fruit is eaten, and rind oil is used to flavour foods and drinks.

stories.summary: A monotypic flowering-plant genus whose sole species is native from southern Europe through South Asia to Northeast Asia. That species is a perennial herb remembered for its large, bright orange-red papery covering around the fruit, resembling a lantern. Its spreading roots can make it invasive.

A bushy shrub hybrid, probably of garden origin. It bears white to rose-pink, urn-shaped flowers in late winter and early spring. Unlike some related plants, it does not require acid soil and is particularly suitable as groundcover.
A tree hybrid growing in the Mediterranean region.
A small genus of flowering plants generally found in the Andes of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia and northwestern Argentina. A cultivated form of Trihesperus latifolius has striped foliage.

A dwarf, perennial bulb native to the mountains of northern Portugal and Spain. It bears small, solitary yellow flowers and needs a cold period to flower. Threatened in the wild, it can nevertheless be cultivated as a cold-hardy garden plant.

A columnar cactus regarded as native to Bolivia and Peru, although widespread cultivation makes its true origins difficult to determine. Its erect stems usually have six to eight ribs, variable needle-like spines, and pale yellow or yellow-green flowers near their tops. Archaeological finds and pre-Columbian objects document human and ritual use over millennia.

A floating freshwater plant originating in tropical and subtropical Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and South America. Juveniles form flat rosettes with spongy tissue beneath the leaves, while mature plants lift their leaves above the water. It spreads by seeds and broken runner segments and is invasive in Chile.

An herbaceous perennial hybrid documented in the wild in Japan and considered by some to be native there. It spreads by seeds and underground stems, and hairs along the underside leaf vein help distinguish it from both parents. It has a worldwide distribution and is considered invasive in some areas.

A tribe of flowering perennials found mainly in woodland or alpine habitats across temperate North America, Central America and Asia, with one species in South America. They grow from bulbs or underground stems and often have off-white flowers with six petal-like parts. Members produce alkaloids toxic to humans and animals.
stories.edibilityNote: Members produce alkaloids toxic to humans and animals; some are seriously toxic.

stories.summary: A short-stemmed rosette plant native to eastern Africa, from Ethiopia to Malawi. Its thick, spine-tipped leaves are elliptical in cross-section, and it is highly drought tolerant, often growing on dry or rocky ground.

A hybrid flowering plant produced by crossing the common and Spanish bluebells. It spans a broad range of forms between its parents and is widespread along woodland edges and roadsides in Britain and Belgium, particularly in urban areas.

An edible climbing gourd first cultivated in Mesoamerica between southern Mexico and Honduras. Its common fruit is wrinkled and roughly pear-shaped, with mild, watery flesh and one large flattened seed; the roots, stems, seeds and leaves are also edible.
stories.edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten raw or cooked; roots, stems, seeds and leaves are also edible, with tubers cooked like root vegetables and shoots used in salads or stir-fries.

stories.summary: A garden-raised hybrid shrub first recorded in Northern Ireland by 1951, produced from Berberis oiwakensis and Berberis japonica. Its variable forms are valued for ornamental leaves and winter-long flowering, and many have a striking upright shape.
A branching cactus native to Bolivia. Its light green to bluish stems usually have four to eight ribs, while its fragrant white funnel-shaped flowers open at night.
A columnar cactus native to northwestern Argentina and Bolivia. It has lime-green cylindrical stems with golden spines that fade toward white, and large white flowers that open at night.
A genus of ferns native to the Old World.

A small cactus tribe found mainly in eastern South America, with its greatest diversity in Bolivia, though some members occur farther north and one reaches the Old World. These cacti grow on trees or rocks, taking hanging, creeping or upright forms, and produce fleshy, berry-like fruits.

A shrub or small tree native to southern China and Vietnam. It is endangered in the wild and remembered for waxy yellow flowers, an unusual colour among camellias; the plant has also traditionally been used there to make tea.
stories.edibilityNote: In southern China and Vietnam, the plant has been used to make tea.

stories.summary: A genus of perennial flowering plants native to temperate and subtropical regions worldwide except Australia, New Zealand and Antarctica. They have leaves arising from the base, and most species bear flowers without petals, with coloured sepals providing the display.

Flowering-plant genus native to Asia, ranging through the Himalayas and much of East and Southeast Asia to Sumatra. Cultivated members, called fall-blooming anemones, usually bear white or pink blossoms alongside globe-shaped seed heads from late July to October.
Shrubby flowering-plant genus found in dry parts of the Old World, across regions from southern Africa and the Mediterranean to Central and eastern Asia.
Liverwort genus with a cosmopolitan distribution.
Shrub and subshrub tribe strictly endemic to Australia. Most members are non-aromatic, except the genus Prostanthera, and any hairs are never woolly.

Evergreen flowering climber, a hybrid of Passiflora racemosa and P. caerulea that may have first been made by British nurseryman Thomas Milne in 1819. It has five-lobed leaves, spiral clinging tendrils, and large purple flowers with maroon and white filaments.

Perennial herbaceous hybrid developed at the Royal Horticultural Society's gardens in 1848 from E. japonica and E. vitifolia. It forms large clumps of dark green leaves and bears loose sprays of white, pink, or rose flowers with silky-backed sepals and prominent golden stamens.
Flowering-plant genus native from Assam across temperate eastern Asia and western and central Malesia, and also to the central and eastern United States.

Hybrid fern first found in Mallorca's Sóller Valley and now recorded around the western Mediterranean. Its leathery, plastic-like fronds have a thick, glossy dark-garnet central stem; during dry summer months they dehydrate and appear dead, then quickly green after autumn rain.
Artificial flowering-plant hybrid grown as a shrub or small tree, derived from Hibiscus schizopetalus and the hybrid H. × rosa-sinensis. It apparently has several cultivars.
A green-algal genus with no supplied native range. Its species often form dense green cushions on stones, shells or aquatic plants, and have both attached and upright filaments with blunt tips.
A genus of flowering plants in the arum family, native to tropical northern South America.
A perennial arum native to southern Brazil and Paraguay. It forms dense clumps with glossy, deeply divided green leaves and flowers enclosed by dark red sheaths.

A perennial hybrid aquatic pondweed widespread globally in rivers and lakes, except where water is very soft. Its broad, translucent submerged leaves may be joined by opaque floating leaves, and identification requires a combination of features rather than any single trait.
A small deciduous flowering-tree hybrid originating in Japan but unknown in the wild. Its parents are Prunus itosakura and Prunus incisa.
